Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:42:50 GMT

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

Decline of deities - the long game the All Blacks cannot afford to lose

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:42:05 GMT

Codie Taylor led the New Zealand haka against England before the 37-12 defeat last Saturday

For decades, the All Blacks have defied gravity.

Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.

Deservedly so. No other team comes close to them.

England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.

But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.

New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.

For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.

A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries,, external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.

But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.

If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams.

But it would be a sixth defeat in a calendar year, a total matched only once before in the All Blacks past, back in 1949 when a split squad played two Test series in Australia and apartheid South Africa at the same time.

New Zealand's win percentage in 2026 is 58.3%, their third lowest for any year since the start of professionalism.

This campaign, marked by an exhausting schedule and four Tests away to the world champion Springboks, is in keeping with a recent trend.

Since the end of the 2010s - a period in which an all-time great team captured back-to-back world titles - New Zealand have come off the boil.

The 2020s are on course to be their least successful decade since the 1970s.

This current crop of All Blacks are suffering not just by comparison to the previous generation, but when set against every other modern predecessor.

One reason may be a source of strength turning against them.

The All Blacks' culture of promoting within and establishing coaching dynasties was seen as key when they were winning.

A thread ran through the Graham Henry, Steve Hansen and Ian Foster succession in the 2010s glory days. The latter two served under their predecessor and the first two earned their Test stripes with Wales, before taking the top job.

All were schooled as coaches in New Zealand and steeped in the country's rugby traditions.

The in-house production line of leaders ensured continuity and protected a team ethos that has been admired and written about everywhere.

But, in a modern world in which opposition tactics are quickly picked apart and best practice spreads fast, has adherence to tradition held back the team?

New Zealand's rivals have all hired coaching talent from outside.

Rassie Erasmus, South African to the core, may front the Springbok coaching operation, but behind him Irishmen Jerry Flannery and Felix Jones and Tony Brown, a former All Black himself, bring specialist knowledge to different areas.

France, famously patriotic in their hiring, benefited from Englishman Shaun Edwards and South African Vlok Cilliers' work behind the scenes in recent years.

England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have or have had head coaches from other countries.

Dave Rennie, who has coached Australia, Glasgow Warriors and Japanese side Kobe Steelers previously, became the first person of Pasifika heritage to lead the All Blacks when he took on the job in March.

He has brought a Scottish contingent to mix up his backroom, with attack coach Mike Blair the most high-profile.

But his regime is still only eight months old. Other issues predate it.

England v New Zealand

Nations Championship

Saturday 28 November, 16:40 GMT

Allianz Stadium, Twickenham

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app

Most pressing is the balance sheet.

New Zealand Rugby is leaking millions. A failure to balance the books means it has built-in annual losses of about NZ$20m (£8.35m), and is projected to lose NZ$66m (£27.6m) between 2027 and 2031., external

The All Black brand is valuable. It has been licensed to sell watches, healthcare and information technology.

The team are still a powerful global draw.

They are among the keenest Test nations to play matches overseas, where they can fill stadiums bigger than Auckland's 50,000-capacity Eden Park and make more money.

A globe-trotting 2026 itinerary has filled coffers, but emptied players.

Still though costs are rising faster than their income.

In turn, that is compromising the All Blacks' ability to keep their centrally contracted stars at home.

As in England, playing for a domestic team is a requirement to play internationally.

Thirty-five-year-old playmaker Beauden Barrett's proposed move to Bristol Bears and out of eligibility at the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup attracted headlines, but New Zealand are more concerned by other departures.

Back-row star Wallace Sititi, 24, is rumoured to have agreed a move to Stade Francais, while Luke Jacobson, 29, has already announced his own switch to fellow French side Bayonne.

"What bothers us is when All Blacks or highly prospective All Blacks leave in their sort of mid-20s," said New Zealand Rugby chairman and World Cup-winning captain David Kirk this week., external

"When they want to go away for two or three years or something like that in their mid-20s, possibly come back, but possibly not come back. That's a problem for us.

"We're not ever going to win on the money. We just don't have the money to compete with Japan and France, who are the two big payers.

"So we have to compete on the desire to play for the All Blacks and to have a career that's memorable representing New Zealand. And most of the time that's absolutely fine.

"That's why the few people leaving become a bit of a cause célèbre - because not many do."

Richie Mo'unga is one of them.

He was New Zealand's first-choice fly-half at the last World Cup and arguably the best in the position in the world.

He spent three years in Japanese club rugby and international exile afterwards, and has yet to fully find his feet on his return.

Richie Mo'unga made his first start for the All Blacks in three years in the team's 35-28 defeat by Wales a fortnight ago

No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series

New Zealand have the talent to cope. Ruben Love is a coming force at 10. Many of their stars will time stints overseas around World Cups. But it robs them of options and makes cohesion and succession trickier.

Sabbaticals – approved overseas stints which allow players to take up short, lucrative stints at overseas clubs and remain available for the All Blacks – have been a compromise.

Ardie Savea, talismanic All Blacks captain, has been playing in Japan on one this season.

But, overseas clubs hungry for Kiwi talent on a longer-term basis are circling.

There is another angle to the issue that cuts against the All Blacks.

Those who do stay and remain eligible are competing in a weakened Super Rugby tournament.

South African sides left in 2020, throwing their lot in with the United Rugby Championship and the European club scene.

With only Australian sides and the Fijian Drua to compete against, Kiwi provincial sides' fixture lists are a significant step down from international rugby.

It is far from ideal preparation for the Test arena.

Then add in the cross-code lure.

New Zealand Warriors, the Auckland-based NRL side, offer a convenient and potentially lucrative route into the 13-man game for young rugby talent.

After taking a hit during Covid, grassroots rugby league numbers have ticked upwards., external Rugby union's equivalent numbers have been propped up by a rise in women's participation.

For the all-conquering All Blacks, suddenly the problems are stacking up.

Win or lose against England, they and New Zealand Rugby know they are playing a longer game. One they cannot afford to lose.

Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:02:25 GMT

For better or worse, everyone recalls their first date. But how will the last one be remembered?

After more than a decade of serving up her awkward, off-the-wall questions, Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date is no longer looking for love, with the YouTuber calling time on her hit series.

From a youth club project to a full-blown media empire with A-listers asking her out, the series has influenced the interview landscape and carved a new path for the next generation of content creators.

"To start my next chapter, I have to close this one," Dimoldenberg told the BBC earlier this month.

"I'm focussing on making sure I say goodbye in the perfect way so I feel ready to do my next thing."

This article contains spoilers for the final episode of Chicken Shop Date.

After much speculation as to who would be the final date, fans were never going to be able to agree as to whether the farewell was indeed perfect.

Names like Harry Styles and Beyoncé had been floated around, but it was Drake who was the favourite with some bookies after Dimoldenberg previously described the Canadian rapper as her dream date.

So when the camera panned to psychotherapist Esther Perel, "everyone was a bit surprised", says fan Sarah Almond, who watched an early cinema screening on Tuesday.

"I wasn't familiar with Esther Perel myself and I don't think anyone else in the cinema was aware of who she was," the content creator tells BBC Newsbeat.

And when the episode went live on YouTube, while most viewers reacted positively to the choice of guest, some said they did not recognise her and asked "where's Drake?!".

"I did hear a few people say they were disappointed, but I wasn't disappointed at all," Almond says.

"Even though I was expecting a bigger name to go off with a big bang, it was exactly what the show needed."

The episode played out like a counselling session, becoming emotional at points, Almond says.

"She's treating the end of Chicken Shop Date like it's a relationship break-up.

"It served her really well. It was a nice goodbye."

Signing off with an interview with a relationships expert is a sign of the journey Dimoldenberg has been on with her pioneering series.

With more than three million YouTube subscribers, Chicken Shop Date has climbed the pecking order to become a key stop on press tours for even some of the world's biggest names, including the likes of Cher and Sir Paul McCartney.

But it wasn't always that way.

Rachel Adeolu watched the series from the very beginning, when Dimoldenberg would mostly date emerging rap and grime artists.

"A chicken shop is somewhere that's very familiar to a lot of people who grew up in London," the 21-year-old says. "It's kind of like a third space where a lot of us built friendships.

"So seeing content creators who also looked like us being interviewed in that same kind of setting with this unconventional interview style, which was also very funny, was unheard of."

By 2021, seven years on from the first episode, the show was starting to look different.

As well as rappers and content creators, Dimoldenberg was bagging interviews with pop stars like Ed Sheeran and Finneas, as well as footballers Tammy Abraham and John Stones.

It was about that time producer Liv West joined the team, and her background at a major music publisher helped the series secure an impressive roster of guests.

"That summer we had a really big line-up," she says, with the likes of Keke Palmer, Charli XCX and Rosalía looking for love at first bite.

"It was then we started to think the tides are changing," she adds.

As the profiles of the dates grew though, so did their teams, with West saying it became a challenge to squeeze everyone in for shoots - with some being put into the kitchen.

The producer feels things ramped up after the episode with documentary maker Louis Theroux, as he was not a typical guest and of "legendary status".

For earlier fans like Adeolu, the take-off came at a cost.

"It feels like the audience who are more interested in seeing A-list celebrities be interviewed, they have definitely been favoured over the people who made the show popular in the first place," she says.

"In terms of just the initial charm of what the show was, I think that has probably had a negative impact on it."

As Dimoldenberg reached new audiences, her success started to balloon and before long she was appearing on major red carpets, in films and magazines - as well as a guest on other people's talk shows.

It also allowed her to work on a passion project: Dimz Inc Academy.

Launched in 2025, the scheme aims to upskill and mentor young people from underrepresented backgrounds who want to get into creative industries.

"It was Amelia's big dream to really make the creative industry, and particularly digital entertainment, accessible from every walk of life for every young person," West says.

Now in its second year, the scheme will be a legacy for the series away from screens - but as for what's next for the series' star, that's yet to be revealed.

"I really want to spend more time writing, that's what I'd like to focus on in the future," Dimoldenberg told the BBC.

"But who knows, the possibilities are endless."

Additional reporting by Naomi Clarke, Miya Chahal and Srosh Khan.

Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:00:40 GMT

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

'Cowardly monster' blackmailed girls to self-harm

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:47:14 GMT

This aticle contains distressing details

A "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others has been detained for 14 and a half years.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was 17 when he began forcing vulnerable girls to send sexual images, hurt animals and carve his assumed name into their bodies, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

One of the girls' mothers said he used the internet to breach the safety of his victims' homes and minds, causing lifelong devastation.

Mensforth, 20 and from Sunderland, admitted 17 offences. They included crimes against nine victims, the youngest of whom was aged 12, and having indecent images of children as young as five.

Mensforth was in online groups who made content for their "com", short for community, by victimising "vulnerable young girls", prosecutor Charlotte Hole said.

They often targeted girls in self-harm support groups and used apps including Telegram and Discord to befriend them.

Abusers convinced the girls they were in romantic relationships and coaxed them into sending indecent images of themselves, then threatened to publish the pictures unless they committed more "extreme" acts, the court heard.

The girls would be forced to carve the names of their abusers into their flesh and write messages and logos in blood promoting the "com" groups.

They were also ordered to "sacrifice" animals under the threat their personal information would be released online or false reports would be made to trigger armed police raids of their homes.

Under the username Yuri, Mensforth targeted girls in the UK, USA and Australia, making them write "I worship Yuri" in blood among a litany of other abuses.

When one of his victims asked him why he was doing it, Mensforth replied "for content", the court heard, with the abuser seeking to rise to the top of the group's hierarchy.

Even after being arrested in October 2023, Mensforth used other hidden phones to message girls and post in his group.

He boasted and shared bloody images of his victims, and complained when other users were ranked higher than him.

Mensforth met one victim in real life, later sharing pictures he took without her knowledge and bragging to his friends about raping the 16-year-old.

He later told police his role was to "recruit leaders who would be taught how to extort girls".

A victim from the USA said she was 16 when she was "lured" into Mensforth's "online child predator group".

Having been forced to harm herself, the pictures of her "mutilated" body then got thousands of views online, she said.

She said she begged her abusers to take the images down but they refused, adding: "The more I cried about it the more amusement it seemed to bring them."

Her mother said she had no idea there were "cowardly monsters" like Mensforth "hiding behind a screen tormenting our baby girl".

A UK-based victim, who was 13 when Mensforth began abusing her, reported himto police.

"Instead of looking back at my early teen years and being filled with joy, I'm reminded of the fear and violation I felt," she said.

Her body was "covered" with scars inflicted at Mensforth's behest, she said, describing him as a "psychopath" who "feeds off the pain" of others.

Other victims said they had ongoing mental health issues and their trauma was worse because the images were still online.

Mensforth admitted blackmail, sexual communications with children, making and distributing indecent images of children and participating in an organised crime group between 2023 and 2024.

Judge Edward Bindloss said Mensforth was a "calculating predator" who groomed, manipulated and blackmailed girls for those who shared his "taste for sexual violence and enjoyed watching females self-harm".

Mensforth "rose to play a leading role" in the harm group and "thrived" on his status, the judge said.

Bindloss said Mensforth, who told probation workers he hoped to push a girl into killing herself, would have to serve six years on extended licence.

GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:39:11 GMT

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.

But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.

Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.

Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.

Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.

Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.

It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.

Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.

While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.

"It never got eyes like it's getting right now," she said.

"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.

The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.

Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.

But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.

He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".

Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.

Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".

"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.

"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."

Only One by New York band Fcukers appears on the official GTA 6 soundtrack and has already had more than one million streams on Spotify.

The group's singer Shanny Wise tells Newsbeat: "It was actually one of the songs we recorded when we were making our album, but it didn't end up making the album."

"We felt like the vibe of it maybe was too much of an outlier," adds bassist Jackson Walker Lewis.

"But when the GTA thing came around... I felt like it perfectly fit."

Lewis says the band didn't know they'd made the official soundtrack album until the tracklist leaked in the days leading up to the game's release.

"The one thing I'll say is, Rockstar operates very fluidly behind the scenes," says Lewis.

"They can change their mind last-minute. I think that's what makes them so good at what they do is because they have flexibility."

The electronic duo agree it was "beyond an honour" to appear alongside huge names such as pop star Dua Lipa and rapper Travis Scott.

"I mean, it's crazy and really... it blows me away," says Wise.

But, Lewis says, it's not the only thing making their big moment special.

"I think it's been a really long time since kind of globally we've had a monoculture moment that we can all share in, you know, in a positive way, in a joyful way," he says.

"Everyone across the globe is, for the most part, enjoying this game, and I just think it's a special thing to be a part of."

Steven Ellison, better known as Flying Lotus, points out the GTA series was already an established cultural phenomenon.

Millions of players heard the US producer, DJ, film-maker and rapper hosting FlyLo, one of GTA 5's in-game radio stations.

He also curated its tracklist - a job he confesses was made easier by the series' profile.

"People just wanted to have any involvement at all," he says.

"It was like: 'Who do we want? Who don't we want?' It was incredible."

He says the role gave him an opportunity to "shine a light on musicians from LA", his hometown, and the inspiration for the game's fictional location Los Santos.

It also influenced his own musical taste, he says.

"I remember when I played GTA: Vice City and it was the first time I actually listened to Africa by Toto.

"I was like: 'Man this song is awesome'. I didn't really know it before."

That curated experience, according to Ellison, is a big part of the appeal, and why the game can generate surprise hits out of neglected songs.

"It's so hard to get an experience like that nowadays with the way we listen to music and find music," he says.

"So this is kind of like that experience from back in the day where you're actually being put on to something by hanging out with people and then someone plays a track.

"It's that genuine connection that I think is possible with this."

Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Jordan Kenny and Naomi Clarke.

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:03:03 GMT

Police have confirmed that a body found in woodland in southern Scotland has been identified as missing 20-year-old Kelsey Hunter.

She had last been seen in Castle Douglas at 17:00 on Saturday and a major search was carried out around the nearby village of Springholm where she lived.

On Tuesday, Daniel McKnight, 21, appeared on petition at Dumfries Sheriff Court charged with murder and two other charges, including defeating the ends of justice. Kelsey's body was found at about 19:15 on Wednesday.

McKnight made no plea and was remanded in custody.

The search operation around the Dumfries and Galloway village concluded when the body was found but police said extensive inquiries remained ongoing with a number of resources being used - including forensic specialists.

Det Ch Insp Stephen McGrath said: "Our thoughts remain with Kelsey's family at this incredibly difficult time, and we are continuing to provide them with support.

"They have asked that their privacy is respected.

"Extensive work remains ongoing and a team of officers are continuing to carry out inquiries."

He thanked everyone who had come forward with information so far and said officers would remain in the area while the investigation continued.

Door-to-door and CCTV inquiries are still being carried out.

Local area commander Emma Dodds said: "We understand how upsetting this has been for the local community, but we continue to have a significant amount of resources dedicated to this investigation.

Dogs, a helicopter and specialist officers were involved in the search while officers made door-to-door inquiries.

Dumfries and Galloway Council has been offering support to the village primary which is close to where a police cordon was in place.

It said a message had been sent to the community to reassure them that the school continued to be a "safe and nurturing space".

The local authority's principal education psychologist has also been working with the primary and Castle Douglas High School to "provide support to learners and staff".

Why snooker could be the most mentally challenging sport

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:00:10 GMT

This video can not be played

The unique psychological challenges of elite level snooker

It is perhaps one of the most visceral and deeply human interviews that any sportsperson has ever given.

When Mark Allen, snooker's world number 11, spoke live on TNT Sports, external in October, he said he was in a "bad place", that he didn't see a future in the game, and that he was "just trying to survive".

Allen had just been beaten at the Northern Ireland Open. It was his first match since the World Championship, when in May he was one black ball away from a place in the final.

He has not spoken publicly since. In a post on social media in early November, Allen said the future is "looking brighter",, external although this week he explained he was having a "very tough" time, external and was "definitely stuck in a major low right now".

While Allen has not publicly discussed the reasons for his struggles, and if it is related to the sport, he had previously said "there is more to life than just a career".

And this would be far from the first time that poor mental health has affected a snooker player.

Right from the 1970s and the sport's first television boom, some of its great characters have spoken openly, and regularly, about addiction, isolation and snooker's unique psychological challenges.

So what is it about the sport that makes it so mentally difficult? And what is being done to help?

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this story you can visit BBC Action Line, which has details of a range of advice and support.

In his emotional interview, Allen said he had spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic and discharged himself to play in Belfast, though he planned to continue his treatment.

Other players have also previously spoken candidly about their own struggles, including multiple world champions Ronnie O'Sullivan and Mark Selby.

Selby considered retirement after a first-round defeat at the 2024 World Championship, while in 2025 O'Sullivan said many players "suffer in silence".

Snooker is, perhaps alongside golf, one of the most intensely individual sports, where players spend long hours alone in dimly lit practice rooms or travelling on the road, and where entire livelihoods can come down to tiny misjudgements.

"At least in golf you have your own ball. You don't have to worry about anyone else," 1997 world champion Ken Doherty told BBC Sport.

"In snooker, when you're sitting in your chair and your opponent is at the table, you can do nothing. Only sit and bear it.

"That is the toughest part about our sport and mentally that is quite difficult for people to comprehend."

Dr Paul Gaffney is a psychologist who has worked with Allen for the past four seasons. Snooker players, he says, can feel like they are inside a "colosseum".

"There are people looking down at you, and you can absolutely thrive, or be beaten in front of the world stage."

Allen considers retirement after NI Open exit

Selby faces tough UK opener, with Allen set to feature

Gary Wilson, the world number 28, has also spoken openly about the bouts of depression he has suffered during his 22-year career.

"It's a very lonely sport," the 41-year-old told BBC Sport.

"You're practising in a club and you could be in there on your own for six, seven, eight hours a day in a dark room, with just a snooker light on.

"It can get unhealthy mentally in itself, but it's what you've got to do. You've got to dedicate yourself to it.

"I think it is a more mentally destructive sport, potentially, than a lot of other individual sports."

When asked how he felt watching Allen's interview, Wilson said: "We can all relate.

"There are a lot of lads who are a lot lower down on the tour struggling.

"Every couple of years, this coming out and nothing being done about it, isn't really good enough."

This video can not be played

Emotional Allen tells the BBC he is contemplating retirement following NI Open exit

Since 2021, snooker's governing body, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA), has put mental health provisions in place for players in the form of a partnership with Sporting Chance, a charity founded by former Arsenal and England footballer Tony Adams.

In the five years since the partnership was formed, Sporting Chance has provided more than 180 sessions of counselling for a wide range of issues.

Players experiencing mental health issues are encouraged to ring a confidential 24/7 helpline, and Sporting Chance will then arrange free treatment with a qualified therapist. This can take place over six to 12 talking sessions.

But some players believe that support could go further. In an interview in January 2025, O'Sullivan and Selby said they would like to see mental health professionals operate on-site at tournaments.

"I think players would have a lot more inclination to use somebody physically there at tournaments. I don't know how feasible that is," said Wilson.

There are benefits and drawbacks to the Sporting Chance service. Players receive a bespoke counsellor, rather than one who may speak to every player, but they are required to reach out themselves for this through a helpline. Doherty, who sits on the WPBSA players' board, believes it is the best solution.

"Players don't necessarily want to go and speak to someone at a tournament," Doherty said.

"We thought about having someone on hand, but then we thought, we don't think anyone would use it.

"This is a free service. Nobody has to know. Nobody will know on the circuit. It's just you and the person you're talking to.

"I know Ronnie [O'Sullivan] and Mark [Selby] spoke about that, but they obviously didn't know that service was there for them, that it's free, and that it's available for the whole tour."

WPBSA chairman Jason Ferguson, a former professional player himself, said: "The highs are very high and the lows are very low.

"If there's anything we can work on, it's continually getting the message out to other players to say those services are there."

This video can not be played

How Tony Adams' charity is helping snooker players - but could more be done?

In 2021, Wilson said he felt "totally gone" when the depression he explained he was suffering with came to a head in a match against John Higgins.

Wilson missed a pot, and while still down on his shot, thrashed the cue ball into a neighbouring red,, external sending the frame into chaos. He was fined £250 and received a formal warning.

But Wilson - known as the Tyneside Terror - believes there could be a more liberal approach to such displays of emotion in this most gentlemanly of sports.

"You're expected to keep your emotions completely in check at all times," he said.

"Now that's just not sport. When you look at any other sport that you play… you've got to be able to vent."

In response, Ferguson said that while snooker's authorities and fans love to see such passion, fundamentally it is a sport of "great etiquette".

Allen is next due to play in the UK Championship - a tournament he won in 2022 - which starts on Saturday. He has been drawn against qualifier Yuan Sijun but has not spoken publicly about whether he will play.

For Dr Gaffney, watching Allen's interview at Belfast's Waterfront venue was "painful". It made him feel "sadness, but also admiration".

"The brilliant thing about what he's done - his courage, his integrity, his class in the last few weeks - is there will be people watching snooker who wouldn't have been watching snooker before, because Mark Allen is playing," said Dr Gaffney, "and I think that says everything about the man."

Tory candidates must sign pledge to scrap net-zero targets, says Badenoch

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:42:22 GMT

All Conservative candidates will have to sign a pledge committing themselves to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and scrapping net-zero emission targets ahead of the next election, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said.

Unveiling her "candidates covenant" at an event in the East Midlands, Badenoch said both policies were "necessary for a stronger economy and a stronger country".

The move could see some senior Conservatives blocked from standing for the party at the next general election.

Lord Barwell, a former Conservative minister and No 10 chief of staff, said: "After a summer in which the impacts of climate change were clearer than ever, this is bad policy."

He added: "Given the seats Conservative strategists say they are targeting, it is also bad politics."

Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative MP and defence minister, told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5Live he had applied to stand as a candidate in the next election but had not passed what he described as "the purity test".

He criticised Badenoch's covenant, saying: "Can you imagine if... prior to the war, you had to sign up to [Neville] Chamberlain's 'peace in our time' speech, you know, [Winston] Churchill wouldn't have been allowed to stand."

"I mean, there must be times where you can have different views and different views within a party are actually helpful," he added.

Addressing party activists in Newark, Badenoch said: "The government that cleans up Andy Burnham's mess is going to have to make some very difficult decisions... it is not going to be for the faint-hearted.

"I need everyone who stands as a Conservative candidate at the next election to know what they are standing for - I don't want to hear complaining from MPs that they didn't know what we were going to do."

The covenant also states that candidates must support staying out of the EU, reducing the size of the state and changing the welfare system.

Sir Mark Spencer, a chief whip in the last Conservative government, became the first to sign the new pledge.

He lost his seat in the 2024 election, but is now standing in Newark, where he hopes to unseat the Conservative-turned-Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick.

A Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch is living in an alternate reality. She says the Tories have changed but the truth is they're the same old Tories."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Kemi Badenoch tells us the Conservative Party has changed - it's hard to believe when she's surrounded by so many Remainers and her party is selecting lots of failed ex-Tory MPs who got kicked out at the last election."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "The Conservatives pretend they care about winning back support from millions of former Conservative voters, yet Kemi Badenoch is now asking her candidates to sign the 'Farage pact'.

"They are taking people for fools."

Both the commitments to leave the ECHR and repeal net-zero targets represent a shift from previous Conservative governments.

The net-zero target was originally legislated for by the Theresa May-led Conservative government in 2019. The party's 2024 manifesto said it was proud of its record on reducing emissions and remained "committed to delivering net-zero by 2050".

In the run-up to the election, then Prime Minister, and Conservative leader, Rishi Sunak resisted demands from some in his party to commit to leaving the ECHR.

Since becoming leader, Badenoch has argued that the net-zero target - which commits the UK to reducing its net greenhouse gas emissions to almost zero by 2050 - couldn't be achieved "without a serious drop in our living standards or by bankrupting us".

Last year, she also announced that, if elected, her party would take the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty that guarantees certain human rights such as the right to privacy, protection against torture and a right to a family life.

Badenoch said the convention prevented the UK from being able to secure its borders and deport foreign criminals.

Over the past year, the Labour government, along with other European countries have agreed to negotiate a new approach to the convention with the aim of making it easier to deport people.

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:40:22 GMT

Police have said they are trying to contact more than 100 gig-goers to help their investigation after an unknown substance was released at a concert at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.

Detectives believe a "small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night".

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

No arrests have been made and the substance has not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We're working to identify those [robbery] suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents.

"All of this work is ongoing at pace.

He said there had been "similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries".

Fans reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.

Jess Kinyata, 20, from West London, who was one of 12,000 people evacuated from the arena, said before the "gas began" his 18 carat gold chain, worth about £1,500, was stolen from him during a set by the concert's opening artist, Victony.

GMP previously said there had been nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert.

Harding said officers had been "working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV".

He added: "There are over a hundred people at the gig that we are working to try and contact to potentially assist with our enquiries.

"We thank all those that have assisted us so far.

"We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically."

North West Ambulance Service said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution".

Those who suffered symptoms had been taken to the Etihad stadium.

Some fans complained the process, which involved them changing into paper white suits and putting their clothes in a plastic bag, was "invasive" and "traumatic".

Many stayed quarantined for several hours before being able to leave in the early hours of Monday.

GMP said: "People's safety, and the safety of the wider community, was at the forefront of officers' minds throughout."

The substance was released at about 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

Concertgoers have described feeling "unsafe" and seeing "distressing" scenes and people "coughing up blood".

Posting on Instagram, Toliver said: "My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured.

Co-op Live, which reopened its doors on Thursday night for a gig by American singer Phoebe Bridgers, previously said its priority remained "the safety and security of all visitors" to the venue.

'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:33:10 GMT

The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.

"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.

"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."

The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

"That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."

Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the House of Commons culture and media select committee, said the media outlets should "not just act as a platform" for Edwards to have a voice.

Any programme featuring him "needs to properly challenge his past actions" she said, along with raising "still unanswered questions" about whether Edwards will return more than £200,000 he was paid by the BBC, after he was first arrested.

The documentary and podcast will both be released on Tuesday, with some material expected to be published by the Observer on Sunday.

The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of.

"I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".

And it is the wrong time to release these programmes, coming during "a reckoning moment" for abuse in the media, he added.

"[It is] in fact giving somebody a platform that, in some way, shape or form, gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross. That is not OK."

He added he does "fundamentally believe in rehabilitation" but that "this doesn't feel like it."

In a promotional clip released by the Observer, interviewer Ceri Thomas is seen saying he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

Craig criticised that choice of words.

"An 'unbelievable terrible fix' isn't somebody sat actively downloading 41 images of child sexual abuse, of which a number of them were at grade A level of of boys aged seven to nine being sexually abused," he said.

BBC broadcaster Nicky Campbell added his voice, saying: "I'm rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?"

The Observer, which is owned by Tortoise Media, has been asked for a response to the criticism.

Meanwhile, journalist Sangita Myska posted: "The rehabilitation [of] Huw Edwards' reputation via a 'personal journey' documentary is contemptible. He's a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?"

Fellow broadcaster Richard Bacon responded: "Why is that rehabilitation? It's a documentary. There are lots of them about lots of different people. About lots of different types of people."

"From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.

McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."

Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans.

"There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure.

"AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."

He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".

McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."

On Wednesday, an Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

On Thursday night, Frostrup completed her fourth bushtucker trial, which is voted for by the public.

Many viewers defended Odudu after the encounter.

They included broadcaster and comic Judi Love who said she felt "triggered by Frostrup's comment, while Britain's Got Talent judge and Strictly Come Dancing judge Motsi Mabuse also gave their support to Odudu.

BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."

An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved.

"The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion as it sees fit".

"If there was any situation where anyone was diagnosed with that and coming into a fight then there is no way the board would let him fight, so that's definitely not the case," he added.

An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.

Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.

In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.

Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.

She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.

"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."

The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".

"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'

He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".

"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.

Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.

Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".

"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.

"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.

"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.

"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 10:10:36 GMT

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:57:37 GMT

A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it."

Suzanna McDonald, who leads the UKHSA's flu programme, said the H1N1 strain was fueling the spread.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the strain "does seem to have picked up a few more changes that we would have expected over the season".

"But the really encouraging news was that last year when we saw a drifted strain, the vaccine still worked very well," she added.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.
