Is it a cold, flu or Covid? How to tell the difference

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:43:38 GMT

There are lots of coughs and sneezes doing the rounds at the moment, so how do you know if it might be covid or flu rather than a cold?

Here's how to spot the difference and hopefully avoid the worst this winter.

NHS leaders are already warning that the UK is seeing a "horrible spike" in flu, with hospital cases higher than usual for the time of year.

Flu has hit a bit earlier than normal.

And we are seeing a 'drifted' strain, say experts, meaning one that is slightly different to what was anticipated when this year's vaccine was being made.

But vaccines still work against the virus that is constantly changing or mutating, they say. The vaccines are updated each year to ensure they continue to be a good match.

So far this season, there's a mix of two flu A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2, circulating in England, says the UKHSA.

The flu vaccine is designed to protect against all three main types of flu - influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and influenza B. Whichever ends up dominating this winter, or if they all circulate at similar levels throughout, the vaccine should offer broad protection.

Some people can get a free NHS flu vaccine. Anyone else who wants one can buy it at a pharmacy.

Flu symptoms tend to start more suddenly than a cold or Covid, and are usually more severe.

Common flu symptoms include a fever, aching muscles and chills.

Cold symptoms tend to be milder and come on more gradually than Covid or flu.

It might include a sore throat, as well as coughing and sneezing.

Research on the extent to which cold weather impacts our immune systems remains unclear.

But darker days mean we typically make a beeline for warm, cosy, indoor spaces.

And this environment is perfect for viruses.

Schools, nursery and even some workplaces can be like a petri dish with lots of viruses circulating. The Christmas season raises the risks as more people socialise indoors.

The same applies to freshers in university halls - where mixing together spreads germs, while heavy drinking and partying further weaken the immune system.

It is still possible to catch Covid. Common symptoms include a high temperature and a cough, as well as feeling exhausted.

One key Covid-specific identifier can be a loss of smell or taste.

While no one is told to isolate any more, the advice is try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people if you or your child have symptoms.

Most people do not need to take a Covid test if they have symptoms, but they are available to buy in chemists and, while not 100% accurate, they can help confirm or rule out infection.

Colds

Flu

Covid

Many of the symptoms between cold, flu and Covid, overlap.

But there are some clues that might help you identify the exact culprit.

If a cold's coming on, then it often does so gradually.

It's going to affect your nose and the back of your throat, while some will get a tickling at the back of the mouth.

Another early warning sign can be a build-up of pressure in the ear.

If the virus spreads further, it can reach your lungs and cause a pesky cough.

Mostly however, these symptoms don't stop us from carrying on as normal.

The same can't be said for flu, which typically adds aches, fevers and muscle weakness into the mix.

Flu doesn't always mean you have to go to bed, but it might make you feel that way.

Since the pandemic, Covid has complicated things further, with similar symptoms to flu.

The recommendation is to stay home and rest and recover.

However, if you have underlying conditions, experience breathlessness or find symptoms don't ease after three weeks, then you shouldn't hesitate to seek medical advice.

Our bodies naturally fight viruses and infection, but we can also give it a helping hand with the right medication.

'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped train attacker

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 07:53:24 GMT

Contains some upsetting scenes.

A student who survived the Huntingdon train attack has met for the first time with the passenger she believes saved her life during the stabbings.

Astrid told BBC News that Stephen Crean's decision to confront Anthony Williams gave her time to escape. "I owe him my life," she said.

Williams was found guilty on Thursday of attempting to murder Crean and 13 others.

The then 19-year-old and 61-year-old Crean were just strangers on a train when she ran down the carriage screaming that there was a man with a knife.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Crean ran towards Williams and was stabbed in the hands, back and neck. She was the last person to reach the buffet car and believes his actions gave her time to get in and shut the door.

Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security

BBC News Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:04:51 GMT

Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.

He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.

He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.

"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."

The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.

According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.

Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.

In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.

As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.

Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.

As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.

The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.

Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.

The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.

But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.

Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.

We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.

"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."

Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.

Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.

The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.

Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite “blind spots” also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are tracked only “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR) describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.”

Advertisement

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel).

Ultracold atoms could help unravel a major flaw in quantum theory

New Scientist November 26, 2026

Extremely cold atoms could help physicists answer a long-debated question about quantum particles and time. This may shed light on the accuracy of different interpretations of quantum physics.

When it comes to time, quantum physics fails to answer even the simplest questions. For instance, predicting how long it will take a quantum particle to travel from some point A to a nearby point B has been debated since quantum theory’s earliest days. There are several competing ideas for calculating the particle’s arrival time in standard quantum theory, as well as in its non-standard versions.

Pascal Naidon and Lucas Happ at RIKEN in Japan and Denis Boiron at Paris-Saclay University in France now argue that an experiment with ultracold atoms could add clarity.

Advertisement

“[Ours] is the first proposal whose concrete implementation has been checked by an experimentalist and has a good chance of being successfully realised in the future,” says Naidon. Boiron specialises in atomic experiments.

Ultracold clocks could reveal how quantum physics alters time

The researchers’ proposal starts with a collection of tens or hundreds of thousands of atoms that have been chilled to temperatures remarkably close to absolute zero, the ultimate coldness limit, by using lasers and electromagnetic fields. Under these conditions, atoms’ behaviour is dominated by quantum effects. In the experiment, the atoms would be corralled into the shape of a cigar, then allowed to fall onto a detector about half a metre below. They would move vertically from their initial position, point A, towards the detector, point B.

Because quantum objects behave probabilistically, neither every atom nor every run of the experiment would exhibit identical behaviour, but repeating the experiment a few hundred times would give the researchers a distribution of detection times. They could then compare this data with different predictions based on various interpretations of quantum theory.

Naidon says the experiment could test ideas such as the “pilot-wave” or “trajectory-based” quantum theory pioneered by Luis de Broglie and David Bohm. In standard quantum theory, quantum objects’ reality is fuzzy and indeterminate until they interact with a measuring device, but this proposes that their behaviour is guided by a very real pilot wave caused by some yet-undiscovered physical field. “It is possible that the trajectory-based interpretations will be ruled out from the results of the experiment,” says Naidon.

‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds

Sheldon Goldstein at Rutgers University in New Jersey says past experiments have failed to discriminate between different versions of quantum theory, but ideas like the new proposal can highlight the limitations of orthodox quantum theory. While it can get to grips with particles’ properties, such as their position, standard quantum theory doesn’t offer a recipe for calculating time, he says. “Usually some analysis of an experiment or a theoretical issue requires a sequence of steps. This issue of arrival times goes off the rails at step zero,” he says. “What is even meant by the arrival time in textbook quantum theory? It’s not clear what it is.”

This makes it difficult to compare standard quantum theory with alternatives that can produce clearer arrival-time predictions, says Siddhant Das at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich. But some ideas for solving the arrival time problem with standard theory have been formulated anyway and could be tested, and even eliminated, by the proposed experiment, he says.

Importantly, the arrival time of quantum particles is often an ingredient in other physics experiments, such as those involving beams of particles, so the stakes of understanding it transcend purely theoretical debates, says Das. “We have had enough theory papers. We can keep arguing about this till the cows come home,” he says. “I would love to see the experiment being done, and then we’ll see how much we can interpret.”

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/683f-3qxt

AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?

New Scientist November 26, 2026

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.

But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.

Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”

But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.

It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.

For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.

If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.

The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate

New Scientist November 26, 2026

Sponsored by

Only five years ago, defence technology start-ups had little choice but to wait for government funding to build and test their inventions – often in complex, multi-year programmes. No longer, however: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has prompted such a fast, furious response that military innovation timescales have shrunk dramatically.

“Ukraine is becoming a real-world lab for military innovation, and it’s innovating at a pace greater than anything that we’ve seen previously,” says Ola Fashade, an air vice-marshal in the Royal Air Force and director of military digitalisation and the rapid AI delivery task force at the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD).

“Agility and tempo of adaptation is critical. In a contested battlespace, technology that works well on day one, by day eight has become a little muted – and by day twelve it’s probably no longer relevant. And if you don’t adapt over that period, what you have is a very expensive and ineffective bag of steel.”

That raises the question of how significant this accelerated innovation could become. In September 2026, New Scientist CoLab, sponsored by BAE Systems, brought together leading thinkers and investors from industry, the military and academia to discuss the factors driving this innovation and the lessons that can be transferred to other industries.

The investment for this step change is coming both from the technology incubators based within military prime contractors – like the Launchpad incubator at BAE Systems – and from a host of venture capital (VC) companies worldwide. “The idea behind Launchpad is to forge an ecosystem that gets technology from defence start-ups into the front line quicker, or into spinouts, before they run out of money and die,” says David Ewing, head of technology commercialisation at BAE Systems. In addition, VC funding is seeing a raft of new multibillion-dollar military tech players, dubbed neoprimes, that complement the work of the primes on bigger-ticket battlespace items.

The poster child for the neoprimes, says Samuel Burrell, a partner at the pan-European VC firm Expeditions Fund, is the nascent British air defence start-up Cambridge Aerospace, which reached a valuation of $3.4 billion with little but a convincing tech narrative: “They had no battlefield data, no product – just a compelling team and an idea on paper.” It wasn’t all talk: Cambridge Aerospace has begun delivering its Skyhammer air defence missile for taking out Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles. A solid-rocket-motor-powered ballistic missile interceptor, Starhammer, will ship in 2027.

In the maritime battlespace, meanwhile, fast-scaling neoprime Kraken Technology Group of Hampshire, UK, has raised $175 million from various VC firms, valuing it at $1 billion, to further develop its uncrewed surface vessel and drone technologies for users including the MoD, NATO and the US Special Operations Command. Key to it all succeeding, according to Amelia Gould, chief technology officer at Kraken, is a culture that actively nurtures iterative speed – to ensure battlefield systems stay ahead of emerging countermeasures: “Having really quick feedback loops from the warfightersin the field to r for high-consequence innovation,” Gould says.

The shortening of feedback and iteration cycles, however, means tacticians must increasingly accept imperfect battlefield technologies. “We need to be much more open to minimum viable products, with relatively few safeguards, because, in conflict, staying alive is what matters,” says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, CEO at Ploughshare, an MoD-owned specialist in turning technology into real-world applications, companies and growth. Ewing agrees: “We’ll definitely see a move away from having so many exquisite platforms, in programmes that take years to define, decades to deliver and decades to wind up, in favour of quicker cycles of technology validation, implementation and adoption.”

What kind of spinoffs could emerge from this new way of refining technology? Westwood hopes some powerful answers on clean energy (see box) may emerge. “If we get ourselves really motivated around the fact that we’re boiling the Earth, that could be a real technology driver here,” he says.

What makes Westwood so confident of a positive dividend outside the military? An example from history, he says: “We went into world war two with propeller-driven biplanes and came out six years later with jet fighter aircraft. And the subsequent innovation around the jet engine seeded the commercial air transport market that’s been such a huge influence on the way we all live now.”

Ukraine’s move has militaries around the world racing to emulate its iterative techniques, which are based on the low-cost technologies behind smartphones and consumer drones: artificial intelligence, mobile connectivity, satellite positioning, cloud storage, digital design systems and 3D printing. “It’s the ability to develop, deploy and iterate these technologies at scale that have been the driver for the drone technology that we see Ukraine using,” says Mark Westwood, director of defence and security at Cranfield University in the UK.

Read more about BAE Systems Launchpad at: baesystems. com/launchpad

One of the leading spinoffs from BAE Systems’ Launchpad incubator is start-up Nuclear Turbines of Manchester, UK, which has raised £15 million from four venture funds to begin developing a novel, passively safe 20-megawatt small modular nuclear reactor.

The reactor is designed to power data centres and industrial plant. Its novelty is a straightforward one, says CEO Jeremy Owston: instead of driving a vast steam turbine, like a regular reactor, its reactor heats and compresses air to much hotter temperatures to drive a small, commercial gas turbine – greatly simplifying and shrinking the overall power plant.

“We’re not building Hinkley Point. We’re targeting the early 2030s to get our reactor up and running and we don’t need tens of billions of pounds to do that. What we’re talking about will need a fraction of the price,” Owston says, adding that he is impressed by the willingness of the VC sector to back such ideas.

There are plenty more opportunities worth investing in, says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton at the MoD’s intellectual property spinoff unit, Ploughshare. “Of the billions spent every year in the UK on defence innovation, only a fraction results in IP being spun out. The track record of that innovation reaching civilian markets is weak.”

VCs are beginning to notice this opportunity. “There are so many of these funds and they just want to take a bet on something, and that’s great,” says Owston.

Vagus nerve stimulation slows growth and spread of pancreatic cancer

New Scientist November 27, 2026

An electrical implant that stimulates the vagus nerve slowed the growth and spread of pancreatic tumours in mice. The approach seems to work by helping cancer-killing immune cells infiltrate tumours, enabling a treatment that doesn’t normally work for pancreatic cancer to become effective.

“It’s very exciting,” says Timothy Wang at Columbia University in New York, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It’s the first study I know where electrical manipulation has been used to treat tumours outside the brain.”

‘Transformative’ pancreatic cancer drug doubles survival time

The intervention made the tumours susceptible to immunotherapy, which helps immune cells destroy cancer but usually fails against pancreatic tumours. “That could be very significant for patients,” says Wang. “Getting immunotherapy to work is the holy grail right now for pancreatic cancer. It’s thought to be key to long-term survival.”

Advertisement

One way to potentially make immunotherapy work is through electrical stimulation. This is already used to treat some kinds of brain cancer, such as glioblastoma. Now, Lu Gan at the Huazhong University of Science and Technology in China and their colleagues have tested it for pancreatic cancer. More than 500,000 people are diagnosed with pancreatic cancer a year, of whom only 13 per cent survive 5 years, making it one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

Prior research by Wang and his colleagues has also shown that blocking electrical signals in the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to other organs, increases the growth of pancreatic cancer in mice. To see whether stimulating the nerve has the reverse effect, Gan’s team developed an electrical device – roughly 1-centimetre long – that wraps around part of the oesophagus.

Free newsletter

When activated by ultrasound waves, sent from outside the body, the device sends electrical signals along a branch of the vagus nerve that runs from the oesophagus to the pancreas.

To put it to the test, the researchers implanted the device, which wasn’t yet activated, into mice. Six days later, cancerous cells were injected into their pancreas. After tumours had formed, the team activated the device for 20 minutes a day in half the mice. It remained inactive in the remaining mice, acting as a control.

About two weeks later, the tumours in the control mice weighed about 230 milligrams, on average, compared with about 190 milligrams in the mice that received electrical stimulation – an almost 20 per cent difference. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted that big an effect,” says Wang.

The pancreatic cancer cells had also spread to more than 10 other parts of the control mice’s bodies, on average – about double the degree of spread that occurred among those that received electrical stimulation.

The more tumours spread, the deadlier they tend to be, however, the researchers didn’t measure the mice’s survival outcomes. This is probably because that would involve tracking a large number of mice over a longer period, and this was just a proof-of-concept study, says Wang. The researchers did find, however, that the device had no known short-term safety issues.

In another part of the experiment, the researchers found that the electrical stimulation seemed to boost the number of cancer-killing immune cells, called T-cells and natural killer cells, in the tumours. It also reduced the abundance of other kinds of immune cells, called MDSCs, which suppress T-cells.

Exactly how this occurred is unclear, but prior studies suggest that stimulating the vagus nerve increases the release of a neurotransmitter called acetylcholine, which can bind to receptors on the surface of immune and cancer cells, altering their behaviour, says Wang.

Finally, the team explored whether the approach could make pancreatic tumours respond to an immunotherapy drug, called anti-PD1, which activates T-cells but is usually ineffective against this type of cancer. “Pancreatic cancer is notorious for having an almost zero response to immunotherapy, and most believe that’s because pancreatic cancer has a tremendously fibrous structure, which stops immune cells getting in,” says Wang. If electrical stimulation allows T-cells to infiltrate the pancreas, immunotherapy stands a better chance, he says.

A cancer-killing virus has stopped pancreatic tumours from growing and spreading in three people in an initial safety trial, raising hopes that it may help to beat the deadly condition

The researchers found that anti-PD1 alone had no substantial effect on tumour growth in mice with pancreatic tumours. But combining it with electrical stimulation slowed tumour growth and stopped cancers spreading more than electrical stimulation alone.

This suggests this combination treatment could improve survival outcomes, says Wang. “Long-term survival in pancreatic cancer really does require T-cell immunity and getting immunotherapy to work.” It may be even more effective when combined with a non-immunotherapy drug, called daraxonrasib, that roughly doubles survival time in people with pancreatic cancer, says Wang.

Further research should first test whether the findings can be replicated in other mouse models of pancreatic cancer that better mimic what happens in people, for instance, by using mice that have been genetically engineered to develop pancreatic tumours, says Wang. These studies could also assess survival outcomes, he says. If successful, trials in people could start within the next couple of years, he says.

Nature Communications DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79002-w

New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history

New Scientist November 27, 2026

Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick?

For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history.

Free newsletter

The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce.

Advertisement

If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet, money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world.

The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia, the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X, part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. In it, the recipe suggests using the “urine of a small child”, although today our understanding of the chemical reaction that creates the effect means we know water is a better alternative.

From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list

Fast-forward a thousand years, and the mass use of urine was commonplace around the world. It was still used for laundry and leatherwork, but was now also part of the burgeoning gunpowder industry. One of the key ingredients of this game-changing superweapon, the origins of which lie in Chinese herbal medicine, is saltpetre, or potassium nitrate. This was gathered from nitre beds, stinking manure heaps mixed with potash and mortar, all moistened with urine to claim the nitrates. This method, used from Europe to Japan, continued well into the 19th century; during the US Civil War, the Confederacy was using urine to keep its guns firing.

But perhaps urine’s greatest contribution came from alchemy. By the 17th century, just as the printing press and improvements in lenses and glassware had finally begun to usher in the scientific method, the old practices and beliefs that blended experiment, philosophy, religion and misunderstanding of the ancient world had their greatest triumph. In 1669, an alchemist in Hamburg, Hennig Brand, was searching for the philosopher’s stone using 1500 gallons of fermented urine he had collected in his basement. To Brand’s astonishment, the concentrated urine at the heart of his experiment began to glow. Brand kept his accomplishment secret for years, but unable to take the next step and turn metals into gold, he eventually sold the recipe to a friend and the discovery was shared with the world. Brand hadn’t performed a magic trick, but isolated phosphorus – the first chemical element to be discovered in modern times.

Today, urine still plays a critical role around the world, particularly in medicine, where it is a source of biomarkers used in diagnostic tests, and was even the original source of drugs such as human chorionic gonadotropin and follicle-stimulating hormone for fertility treatment. As Emperor Vespasian said almost 2000 years ago, money doesn’t stink – and nor do the benefits of the amber liquid we all produce every day.

Kit Chapman is the author of The Age of Alchemy, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman

New Scientist November 27, 2026

“A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder.

Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child.

Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood.

Advertisement

Decant this properly, and use.”

Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X, c. 300 CE

In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements.

For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it.

The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway.

Free newsletter

When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands.

Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X, written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. These are all real instructions, and all recipes that work (even if, today, there are cheaper ways to get the same result).

Among them is the greatest secret in alchemy. It’s called the “invention of sulfur water” and is the recipe at the start of this chapter. Sulfur and lime (calcium oxide, not the fruit) are gardening supplies that you can buy in a hardware store, and if you don’t have a small child that needs a wee to hand, strong vinegar from the supermarket will work just as well. While you shouldn’t try this at home, the result, after you heat the mix for an hour, is a red-brown goop and a kitchen that reeks of rotten eggs. These are calcium polysulfides, making up lime sulfur. It’s a nasty substance – an alkali that can cause skin irritation and even blindness if you get it in your eyes. Today, we use this for pest control, but in ancient times it was how you created gold. Well, the appearance of gold. Once you’ve got your “sulfur water”, any metal object submersed – a coin, nail or paperclip – will gain a thin, yellowy film coating.

The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t just the oldest alchemy book in history. It’s a tried-and-tested guide for tricksters. We may not know who wrote the document, but we do know that if you had walked into the author’s workshop 1,700 years ago, you’d have been swindled. Or that’s how it seems. The truth, as we’ll learn, is that something else was going on that’s even more fascinating. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list

The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t what most people think of when they picture alchemy. We think of it as a pseudoscience, a blend of religious beliefs, ancient superstition and gilded dreams, with only the occasional glimpse of something that might work underneath. If you subscribe to the traditional view, this is the best you can hope for when it comes to studying any chemistry earlier than about 1650. Before the Enlightenment, there were only wizards, witches and wishful thinking. Then suddenly, whoosh, in a flash of gunpowder, a crackle of electricity and bubbling fizz from a test tube, a new science arrived to change our world.

This book turns that idea on its head. No one person created chemistry, and even if they had, it certainly wouldn’t have been some white European in a powdered wig. Chemistry didn’t appear overnight and there is no one moment when it came into existence. It was a gradual transformation that built on millennia of knowledge. Choosing to ignore chemistry during the Age of Alchemy does a disservice to thousands of men and women, across the world, who guided us from the first campfire to the modern age.

This book is divided into three parts. In the first, we look at how early chemistry worked, from the Stone Age up to the emergence of alchemy, and how it set the basic principles for what alchemy, and later chemistry, would become. In the second, we go on a trip around the world. Practically every history of alchemy just focuses on the western traditions – mainly because they are the best studied. But we’re going to look at what was happening with chemistry in the Islamic world, China, the Indian subcontinent and even the Americas. Some of this is alchemy, and some of it isn’t, but it all plays a role in the tapestry of science. Finally, the third section returns to Europe, where we’ll look at how alchemy changed (or, to use the alchemical term, transmuted), over the course of several hundred years, into the science we know today. My journey has led to travels across six continents and taken me on adventures through deserts and jungles, tombs and tomes, and some of our most fabled cities. I have explored old roads and met the researchers busy paving new ones. The result is a story that is both a mirror to progress and a love letter to science, one that offers a glimpse into the past and shows how it all connects to our daily lives, often in surprising and roundabout ways. Chemistry is everywhere and is linked to everything. It is painfully human. It is filled with our mistakes, beliefs and hubris. It showcases our noble endeavours, destructive potential and indomitable spirit. And it allows us to appreciate how science, whether through petty rivalries, oppression and colonisation, or religious fervour, has always been political.

Particles not seen before have been observed in a quantum simulator

New Scientist November 27, 2026

After decades of being dismissed, a group of particles called paraparticles have been seen emerging inside a quantum simulator. Coming only a year after a mathematical breakthrough in our understanding of paraparticles, this experiment complicates our view of the quantum world.

Quantum particles are classified by what happens when two of them swap places and by how many can have the same quantum state simultaneously. Bosons, for example, can be swapped at no penalty, and infinitely many can share a quantum state. Fermions are their opposite; swapping them incurs a change in their quantum states, and two or more fermions can never occupy the same quantum state.

The ‘impossible’ particle hinting at the universe’s biggest secrets

In the 1950s, researchers theorised other types too, but it seemed impossible to experimentally distinguish them from fermions and bosons. But in 2025, Kaden Hazzard at Rice University in Texas and Zhiyuan Wang at the Perimeter Institute in Canada argued that this doesn’t have to be the case.

Advertisement

Their mathematical work made the case for the possibility of finding signs of paraparticles in experiments. Now, Max Hays at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and his colleagues have used a quantum simulator do exactly that.

“They’ve seen emergent paraparticles,” says Hazzard. “They have a system whose dynamics obeys exactly the same mathematical equations that a paraparticle is expected to satisfy.” He says he is surprised by how quickly the team managed to complete this work.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers used 16 qubits, which are the building blocks of quantum computers, made from tiny superconducting circuits and arranged in a grid. By using electromagnetic interactions, the team connected qubits into pairs, like rungs on a ladder. Each rung behaved like a paraparticle.

Three tests confirmed this: the researchers swapped two paraparticles, made them crash into each other and, ultimately, checked how they pile together. It all took a year and lots of careful control and calibration of the qubits, says Cora Barrett, also at MIT, who worked on the experiment.

“This work provides a proof of concept that paraparticles are not merely theoretical curiosities,” says Kristian Hauser Villegas at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

Particles seen emerging from empty space for first time

Unlike a simulation on a conventional computer, the new experiment uses the qubits’ quantum characters as building blocks of paraparticles, says Hauser Villegas. It may even be impossible to faithfully reproduce this on a conventional computer.

“In a regular computer, you are writing code and it’s very abstract; there’s no way in which these things are actually really existing in the computer,” says Hays. “In this case, you can say the particle is right at this spot physically.”

Going forward, the team wants to expand their experiment to include paraparticles that interact with each other, as well as paraparticles in more complicated geometrical configurations, says Hays.

Many open questions about paraparticles remain, and these more complex experiments will stand a chance of answering some of them, says Wang. “This is the just the beginning of an exciting journey,” he says.

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2611.03908

Waikanae Beach murder: Keri McIlroy jailed for the murder of his father, James McIlroy

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

Keri James McIlroy was sentenced in the High Court at Wellington for the murder of his father, James McIlroy, 72. Photo / Mark Mitchell

WARNING: This story contains violence and distressing content that may disturb some readers.

After a father punched his son in the face during an argument at their home, the son grabbed the first thing he could see - a fire poker.

In the frenzied and fatal attack that followed, Keri McIlroy repeatedly struck his father, James McIlroy, with the metal rod, even after the 72-year-old fell to the ground at their Waikanae Beach house, north of Wellington.

He later told police his father had been “going at him all day” and “had punched him in the eye”.

Yesterday, McIlroy, 34, who had earlier admitted to murdering James in June 2024, was sentenced in the High Court at Wellington.

His family described James as a kind and generous man and spoke of the devastating and ongoing impact his death had on the family more than two years on.

His wife, Wendy McIlroy, described at the hearing how her life was cruelly shattered that day when her husband of 37 years, the father of their children and grandchildren, was taken from them.

“My life has, and will never be the same ever again,” she said in her victim impact statement.

“A once very happy house full of love [and] laughter, now empty and silent; if only one second of thought, this would not be.”

Wendy said she cried herself to sleep most nights and was “very depressed”, trying her best to face each day.

“I wanted to end my life too and go be with James.

“Not only on that day did I lose the love of my life, [but] I also lost my son. It is me the one doing all the loss and upset. I wished it was me taken that day.”

However, Wendy concluded her victim impact statement with a message to her son.

“Keri, you have apologised and told me how sorry you are. For this I will always be grateful.

“A mother’s love is always unconditional, and I hope that one day, I will be able to forgive you.”

At the sentencing hearing, it emerged that McIlroy had undiagnosed schizophrenia.

Prone to angry outbursts as a child, attempts to have him assessed as an adult came to nothing, or he was diagnosed with drug-induced psychosis, the court heard.

“The family has been let down by the Australian and New Zealand health systems,” Wendy had told the court.

“For years we were reaching out for help and never received it. Had we received some help, none of this would have happened, and we would all be living our happy life.”

The court heard that in the months leading up to the murder, McIlroy became increasingly paranoid, to the point that Wendy moved out.

McIlroy reported hearing voices and believed his family had installed cameras behind paintings and buried body parts in the backyard.

“You described your home environment as toxic in the years before your murder, especially with your stepbrother, but you got on well with your father and acknowledged that you were his favourite,” Justice David Boldt said.

While McIlroy denied his paranoia prompted him to kill his father, his lawyer, Elizabeth Hall, told the court the psychiatric condition contributed to it.

According to the summary of facts, James punched McIlroy in the face during an argument on June 11, 2024.

McIlroy grabbed a knife and stabbed his father in the neck, causing a superficial cut, before running down the hallway.

To stop his father from chasing him, McIlroy grabbed the closest item he could find, a fire poker, and repeatedly struck his father’s head and body, not stopping until he fell to the ground.

The blows were inflicted with such force they bent the poker and left blood spatter on the walls, curtains and nearby kitchen, the summary said.

They were also so severe that James’ teeth were later found in his stomach.

Afterwards, McIlroy dragged his father towards the front door and used his father’s phone to call his mother.

“Dad stabbed me. It’s real bad, I was unconscious, and I’ve just come to. Can you call the police?” he falsely claimed.

After hanging up, McIlroy called emergency services, telling them his father had attacked him with a knife and smacked him with a “ball thing”, so he had grabbed it back and beaten him to death.

Asked whether his father had any other injuries, McIlroy replied, “Yes, because I went mental.”

When emergency services arrived, they found McIlroy attempting to administer first aid, only stopping when police pulled him away from his father’s body.

Paramedics declared James dead at the scene. His catastrophic injuries were deemed unsurvivable.

Meanwhile, McIlroy had a 1cm cut on his chest, along with other superficial cuts and bruises.

At sentencing, the question for Justice Boldt was whether it was manifestly unjust to impose a sentence of life imprisonment.

The Crown submitted such a sentence was appropriate and sought a 12-year minimum period of imprisonment (MPI) before a guilty plea and other factors were taken into account.

Hall, meanwhile, argued a life sentence would be unjust and urged the court to impose a finite sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment.

Crown prosecutor Tim Bain told the court this was not a case where the presumption of life imprisonment should be displaced.

He submitted it was not enough for a person to be struggling with mental illness, nor was there evidence of prolonged abuse, a factor in other cases cited by the defence.

The court heard McIlroy refused to blame his mental health for his offending, and the psychiatrist who examined him to determine whether he was fit to stand trial did not make a link between his schizophrenia and the killing.

But in response to a question from Justice Boldt, Bain agreed there was a connection between McIlroy’s mental illness and the ferocity of the attack.

Hall began her submissions by acknowledging members of the McIlroy family, telling the court that nothing she said could diminish their loss.

In seeking a finite sentence, she referred to her client’s long history of psychosis and complex psychiatric profile, including a serious, chronic and untreated mental illness.

Hall said he refused to accept there was a nexus between his mental health and the killing, believing he acted in self-defence and “then went mental”.

But rather than a cold, calculated and callous killing, Hall told the court it was a single, unbroken episode in which the victim threw the first punch and the blows were struck in the heat of the moment.

“While there may not be a causal nexus with psychosis, it was close,” she said.

In sentencing McIlroy, Justice Boldt noted the aggravating factors of the offending included a frenzied attack on McIlroy’s father in his own home, a place where he was entitled to feel safe.

His father was vulnerable because of his age and a limp following a knee replacement.

Justice Boldt ruled McIlroy’s mental illness reduced his culpability, noting that in the lead-up to the killing he experienced auditory and visual hallucinations and complex persecutory paranoia.

Contact the Open Justice team

“You feared for your safety at home and believed other family members were conspiring against you.”

He also noted McIlroy was remorseful and had undertaken restorative justice with his mother, where he apologised and tried to answer her questions.

But Justice Boldt said the circumstances were not enough to determine it was a rare case where a sentence of life imprisonment could be displaced.

Instead, he sentenced him to life and imposed an MPI of 10 years, with the Parole Board responsible for determining when McIlroy could be released.

The judge also made two final orders, following requests from McIlroy’s lawyer and his mother.

Hall requested that McIlroy be required to continue his psychiatric treatment in prison, and Wendy wanted her son to serve his sentence at Rimutaka Prison near Wellington so they could continue rebuilding their relationship.

Catherine Hutton is an Open Justice reporter, based in Wellington. She has worked as a journalist at the Waikato Times and RNZ. Most recently, she worked as a media adviser at the Ministry of Justice.
