NZ Defence Force: The day Tony Davies lost access to NZ’s deepest secrets

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

New Zealand’s spy chief moved to suspend Tony Davies’ security clearance on the day of his resignation as Chief of Defence Force – informing military officials of the decision before telling Davies himself.

The revelation comes as Inspector-General of Defence Tim Brewer prepares to investigate Davies’ departure.

Brewer has warned that the probe will be hampered by a shortage of investigators, and the fact the office he has been provided is in a highly secure environment that doesn’t allow laptops, mobile phones or recording equipment to be brought in.

Documents released through the Official Information Act (OIA) show that on the day Davies’ resignation was announced and while the formal resignation process was still underway, NZ Security Intelligence Service Director-General Andrew Hampton ordered an urgent review of his security vetting file and then “suspended” his security clearance.

Davies held Top Secret Special clearance, New Zealand’s highest clearance level, provided only to those requiring access to the country’s most sensitive national security information.

The documents also reveal the behind-the-scenes lead-up to Davies’ resignation on October 23 as a result of what he called an “inappropriate relationship… when in a position of unit command”.

Davies’ disclosure of “errors of judgment” was followed by his departure from the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) a week later, ending his 42-year military career.

The Herald previously revealed how allegations about Davies’ historical relationship with a young flight steward at 40 Squadron were raised in a letter sent directly to him on October 21 by a former flight sergeant seeking to highlight what she considered the military’s departure from its values.

The letter, subsequently circulated to hundreds of NZDF personnel at 4.24pm on October 21 – a Wednesday – described a friend who had served with 40 Squadron in 2005-06 and been investigated over an inappropriate relationship with her commanding officer. Davies commanded the squadron at the time.

The letter said: “This investigation, which tested her profoundly, ultimately led to her departure from the service. Others who were aware of the alleged inappropriate conduct said nothing, choosing instead to stand by and allow the young woman to deal with the aftermath entirely on her own.”

Davies’ resignation was made public through an NZDF press release at 4.02pm on Friday October 23, less than 48 hours after the letter was sent to hundreds of military personnel.

The events leading to the announcement began unfolding on Thursday afternoon when Davies telephoned Minister of Defence Paul Goldsmith – also Minister for the NZSIS – to disclose the relationship and his intention to resign, according to documents released to the Herald.

The documents show – and the NZSIS has confirmed – that spymaster Hampton was told “late in the evening” of Davies’ impending departure.

Documents show that Davies then spoke with Hampton personally on Friday morning “to advise of his undisclosed relationship and that he had resigned”. The NZSIS subsequently confirmed it was Davies who contacted Hampton.

An NZSIS spokesman said: “Following the conversation with Mr Davies, the Director-General initiated the urgent review of the vetting file and made the decision to suspend his clearance.

“Mr Davies was not advised of this decision until early afternoon as NZSIS needed to inform relevant NZDF staff of the clearance suspension decision.”

Cabinet papers released by the Public Service Commission show a Top Secret Special security clearance was a condition of Davies’ appointment as Chief of Defence Force.

Such a clearance requires a high-level security review – the vetting file Hampton ordered reviewed - that seeks highly personal information about an individual’s relationships, conduct, finances and other aspects of life.

Applicants are required to provide full and honest answers, including about matters they might find embarrassing or damaging. Failure to disclose relevant information can itself raise doubts about a person’s trustworthiness and jeopardise their clearance.

But the law tightly restricts how information gathered during security vetting can be used.

Contact journalist David Fisher

In briefing notes prepared for Goldsmith’s office, the NZSIS said the information “can only be used for the purpose of a security clearance assessment, another clearance assessment, or counter-intelligence purposes”.

The agency has declined to say whether Davies previously disclosed the relationship during security vetting, citing those legal restrictions.

The briefing notes also stated: “Individuals holding a national security clearance have clear obligations to report any information which may be relevant to their ongoing suitability to hold a clearance.”

The OIA documents show how the shock news radiated out from the select few who knew on Friday morning.

A flurry of text messages across the day began with Goldsmith to an adviser at 6.53am: “Keen on update on CDF before I leave Whenuapai if possible.” He was told there was no update available.

At 8.48am, the Public Service Commission – which manages the appointment of the Chief of Defence Force – was being asked about developments.

Text messages show officials were expecting an announcement.

“Definitely looking like this afternoon, not this morning – we don’t have his statement yet,” commission official Gabrielle Wilson wrote. “But are working with him and his people on the wording.”

Then, at 11.27am, Davies sent an email to senior Defence Force officers declaring himself unable to continue exercising the powers of Chief of Defence Force.

“I write to advise you that I am unable to perform the functions, duties, or powers of the office of CDF,” he wrote.

The email was sent to Chief of Army Major General Rose King, who would take over as acting Chief of Defence Force while the military’s Vice-Chief, Rear Admiral Mathew Williams, made plans to return to New Zealand from overseas early, the documents show.

At 12.59pm, Wilson confirmed the commission had received Davies’ statement and was assembling material to send to the ministerial office.

Then, at 1.24pm, senior commission official Heather Baggott texted Goldsmith to confirm Davies had activated the military succession order and King had taken command as Acting Chief of Defence Force.

“We have tracked her down at Waiouru and asked that she call you,” Baggott wrote.

In an email at 3.01pm, the commission was providing advice to Goldsmith’s office on the transfer of command.

An existing Defence Force order – signed by Davies in 2025 – provided for the temporary transfer of command and set out the order in which military commanders should step into the role.

The September 2025 succession order placed Williams first in line, followed by Chief of Air Force Air Vice-Marshal Darryn Webb, then King, and then Chief of Navy Rear Admiral Garin Golding.

The order also allowed Davies to override that sequence, which he did by directing King to assume command ahead of Webb. The released records offer no explanation for that decision.

The commission’s Wilson said a formal appointment should be made as soon as possible, which required the Governor-General acting in Council, conventionally on the recommendation of the Minister of Defence.

By 3pm, the focus had shifted to finalising the public announcements by the commission, NZDF and the minister’s office. One official texted: “PM needs to see [the material] asap.”

Even at 3.35pm on Friday, when Goldsmith sent his proposed resignation statement to the Prime Minister’s Office, he was still saying he would recommend that the Governor-General accept Davies’ resignation.

Davies’ resignation letter was not received by the commission until the next day, although it was dated the day before.

The circumstances of Davies’ resignation are expected to come under scrutiny from Brewer, whose investigation will face significant obstacles before it begins.

The investigation sparked by Davies’ resignation will be a significant test for the newly created oversight office, which already has a hefty work programme.

Brewer – a former High Court judge and brigadier (retired) in the Reserve Force – told the Herald he expected to go ahead with an investigation.

He said he had received draft terms of reference from NZDF and made amendments to those, which would be returned to NZDF for consideration. He said he had yet to complete an investigation plan or assemble the relevant NZDF documents.

Brewer said: “The investigation will not be done quickly.

“I have only three investigators, all of whom have existing full-time assignments.”

The staffing shortage was compounded by security restrictions at the building housing his office – the Herald understands his office was set up before his appointment in Pipitea House, where the spy agencies are located – which made it difficult to interview witnesses or handle evidence.

“The security requirements mean that I cannot bring mobile phones, dictaphones, laptops or any other electronic devices into my office. That makes recording, storing and processing data difficult.”

Brewer, who took up the role a year ago, said he had been trying to find other office space since February but was constrained by funding restrictions.

“I will try to find some temporary space that will allow me to interview people, record and store what they say and work productively.”

Brewer said the investigation needed time to follow proper procedures. “The investigation must be planned, be thorough and be fair.”

In a statement, the Public Service Commission said Davies had failed to disclose the inappropriate relationship during his 2024 appointment process, saying the information would have been material to its advice to the then-Minister of Defence, Judith Collins. It said its internal assurance review of the appointment process was underway and being prioritised.

The Herald has established that there were two inquiries in the early 2000s that looked into allegations Davies was involved in an inappropriate relationship, which he denied at the time.

David Fisher is based in Northland and has worked as a journalist for more than 30 years, winning multiple journalism awards including being twice named Reporter of the Year and being selected as one of a small number of Wolfson Press Fellows to Wolfson College, Cambridge. He first joined the Herald in 2004.

Nestlé recalls Alfamino Junior 1+ Years toddler milk due to cereulide toxin fears

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

Nestlé is recalling a specialist milk product for toddlers after contamination concerns. Photo / AFP

Nestlé is recalling a specialist milk product for toddlers with allergies and medical conditions due to the presence of the cereulide toxin.

The company said 103 cans of its Alfamino Junior 1+ Years (400g) with a use-by date of 10/12/2027 and batch number 53440017Y1 were affected by the recall.

Food Safety (NZFS) deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said the affected products were mainly available through pharmacies and had been removed from shelves.

“The problem with one batch of this specialist toddler milk is that it could contain cereulide, which is produced by the microorganism Bacillus cereus and can cause gastrointestinal illness. Fortunately, there have been no reports of associated illness,” he said.

A new, unaffected batch would be available at stores in the coming week.

“In the meantime, if you have the affected specialist Alfamino toddler milk at home, do not feed it to your child and return it to the place of purchase,” Arbuckle said.

“Should you urgently need an alternative before Monday, your pharmacy will have other products available. If you cannot access alternative products, please contact Healthline for advice.”

Symptoms linked to cereulide could include vomiting, diarrhoea or unusual lethargy. They would typically appear between 30 minutes to six hours after exposure and usually resolve within 24 hours.

The imported product was manufactured in Switzerland.

“As is our usual practice, NZFS will work with Nestlé to understand how the contamination occurred and prevent its recurrence,” Arbuckle said.

Anyone with concerns about their child’s health should contact their healthcare provider or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free advice.

Chiefs of staff of the current coalition parties are expected to be talking this weekend.

Winston Peters has yet to break his silence or address the media after the special vote results were announced.

NZ First hints at a long wait for final negotiations in message to supporters.

Richard Prebble says Christopher Luxon should resign, with Erica Stanford, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop - via a Botany by-election - possible successors.

There were about 400,000 special votes – about 14% of all votes cast – including about 100,000 overseas votes.

How NZ voted: Dig into results for every seat in our interactive and read Herald political editor Thomas Coughlan's explainer on what happens now.

National erred when it pivoted to education and gangs during the election campaign - “a mistake" that political commentator Liam Hehir says he also "bought into".

“The public was with the party on the crime issue but crime is not a pressing concern. The edge in education was slight and not a priority in a cost of living crisis,” the Palmerston North-based lawyer and National Party member wrote on X.

“And that’s why things stabilised when they pivoted back to tax and the economy.”

Former Labour Minister and ex-Act Party leader Richard Prebble says National’s Christopher Luxon should resign as leader and MP, suggesting outgoing Hutt South MP Chris Bishop could return to Parliament through a Botany by-election.

“If Luxon had self-awareness, he would know he has neither the mandate nor the credibility to negotiate with Opportunity,” Prebble wrote on social media.

“He should also realise the National Party cannot have another election with him as leader.”

Prebble named Bishop, Erica Stanford and Mark Mitchell as potential successors, noting that while Bishop failed to retain his seat in Hutt South, his personal vote was still 18 points ahead of National’s party vote.

National’s constitution does not explicitly require its leader to be an MP, he added, citing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s path to leadership before entering Parliament.

“The caucus should now ask Luxon to resign both as leader and as an MP,” Prebble wrote.

“Bishop could stand in a Botany by-election, which could conceivably be held as early as 9 January, before Parliament must meet on 14 January.

“A National Party led by Bishop or Stanford would be in a much stronger negotiating position knowing it was able to fight another election.”

New Zealand’s final election result comes after a campaign “shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters”, the BBC told its readers.

The international news behemoth noted the incumbent coalition had fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, and now needed the support of "the centrist Opportunity Party" to remain in power.

“If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.”

The report linked to a previous BBC story on the apathy and dread expressed by some Kiwi voters soon after the country went to the polls three weeks ago.

More than half the country no longer saw New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the public policy think tank The Helen Clark Foundation, the BBC wrote.

“Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, moving to Australia.”

The Guardian’s Wellington-based correspondent has told the UK publication’s readers New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become the country’s “first ever four-party coalition”.

“In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.”

That’s if the country isn’t forced back to the polls, an "unprecedented" but not impossible outcome given negotiations between the four parties would be “so complex”, Victoria University of Wellington political scientist Lara Greaves told the Guardian.

“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election.”

Chris Bishop has been heckled while walking in public, with a motorist asking if he’d applied for a benefit yet and telling the outgoing Cabinet Minister he'd been part of the “most racist Government" ever seen in New Zealand.

Footage taken at the intersection of Gore St and Customs St E in downtown Auckland was posted to the Instagram pages of Public Housing Futures and Zane Wedding - who has been involved in activism and whose LinkedIn describes him as general manager at Auckland Council-controlled Mangere Mountain Education Trust.

“Is that f***** Chris Bishop?”, a person in the car says, before the camera zooms in on Bishop waiting to cross the street.

The former Hutt South National MP gives a thumbs up as a man in the car calls out to ask him, "What’s it like being unemployed?"

Bishop’s replies couldn’t be heard as the heckler continued.

“Must be good, brother. You applied for a benefit bro? You should be. Find out what it’s like to live on this side.

“Part of the most racist Government that we’ve ever seen in Aotearoa. Swear to God the harms that you will do will last for generations.”

Bishop was a senior member of the coalition Government but won’t return to Parliament this term after he was defeated in Hutt South and the party failed to get any list MPs elected.

Outgoing Mt Roskill National MP Carlos Cheung says he remained committed “to our community” despite losing the seat to Labour rival Michael Wood.

“While the outcome is not what we had hoped for, I accept the result with humility and respect for the democratic process”, Cheung wrote on Instagram.

“I would also like to sincerely congratulate Michael Wood on his election victory. I wish him all the very best as he takes on the responsibility of representing the people of Mount Roskill.”

Cheung thanked “every supporter, volunteer, friend, family member, and everyone who stood alongside me throughout this journey”, and promised to keep working for the community.

“Although this election journey has come to an end, my commitment to our community remains.”

Carlos Cheung has thanked the Mt Roskill community for its support. Cheung was defeated in the Mt Roskill seat by Michael Wood. Photo / Carlos Cheung

The wife of defeated National MP Ryan Hamilton has written of the “personal attacks, threats and abuse” those in public office face.

Hamilton won the Hamilton East seat by 5000 votes in 2023, but was beaten by Labour’s Georgie Dansey by 173 after special votes were announced yesterday, flipping Hamilton's earlier 456-vote advantage.

Marie Hamilton wrote on Facebook that her husband had immediately gone to Dansey’s home to “shake her hand and congratulate her”.

“Georgie thanked Ryan for his kindness, recalling how when she was standing alone at events, he would always come over and talk to her. That is the Ryan that we all know, he treats everyone with the same respect regardless of their background, ethnicity, financial status or political beliefs.

“From a wife’s perspective, our partners choose public life because it’s their passion. As spouses, we don’t necessarily choose it, but we are thrown into it.”

She’d witnessed “the personal attacks, the threats, the middle fingers and the abuse directed at one of the kindest humans I know and that’s been hard”, Marie Hamilton wrote.

“Politics can be brutal. It’s a job where you can work 12–18 hours a day, give it everything you have, serve your community wholeheartedly and still find yourself publicly out of a job.”

However, the outcome wasn’t all bad, one person commenting on the post noted: “Positive note, more time with his new mokopuna”.

“This is true,” Marie Hamilton replied, adding a heart emoji.

There are 35 new faces among the MPs who have won a seat in Parliament.

However, not all are first-time politicians, with several returning to the House after stints away.

Here’s a rundown of the new MPs.

Despite having no list seats, National has seven newcomers to Parliament via their electorate seats.

They include Lloyd Budd (Whangārei), Blair Cameron (Nelson), Mahesh Muralidhar (Tāmaki), Katie Milne (West Coast-Tasman), Emma Chatterton (Papakura), Matthew Paul (Port Waikato) and Jessica Rowe (Kaipara ki Mahurangi).

Two of those seats have flipped: Nelson, from Labour’s Rachel Boyack, and Tāmaki, from Act’s Brooke van Velden.

Rowe was selected as a candidate for Kaipara ki Mahurangi after incumbent Chris Penk elected not to run, having been sacked as a minister.

Labour also has seven first-time MPs, including three who will claim some of the party’s 14 list seats: Rakesh Naidoo (5), Chris Flatt (11) and Kingi Kiriona (12).

Labour’s electorate winners include Michael Wood (Mt Roskill), Dominik Yanzick (Wigram), George Hampton (Christchurch Central) and Mananui Ramsden (Te Tai Tonga).

Wood is not entirely new to Parliament, having been the Mt Roskill MP from 2016 to 2023, when he was beaten by National’s Carlos Cheung in his first bid for Parliament.

After three attempts to make it into Parliament, Opportunity has secured seven list seats.

It will fill those seats with leader Qiulae Wong, deputy leader Daniel Eb, Jessica Hammond, Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, Jodie Kuntzsch, Sarah Lucas and Eden Skipper.

With this result, Opportunity is pondering whether it can form a Government with National, Act and NZ First, or if it will send Kiwis back to the polls.

The Act Party has secured 13 seats, some of which it will fill with newcomers Antonia Modkova, Iain Murray, James Christmas and Paul Henry.

It was broadcaster Henry’s first attempt with Act – having unsuccessfully run for the Wairarapa electorate for National in 1999 – and Murray’s first foray into politics, after a career in education.

Christmas, a lawyer, was a candidate for the National Party in 2023.

Filling four of the Green Party’s 14 list seats are Bhen Goodsir, Rohan O’Neill-Stevens, Craig Pauling and Tania Waikato.

The new faces entering Parliament via the NZ First Party list are Taine Randell, Craig Stobo, Harete Hipango-Brownlie, Michael Laws and Alfred Ngaro.

However, only Stobo and Randell – a former All Black – are completely new to politics.

Laws, a broadcaster with The Platform, was National’s MP for Hawkes Bay from 1990 to 1996.

Hipango-Brownlie also served for National as the MP for Whanganui from 2017 to 2020 and as a list MP from 2021 to 2023, when she missed out on a seat.

Ngaro was a National list MP from 2011 until he lost his seat in the 2020 election.

Aperahama Edwards is Te Pāti Māori’s new face, having been elected to Te Tai Tokerau, unseating Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, who was expelled from the party last year and failed to win the seat back under the Te Tai Tokerau Party ticket she founded.

World Fireknife Championships: Hamilton teen Vandross Pere raising funds to compete in Hawaii

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

Vandross Pere is hoping to compete at the World Fireknife Championships in Hawaii. Photo / Tom Eley

A 14-year-old Waikato fire knife dancer hasn’t missed a single day of training in a year.

Even when he’s sick, Vandross Pere practises with his blade in his backyard.

Vandross is now raising funds to help take his cultural passion to the World Fireknife Championships in Laie, Hawaii.

The cross-Pacific journey is a rare opportunity for the Hamilton teen to connect with the world’s elite cultural performers.

“I want to go learn more, meet more, and collaborate with finer people over there,” Vandross told the Waikato Herald.

He’s already planned his first stop for when he lands next April.

“I want to go to 7-Eleven and buy a slushy with all the flavours.”

Vandross became interested in fireknife dancing a year ago, after watching five-time world champion Mikaele “Mika” Oloa complete a speed test in New Zealand.

“I’m shocked people can go that fast,” he said.

He was inspired.

“It means so much to me that I have to try.”

Siva afi, a Samoan fireknife dance, has become a sacred tradition.

“I want to inspire other people to start celebrating their own cultures too,” Vandross said.

Training requires plenty of physical conditioning and deep mental clarity.

“When I pick up [my] stick, it’s just where I can block everything and the world out.”

Since seeing that video of Oloa, Vandross said he has felt the need to practise every day.

“If I don’t pick up my stick, I don’t feel like I’ve accomplished anything. It helps with anxiety.”

Despite only training for a year, Vandross could already be considered a strong competitor.

In March, he won the Siva Afi Aotearoa intermediate division title in Māngere.

He credits his calm composure under pressure to a strict mindfulness routine, which also includes not watching others compete.

“I breathe three times in and out, and then I just relax. You’ve got to have a good mindset.”

Aside from Vandross’ fierce stage presence, he is also the eldest of five siblings, two of whom are living with autism.

His balanced routine involves helping care for them in the morning and completing chores between training sessions.

The upcoming competition also gives the family a rare opportunity to holiday together.

“My parents sacrifice a lot for me,” he said.

“It’s very important to my mum and dad that they get a rest.”

Vandross credits much of his success to his father and coach, Kelly Pere, who always “encourages me to reach my limits”.

“I wouldn’t be where I am without my coach,” he said.

“He tells me, ‘You can be tired now, but you’re not going to be tired when you get your chance’.”

His mother, Audrey Pere, said she gets emotional when she sees her son train and perform.

“He found a healing, creative and powerful space within himself,” she said.

“Tapping into that warrior spirit helps him overcome anxiety, self-doubt and the pressures of being a young brown male in this world.”

In a home with people with different neurodivergent needs, Audrey said Siva afi is a critical grounding purpose.

She said there is something in Vandross’ body that “needs that movement to regulate himself because there’s so much going on in our home”.

“He sleeps with his sticks; they are like his dreamcatchers in the nighttime,” she said with a smile.

Audrey describes watching her son perform as an absolute honour. “This is his flow state, his happy place.”

Navigating extra costs alongside the cost-of-living crisis was tough, Audrey said, but they were grateful for the life they were living.

“Even though life is expensive, me and my husband, we are so happy,” she said.

She said her mindset is that “anything is possible, and we live in abundance”.

“We don’t want [our] Givealittle to feel like we are begging. We want it to be there if you feel inspired by a dream.”

The family was especially moved by a donation from an 8-year-old boy, who watched Vandross perform on television and gifted him his birthday money.

For Vandross, “that meant a lot”.

“I want to inspire more little kids like them. I won’t forget it.”

If Vandross has it his way, Hawaii will be the first step towards a larger journey.

He said he dreams of taking his Siva afi skills internationally, eyeing the stage at Disney World’s The Lion King show that some of his uncles are part of.

“I want to perform around the world ... That’s where I want to work.”

NZ casting director Liz Mullane recalls casting NZDF soldiers in Lord of the Rings

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

New Zealand casting director Liz Mullane talks tanks, orcs and watching trained soldiers scale Ruapehu’s mountains in full monster make-up after being cast in The Lord of the Rings 25 years ago. Erin Smith reports.

Of all the high-profile movies Liz Mullane has worked on, The Lord of the Rings (LOTR) is her proudest.

“I’m proud of a lot of the things I’ve done,

“But this was absolutely the extreme of all extremes of filmmaking.”

Mullane has worked on blockbuster films including King Kong, The Chronicles of Narnia series, The Hobbit and, most recently, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum.

Years ago, she was casting New Zealand talent in a fantasy action movie she had “no idea” would become part of the country’s history and identity.

“I had no idea how big it was at the time. In fact, I don’t think many of us did, to be honest, and it was just a fly by the seat of your pants every single day [project].”

The budget was modest at $93 million, compared to The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey 11 years later at $180m, according to IMDb.

“We didn’t have a budget that meant we could just spend gazillions,” Mullane said.

“It feels like it now, but not back then. We were all just trying to make do with what we could do.”

“I think Kiwis are brilliant problem-solvers ... and that’s true filmmaking.”

One problem was the need for many extras, especially for expansive fight scenes and the orcs’ Uruk-hai army.

The solution: use real soldiers.

“I remember being at a production meeting early on and that there had been some agreement made ... that they [NZ Army] would provide some extras for us.”

Many scenes were filmed around Ruapehu, the set location for Mordor, and nearby Waiōuru Military Camp became a convenient source of orcs and elves.

Mullane said the ever-changing on-set schedule and the army’s rigid, highly organised one quickly became a mismatch.

They scrapped official casting, instead using whoever was available.

“Our schedules changed every five seconds due to weather and all the logistics that go with a massive film crew.

“I think some of them became very frustrated.”

One morning, the crew woke to one of their massive production tents collapsing under overnight snowfall, she said.

“We had to ring the army and say, ‘Plan Z is being put into place’.”

The soldiers also had to adjust to scaling difficult terrain in costume, with prosthetics for the first time.

Many prop weapons, not designed to withstand actual fighting, were destroyed by the soldiers, Mullane said.

“There was a bit of a joke about how many weapons were we down after a day with the army.”

Mullane also experienced some of the army’s world, riding in a tank.

“That was really cool.”

Looking back on the project, Mullane said she was “immensely proud” of what they achieved and of being part of it.

“Whenever I watch the films, I’m blown away by how good they are.

“We didn’t have AI back then. I didn’t even have an iPhone. I didn’t have a laptop computer. I actually don’t really know how we did it, frankly.”

Mullane met her husband, Weta special effects and prosthetic art director “genius” Gino Acevedo, on LOTR.

Their daughter, Ruby Acevedo, returned to Ruapehu with them earlier this year to work alongside her father in prosthetics on the set of the new Gollum film.

“It’s really terrific to be back ... we’re back at Mount Doom [Mt Ngauruhoe].”

Erin Smith is a multimedia journalist based in Whanganui.

New house, but just a squab to sleep on: The helpers who furnish homes for the homeless

New Zealand Herald November 27, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Providing hundreds of struggling people with new homes in Hawke’s Bay has doubled the demand for charities that provide household essentials in the past five years.

The pressure is felt by the volunteer sector, including Christian Lovelink, which, according to operations manager Ian Jones, has seen demand grow over the past five years from about 500 “clients” a year, to over 1000 in the past 12 months.

A team of up to 50 volunteers has collected, in some cases repaired, and delivered 15,000 items in that last year, including 900 beds.

They may be single people living alone, or they may be larger families.

Jones, and Joy Shaw, who links through the Teen Parent Unit based at William Colenso College and has had 62 years in community service, have seen families with as many as eight children needing immediate help.

Shaw’s experience includes more than 30 years referring to Christian Lovelink, which she says has been “amazing and very creative” in setting up full house lots.

Many of those helped have spent three years or more in transitional accommodation, such as motels, and have little in the way of possessions.

“With the increase in poverty and increasing social issues, homeless people in and out of housing don’t have household items,” she says. “Often, it’s just the clothing on their backs.”

Many also have little in the way of family or network support, such as on Friday when she filled the station wagon and headed out of the Onekawa complex to a young mum whose only extras on her first night in new surroundings had been a bargain-priced foam squab to sleep on.

The reward for the volunteers comes in some of the unforgettable looks on the faces of those who have been helped, especially children who, in some situations, might never have had a bed of their own.

“For many of them it is life-changing,” Jones said.

The pressure has been heightened in Napier with new accommodation, such as four developments opening up over 100 new homes within barely 2km of the CBD, in 3-4 months to early 2027.

Among them is the three-storey complex of 30 one- or two-bedroom units in Wellesley Rd, built by developers for the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development. They lay unoccupied for the first 15 months until purchased by TW Properties, put in the management of Auckland-based community housing provider Home in Place New Zealand and opened in October.

There are 24 rental units in the three-storey Pukemokimoki on the corner of Kennedy Rd and Owen St, and 14 free-standing, two-storey, two-and three-bedroom homes in Te Kererū, a former retirement home site fronting McDonald and Latham streets, near McLean Park, and now aimed at pathways to ownership in affordable homes; both developments led by Treaty settlement entity Mana Ahuriri.

Napier District Masonic Trust also has 34 new retirement villas nearing completion, replacing its demolished rental flats village off Morris Spence Ave.

In addition are several other developments, including 98 homes in the first stage of Te Roropipi, a Mana Ahuriri development off Wharerangi Rd, Greenmeadows (including 28 kaumatua flats), the first of which are expected to be occupied by March 2027.

The big demands needing public support and donations are for beds and bedding, tables and chairs, for children and families, and kitchen and laundry items, including whiteware.

Jones said most of the donations come from families who want to help other people, by taking steps such as downsizing their own homes or redirecting estates of the deceased, sometimes entire households.

The store rooms are heavily stocked with mattresses, which often come from homes that have replaced their beds.

They’re usually in good condition, but a workshop, with over $10,000 worth of timber donated each year, helps overcome one of the problems.

“With so many mattresses, we had to come up with a solution to build bed bases,” Jones said.

Community workshop Menzshed came up with a design to fit most purposes, and volunteer carpenters and other tradespeople, such as a retired electrician, make sure everything that goes out is safe and in working condition.

Jones said the biggest numbers of referrals come from the child health team at Hawke’s Bay Hospital, including recognising the need for better living conditions for children in troubled homes, Te Taiwhenua o Heretaunga, and health, housing and social services providers such as Emerge.

But he said modern cost-of-living crises bring problems at both ends, saying the need increases but donations of goods may slow as people spend less.

Jones said it costs about $100,000 a year to run the service, which includes washing and drying donated bedding, and about $5000 a year on waste disposal.

Nationwide, there were 18,837 applicants on the Ministry of Social Development Housing Register, down 3.1% from September 2025, with the cut attributed not only to new housing supply and pathways but also to tighter eligibility rules and tenancy reforms.

The Government introduced tighter prioritisation and stricter assessment criteria in May to ensure social housing is targeted strictly toward those with severe and persistent barriers.

Despite those measures, the number in Napier on the Housing Register was 492 at the end of September, up 15.5% in a year since the 426 in September 2025. It had been 717 at the end of 2023, and the peak was 801 at the end of March 2022.

In Hastings, there were 504 at the end of September, up 10.5% in a year, compared with a high of 804 in March 2022.

Doug Laing is a Hawke’s Bay Today reporter based in Napier, with 53 years in journalism, including more than four decades covering news and sports events and issues in Hawke’s Bay.

Rotorua’s visitor information centres lost more than $400,000 in the last financial year, missing a stated goal of breaking even.

RotoruaNZ, the council-controlled organisation which runs the city’s three isite locations, reported a loss of $438,080 across those operations, despite a near 50% increase in retail revenue.

Chief executive Andrew Wilson said the result reflected spending on new income-generating opportunities and one-off costs.

“We’ve been pursuing a strategy to grow and diversify isite trading revenue,” Wilson said.

“The longer-term aim is to reduce reliance on ratepayer funding for RotoruaNZ as a whole.

Despite the 48% overall trading revenue increase across its Fenton St, Redwoods and Waipa mountain bike park locations, Wilson said a drop in revenue from ticket sales also offset those gains.

He said the organisation had now reviewed its isite operations and made changes aimed at reducing costs. Those changes included closing a satellite isite operation attached to the independently run 3Mirage attraction.

“The past year has involved investment to grow revenue and diversify income streams,” he said.

“With that growth achieved, our priority is ensuring the operation becomes financially sustainable while continuing to support visitors and local tourism businesses.”

The latest result marks a sharp turnaround from recent years.

RotoruaNZ’s isite operations recorded a loss of $827,153 in 2021/22, when international tourism was still suffering from Covid-19-related issues.

That improved to a loss of $189,880 in 2022/23 before rebounding to a $177,654 surplus in 2023/24 and a smaller $3531 surplus in 2024/25.

Last year’s loss was the largest deficit recorded since the Covid recovery period.

Rotorua Lakes Council said it was not concerned by the result, with destination development manager Jean-Paul Gaston noting the loss was absorbed within RotoruaNZ’s overall financial result, a $14,658 surplus.

RotoruaNZ received $9.3 million in council funding during the 2025/26 financial year, increasing slightly to $9.33m this year.

Gaston said that funding supported RotoruaNZ’s wider activities, including economic development, destination marketing, events and venues, as well as isite operations.

He also noted the break-even target was one RotoruaNZ had set for itself, rather than a requirement imposed by the council.

Gaston described it as a “stretched target” and said the council expected RotoruaNZ to continue working towards it.

The result comes as visitor information centres around the country continue to adapt to changing travel habits, with more visitors researching and booking accommodation, transport and activities online.

A 2025 Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment survey of regional tourism organisations found seven had stopped operating isites altogether since 2019, while another nine had reduced their operations.

The report identified changing visitor behaviour, high operating costs and the withdrawal of council contracts among the challenges facing the traditional isite model.

Recent casualties include visitor information centres in Golden Bay and Cambridge, which closed in 2025 as operators grappled with funding, tenancy and financial sustainability challenges.

Visitor Information Network Incorporated (VIN), the company which manages Tourism New Zealand’s isite brand, confirmed there has been a decline in isites in recent years, dropping from 74 in 2019 to 44 today.

VIN executive manager Paul Yeo said many centres had been forced to rethink how they operated following the disruption caused by Covid-19 and ongoing funding pressures.

“Many isites readjusted their business plans, but not all have been sustainable,” he said.

Yeo said most isites received financial support from their owners. Rotorua’s isite operations also received more than $50,000 in central government-backed funding during the year, including grants for a store refurbishment and digital upgrades.

But despite the on-paper financial struggles, the overall benefit to local economies was hard to quantify, Yeo said.

“Providing advice and information to visitors is known to deliver downstream economic benefits for a region as visitors stay longer and spend more locally, but this is not always reflected in direct income to isites.”

Despite a decline in the number of centres, visitor demand remains strong, with the national isite network welcoming 2.64 million visitors and generating $34.9 million in sales in the 2025/26 financial year, both up on the previous year.

As for the current financial year, Wilson said RotoruaNZ’s isite operation was on course to meet a target of breaking even.

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in the UK for eight years.

Anger, uncertainty and ‘deals with the devil’: Countdown on to an election like no other

Sydney Morning Herald November 28, 2026

Political operatives are discarding everything they thought they knew about NSW elections as the March poll looms.

On a stage inside the auditorium at Trades Hall on Goulburn Street, Unions NSW secretary Thomas Costa grips a lectern and talks about anger.

“Workers are worn out and, for many, they have run out of options,” Costa tells a crowd of union delegates and members in mid-November.

“All that’s left is anger at a system they feel is failing them. That anger is real, and we shouldn’t dismiss it.”

In front of him as he speaks is a poster of One Nation’s leader in NSW, Mike Newman. In a building where union bosses have cooked up campaigns for more than a century, Costa is launching the Unions NSW pitch for next year’s state election. “The risk you can’t afford,” the poster reads.

It is a sign of the times that the old enemy – the NSW Liberal Party – barely rates a mention. In his speech, the Coalition is a foil. “The only way that One Nation can win is in coalition with the NSW Liberals, and they will bring out the absolute worst in each other,” he tells the crowd.

This is not the campaign Costa, only recently appointed to the job as the state’s top union official, thought he would be running.

A day earlier, seated at a long table inside Trades Hall, he recalls a meeting at the end of 2025, when 40-odd union leaders gathered for a roundtable for their first talks about the upcoming election.

An official stood up and mentioned One Nation. “He said he was really worried,” Costa remembers. “He said, ‘These people are pitching to our people. They’re going after blue-collar workers’.”

He admits he was dismissive. “My initial statement was: ‘These people were never our people.’ I said our people would never be attracted to this type of ideology. We’ve got nothing to worry about. Clearly, I was wrong.”

He was not alone. Only a year ago, it seemed a fait accompli that Premier Chris Minns and Labor would romp in for a second term. As a rule, NSW doesn’t like switching parties. You have to go back to the 1920s and 30s to find the last time a first-term government lost power in the state.

But the past 12 months have prompted a radical reevaluation of Australian politics, as the rise in One Nation’s polling translated first to big swings in the South Australian election, then to victories in byelections in the federal seat of Farrer and the Western Australian state electorate of Secret Harbour.

The once-fringe party has consistently polled in the mid-20s in NSW since this masthead began tracking its vote earlier this year. After Victoria votes this weekend, attention will turn to NSW, where an election is due on March 13.

It promises to be a poll like no other in the state’s modern history. The combined effect of One Nation’s rise and NSW’s optional preferential voting system has political operatives discarding everything they thought they knew. Optional preferencing means voters are not required to number every box, and ballots can be put aside, or “exhaust”, if there is no preference for a remaining candidate as counting progresses.

When Sonia Hornery, the long-time member for Wallsend, announced her retirement earlier this month, her seat immediately came into play, despite Labor holding it on a margin of almost 32 per cent. “Margins don’t mean anything any more,” one Hunter Labor official said.

Political operatives in Sydney’s south-west are gearing up for genuine three-cornered contests in seats such as Penrith, Camden and Holsworthy. In the Hunter, Central Coast and down south, long-time Labor seats risk flipping orange. Polling conducted for Unions NSW in 10 target seats in September showed a combined One Nation and Liberal vote of almost 50 per cent in some battleground Labor electorates.

At the same time, optional preferencing and Minns’ courting of conservative voters mean Liberal suburban Sydney strongholds are under severe threat, including seats such as Miranda and Lane Cove. The Nationals are prepping for the apocalypse.

“It’s not just total random chaos, but it’s going to be a mess,” election analyst Ben Raue, from the Tally Room website, says of the dynamics.

In the Hunter, One Nation has its sights on seats including Cessnock – where state party leader Mike Newman is running – Maitland, Swansea, Port Stephens and Wallsend. After barely visiting the region for most of his term as premier, Minns has made near-weekly visits for months.

Yasmin Catley, minister for police and Swansea MP, is blunt about the prospects of a One Nation surge in her seat. “Will I take a hit? Most likely,” she says. “I mean, you’d be a fool not to take them seriously.”

Catley, like most Labor MPs, has seen a surge in voter frustration amid five consecutive interest rate hikes and the bite of cost-of-living pressures. Even if the state government is not directly to blame, she is certain it will face the consequences. “They want to blame someone, and I think it will be incumbent governments,” she says.

“People are super frustrated. They’re struggling. They want to make change. I really feel that.”

But it’s not just Labor MPs in the region staring down One Nation. Along with Labor’s Clayton Barr in Cessnock, Nationals MP Dave Layzell in neighbouring Upper Hunter, held on a 3.8 per cent margin, is also in the firing line.

“Honestly, they will go well,” Layzell tells this masthead. “In our seats, there will be a tough contest. Minns says that the real opposition is One Nation. It is for me too.

“If you take the polling, they’re double me. I have the same support, but Labor has fallen off the Earth.”

The shift in the electorate’s mood outside inner Sydney has been so dramatic that even the newest MP, Katelin McInerney, who won the seat of Kiama for Labor at a byelection after the resignation of Gareth Ward a little more than 12 months ago, has felt it.

“I think one of the differences I’ve felt between even 2023, but also the byelection, is, you know, you’d rock up in the afternoon, there’d be a ute in the driveway, pair of boots on the front doorstep. You’d knock, the dog would go off, someone would get up, take the [printed] materials, and you’d get a chance to introduce yourself and have a chat,” she says.

“Now, you knock on the front door, dog goes off, but you’re just not getting the engagement. People don’t want to talk to me as much.”

Costa takes heart from focus group research which shows One Nation support is often quite shallow, and dissipates once people differentiate between Pauline Hanson and the NSW party, led by the relatively unknown Newman. “It’s fascinating how gendered the language around One Nation is,” he says. “People refer to them as ‘her’, or ‘she’. It’s just getting that message across that Hanson’s not on the ballot.”

Liberal Party research shows the same. While the primary vote has taken a hit, insiders familiar with the party’s internal research say One Nation support, particularly among women in their most marginal seats, tends to flow back to the Liberals the more voters hear about Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane.

While One Nation’s surge has already resulted in electoral victories, NSW’s optional preferencing system has made it a key focus for the populist-right party. Perhaps the closest analogue is the 1998 Queensland election, which also had optional preferences. Hanson’s relatively new party won 11 seats with almost 23 per cent of the vote.

While six of those came from Labor, the ALP won six back from the Liberals and formed a minority government.

In other words, even the ALP’s worst-case scenario could see it emerge in NSW with the same or more seats, as long as the Liberals are in worse shape at the end of it. That dynamic helps explain the peculiar contours of this election.

While Labor believes it is at risk from One Nation in as many as a dozen seats, it could also benefit from the flow of preferences – or lack thereof – in Liberal-held electorates. The Liberals hold seven seats on a margin of less than 2 per cent, and a clutch of others – Miranda, Epping, Willoughby, Lane Cove, Hornsby and Hawkesbury – on less than 10 per cent.

While some of the most marginal Liberal seats could fall to Labor – including seats such as Ryde and Oatley following the retirement of sitting MPs Jordan Lane and Mark Coure – the party insists it is still in the running in most of them. But the form of the problem facing the Liberals is best encapsulated by two seats in Sydney’s aspiration belt in the north-west.

Monica Tudehope, in Epping, and James Wallace, in Hornsby, entered parliament after byelections this term prompted by the resignations of two of the party’s most dominant figures from the previous 12 years – Dominic Perrottet and Matt Kean.

Both are factional allies of their predecessors – Tudehope, whose father Damien is also a senior NSW Liberal, worked for Perrottet and is from the right, while Wallace, a longtime ally of Kean’s, is a moderate – and are highly regarded within the party as potential future leaders.

On a humid Friday morning in mid-November, Tudehope is knocking on doors with her very own “heat vest” – seven-month-old son Jude – strapped to her front.

Epping is a seat the Liberals have always held, one in a clutch of blue in the north-west along with Ryde, Castle Hill, Kellyville and Winston Hills. But increased density and changing demographics have ebbed away its margin. Tudehope now holds it on a slim 4.8 per cent. It’s precisely the type of seat which, on a bad day for the Liberals, could end up red.

As she knocks on doors in Epping, there are certainly no brickbats, nor any mention of One Nation. Instead, the issues are hyper-local. One resident wants a zebra crossing outside his house. A few doors down, a neighbour thinks that’s a terrible idea. There are concerns about traffic, construction noise from the new apartment developments surrounding the metro a few blocks away, and how crowded the public transport is.

But it won’t take much. A small swing to One Nation that does not flow back to the Liberals via preferences could flip it. Tudehope knows this. Her biggest fear is voters could assume a Liberal victory in the seat, and park their vote elsewhere.

“I guess it’s always been a Liberal seat, right? I don’t think any seat is safe any more, but for voters that have voted kind of recently in Epping ... there’s a risk, I guess, or I worry that those people might consider putting their vote elsewhere [because] there’s an assumption I’ll win,” she says.

“[But] I’m optimistic that people will understand that a vote for the Liberals is a vote for a plan. You can park your vote with a protest, but I think people can grapple with the idea that if you genuinely want change, we have a plan, not just grievance.”

Minns, a centrist premier who has alienated some within his own party because of his conservative stances on issues such as protest rights, has not been shy about courting Liberals. His popularity with more conservative-leaning voters is an opportunity the government is keen to seize on.

Last week he announced the latest in a string of captain’s picks by unveiling Tanya Raffoul, a former chief of staff to Liberal minister David Elliott, as his candidate in the seat of Epping. Raffoul had been lobbying to run for the Liberals in the seat of Winston Hills as recently as June, before quitting the party in September.

The potential for a wholesale realignment of the political map after March is forcing both major parties to face uncomfortable questions about what they stand for.

For Costa, a scenario in which Labor picks up traditional Liberal seats while shedding its base in places such as Cessnock and Wallsend presents an uncomfortable vision of the future.

“It worries me in terms of a kind of existential view of where politics is going, definitely,” he says. “I’m very concerned about the long-term horizon. If that were to happen, how would we deal with a Labor government where its MPs are based in seats that don’t represent our members and the people we seek to represent?

“How would we influence that Labor Party to do right by working people when they don’t have MPs in parliament from those communities?”

Key too for the Minns government is distancing itself from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose growing unpopularity weighs heavily on the party. “He’s toxic,” a Labor MP in an at-risk seat speaking on the condition of anonymity to speak openly said. “As soon as people on the doors find out I’m Labor, they launch into a rant about Albo.”

The NSW party is doing everything possible to distance itself. Campaign corflutes and material contain very little Labor branding, instead promoting candidates as part of “Chris Minns’ NSW team”.

“There is a lot of disgruntlement with the federal space,” McInerney says. “It’s just, you know, it’s a sense that things are not going as well for people.”

On the other side, the Liberals know their only prospect of forming government is likely to involve some form of supply agreement with One Nation. “It would be a deal with the devil,” one Liberal MP says, “but it’s a deal we’d probably have to take.”

The nervousness among Liberals is exacerbated by the uncertainty surrounding their junior Coalition partner. The Nationals face the full spectrum of possibilities, from total wipeout to potentially holding most of their seats.

While a Nationals MP puts the likely losses at two or three of Upper Hunter, Tamworth and Myall Lakes, others believe the only seats that will survive will be Cootamundra and Northern Tablelands.

While Clarence MP Richie Williamson acknowledges the idea of a safe seat no longer exists, he believes the party is in good shape ahead of the election. “If anyone writes the Nats off, they’re a fool,” he says.

A similar dynamic to Epping is at play in Hornsby, though with a slightly different tilt. After the announcement that Nathan Tilbury, a former Liberal councillor who quit the party in 2024, would run as an independent, a Coalition frontbencher texted this masthead: “This has now become a seat in play, unfortunately.”

For the Liberals, losing blue-blooded Hornsby would be gut-wrenching. Both because it is an electorate they’ve held since its reincarnation in 1999, but also because it would end the nascent career of Wallace, a former lawyer widely tipped as a future minister.

Like Tudehope, Wallace hopes he can convince voters to stick with the mainstream in the face of a global shift towards short-termism and easy solutions. “The approach is to be extraordinarily honest with people about what the problem is, the complications of that problem, and then to demonstrate what the pathway forward is,” he says in his parliamentary office.

Here’s a different scenario, though, one that keeps Minns up at night. The ALP is decimated in the Hunter, South Coast and south-west Sydney, but fails to pick up enough seats to offset its losses. In that case, Labor is left governing deep in minority and reliant on the support of the growing crossbench and Greens.

State political editor

Or, the party is foisted out of office and whoever finishes with more seats out of the Coalition and One Nation forms government with a supply deal from the other.

To blunt the One Nation protest vote, Labor officials have rammed home the importance of pointing to tangible achievements, holding a series of workshops with rank-and-file members and MPs to brief them on the party’s strategy.

As the MP for Swansea since 2015, Catley believes she has the track record to convince voters to stick with her, and despite holding a senior ministry, is homing in on local achievements as the election draws close. “That’s building and developing trust with the people that have voted you in,” she says.

For newer MPs, such as Sally Quinnell in Camden, Karen McKeown in Penrith, or McInerney in Kiama, that is a tougher challenge. McInerney draws optimism from the “green shoots” coming from the government’s investment in local infrastructure such as new roads and housing. But, she concedes, the hurdle is communicating that.

“Things take time to build,” she says. “It takes time to build a school. It takes time to build a road.”

Eight ways Labor has changed the face of Victoria in 12 years

Sydney Morning Herald November 28, 2026

For 12 years, Victorians trusted Labor to teach their children, care for their sick, manage their money, keep the lights on and ensure their safety.

Three times, voters gave Labor a mandate to make major changes to the state. On Saturday, if the polls are correct, those same voters will send a message to the state government that at some point things went awry.

This is how Labor has changed Victoria – for better and for worse – under the leadership of Daniel Andrews, Jacinta Allan and Ben Carroll.

When Labor came to power in 2014, Victoria’s net debt was $22.3 billion. The government’s latest financial update projects it will reach $172.5 billion by mid-2027, and $196 billion by the end of the decade. The debt-to-GSP ratio was 5.6 per cent when the Andrews government was elected – now, it’s 24 per cent.

This rapid increase in borrowing has pushed Victoria’s interest bill this year to $8.85 billion, according to the May budget, equating to about $1 million an hour. This is more than what the state spends annually on police, public transport or ambulance services.

Expenditure rocketed during COVID-19 to fund stimulus packages and welfare payments, but Labor has continued to spend intensely following the pandemic, especially on infrastructure.

Economists have warned the government can only start to reduce debt when it delivers a net surplus, which there has not been in Victoria since 2008-9.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said Victoria had grown too reliant on population growth to boost the economy.

“And that in turn has meant that to a greater extent than in the rest of Australia, Victoria’s economy has come to depend on intrinsically low productivity industries, while intrinsically high productivity industries have declined by more as a share of Victoria’s economy than that of any other state,” Eslake said.

During its 12 years in power, Labor has battled a roller-coaster crime rate, which hit a record high last year as the party’s primary vote began to evaporate.

In June 2015, the rate of criminal incidents per 100,000 people was 5750. It plunged during the pandemic lockdowns, hit a peak of 6716 in 2025, and then fell to 6310 this year.

The rise has been driven by retail and car theft, as well as increases in assault and aggravated burglaries. High-profile violent crimes, especially those carried out by young offenders, put Labor under pressure to change course multiple times on law and order, abandoning progressive reforms to the age of criminal responsibility and introducing its blunt “adult time for violent crime” laws.

Labor came to power promising to address family violence, and immediately called a nation-leading royal commission. It made 227 recommendations and resulted in huge investments in the area. However, family violence assaults rose steadily after the inquiry and peaked in the pandemic, though police note these offences were previously underreported due to stigma.

Family violence experts said that while the royal commission was momentous, domestic violence was getting worse in Victoria, underscored by falling investment and overwhelming demand for services.

Polling shows crime and policing were among voters’ top concerns in the run-up to the election, and both parties have brandished their tough-on-crime credentials.

Labor invested billions in public health and built a dozen hospitals across the state. Throughout the campaign, Carroll leant heavily on Labor’s record on health, and attacked the Coalition on the issue, claiming Opposition Leader Jess Wilson would “Americanise” the system.

But Labor has also struggled to address some major public health issues during its rule.

Ambulances have not once hit their 15-minute response time benchmark under Labor, with standards falling since the pandemic. Waiting lists for elective surgery have climbed, and emergency departments have struggled under the weight of rising demand.

Simon Judkins, Victorian president of the Australian Medical Association, said a major failure had been on mental healthcare.

As part of Labor’s 2018 re-election campaign, Andrews promised a royal commission on Victoria’s mental health system, which made 74 recommendations, including establishing community mental health services.

Early action was encouraging and reforming the system became a priority of the government, including creating a specialist tax designed to significantly boost mental health funding.

But the promised funding hasn’t been delivered, progress has stalled, mental health patients are languishing in emergency departments due to a lack of specialist beds, and workers face high rates of abuse.

Judkins said there was “significant lag time” acting on the recommendations from the royal commission, which made it challenging for mental healthcare workers and for staff in emergency departments. More funding was needed at a community level and also to staff more inpatient hospital beds, he said.

“I think we’ve never had significant change there,” he said. “So I think that’s been ... for me, one of the standout things.”

And of course, Labor was in charge during the COVID-19 pandemic. Andrews initially won plaudits for his efforts to keep the virus at bay, only for the government’s lengthy lockdowns to become a source of controversy, along with the problem-plagued hotel quarantine system.

The $100 billion Big Build will define much of Labor’s success – and its likely downfall. Andrews won elections promising major transport infrastructure works, and hard hats and high-vis became a natural look for the premier and his ministers.

More than 130 projects have been completed, notably including the city-shaping Metro Tunnel and West Gate Tunnel, as well as 96 level crossing removals. The North East Link is due to open in 2028, while construction is under way on the controversial Suburban Rail Loop, although its future is under a cloud as the Coalition is promising to pause and review the project.

The major projects and infrastructure boom has been marred by cost blowouts and corruption scandals.

Revelations in this masthead of serious misconduct and the infiltration of criminals on the Big Build became a major political problem for Allan, and ultimately led to Carroll calling a royal commission. Its public hearings began in September, with explosive evidence already aired.

3:30

How Melbourne got its Metro Tunnel

After eight years and a total cost of $15 billion, the Metro Tunnel is opening. Find out all you need to know about the tunnel and how we got here.

Data from the Commonwealth Grants Commission also reveals Victoria’s infrastructure has come at a premium. The state has paid 10 per cent more than others in Australia to provide an average level of infrastructure.

Economists have urged the next Victorian government to slash infrastructure spending to regain control of the budget.

Labor supercharged the energy transition in Victoria, legislating ambitious renewable energy targets of 65 per cent of the state’s power generation by 2030, and 95 per cent by 2035. Labor set a target to reach net zero by 2045.

The government has subsidised rooftop solar and banned gas connections in new home builds, and has negotiated the closure of all the state’s remaining coal-fired power stations by 2038.

In 2021, Labor lifted a moratorium on onshore drilling for gas. It has approved significant offshore gas exploration to act as insurance against any future energy shortfalls.

Analysis by Rystad Energy recently rated Victoria as having the cheapest wholesale power among economically developed countries.

But the state’s offshore wind projects, a key plank in the government’s plan to offset the loss of coal-fired power, are behind schedule, and the auditor-general has warned of further delays.

Community backlash over controversial transmission lines, in particular VNI West and the Western Renewables Link, has stalled progress on the energy transition. Gas reserves are declining rapidly in the Bass Strait and greater reliance on the fossil fuel would stretch supplies.

Grattan Institute climate and energy program director Alison Reeve said Labor’s plan to transition from gas was nation-leading, but the government had failed to address emerging gaps in gas supply and continued demand for the fossil fuel from Victorians.

Reeve said Labor had done well to get more renewables into the system but hadn’t thought through what “firming” – on-demand energy generation for when renewable output is low – was needed to supplement it.

“It was not really that well co-ordinated with having to get more batteries, potentially more gas generators, and also ... how that was going to sequence with the closure of the coal-fired power stations,” Reeve said.

“Because the two big problems that are sitting there for whoever gets in on Saturday are: how do you deal with the looming gas supply crunch? And how do you deal with Yallourn closing?”

Under Labor, Victoria has consistently built more homes than any other state every year.

It’s become a beacon of relative housing affordability: Melbourne’s median house price is cheaper than all other Australian capitals, bar Hobart and Darwin, and the city also has some of the nation’s cheapest rent.

Labor introduced a townhouse and low-rise code which fast-tracked new housing in established suburbs by limiting the rights of neighbours to appeal against developments.

It also instituted the controversial activity centres – 60 rezoned areas in metropolitan suburbs that allow for towers up to 20 storeys. This scheme has faced a backlash from local councils and some communities, who worry that high-rise developments will destroy neighbourhood character.

During the 2014 election campaign, Andrews said that new number plates would read “The Education State”. Labor’s first budget after its victory was spruiked as “the biggest education budget in history”.

Throughout Labor’s 12-year rule, Victoria has consistently led other states in NAPLAN results.

Labor introduced free kinder to the regions in 2020, and provided it statewide for three- and four-year-olds from 2023. In 2019, the government established Free TAFE, which has educated more than 230,000 students across 80 courses. Since 2017, the government has built 121 new schools.

Last month, the state government signed an agreement with the Commonwealth to fully fund public schools by 2031 by meeting the minimum standard set by the Gonski review. But in 2025, Labor secretly delayed its promise to meet the standard, denying public schools $2.4 billion in funding.

Long viewed as the nation’s most progressive state, Victoria has seen major social policy changes under Labor.

4:54

What is Victoria’s treaty with First Nations people?

Victoria is the first state in Australia to legislate a treaty with Indigenous people. We explain how we got here and what the treaty will mean in practice.

In November 2017, the parliament passed assisted dying laws, becoming the first state to do so. And when it became clear, eight years later, that the laws were too narrow, amendments passed the upper house to allow more people access.

Labor also introduced pill testing, allowing Victorians to test drugs to detect harm. In its first year, the program tested more than 5000 samples and detected an unexpected psychoactive substance in 12 per cent.

After more than a decade of work, the government signed Australia’s first treaty with its First Peoples. It established Gellung Warl, a body to advise parliament and represent Indigenous Victorians, embed truth-telling bodies to monitor government, and set out formal engagement between First Peoples and state bodies.

Wilson has pledged to scrap the treaty within 100 days, though that may prove practically fraught.

The Coalition will also close Victoria’s only safe-injecting room, which was opened by Labor and has reduced overdose deaths. The room has faced a backlash from nearby residents and traders in North Richmond.

Inside ‘Rinehartworld’: Buckle up. We’re going in

Sydney Morning Herald November 28, 2026

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart is increasingly using her outsize influence to push her political views. And Australia’s richest person is used to getting her way.
