Gina Rinehart is wearing a cowboy hat, which adds to her natural air of authority. From the stage, she looks out at the politicians, businesspeople and community leaders who have gathered for a conference on North Queensland’s economic future. “Can you all sound like bulldozers, please?” she asks. Her tone is pleasant but firm. By way of encouragement, she demonstrates an engine-like growl: “Grrrrrrr.”

Uncertain laughter in the audience. She doesn’t really expect them to …? “Come on,” says Rinehart, a little more edge in her voice. “I want some bulldozer noise.”

As I sit at my desk watching a video of the event, which was held in Townsville mid-year, I remember the first rule of engagement with Rinehart: what Gina wants, Gina gets. Sure enough, after the briefest hesitation, the crowd growls: “Grrrrr.” The mining magnate’s face lights up. “Beautiful,” she says.

Rinehart asks One Nation leader Pauline Hanson to join her on stage, then reminds everyone that US President Donald Trump appointed billionaire Elon Musk to dismantle federal agencies and slash government spending. Musk brandished a chainsaw to signal his enthusiasm for the task. In Australia, heavier machinery than a chainsaw is required, Rinehart says. “We actually need a beautiful, big, fat… Where is it?”

A neatly dressed young man carrying a toy bulldozer appears. He presents it to Hanson, who laughs. She has the look of a person who isn’t entirely sure what’s going on but has decided it’s safest to play along. Rinehart beams under the cowboy hat. “I don’t hear that noise,” she says into the microphone. “Let’s hear a bit more. Grrrrr!”

Rinehart is Australia’s wealthiest citizen. In the 2026 edition of the annual Rich List published by The Australian Financial Review, her fortune was estimated at $39 billion – up from $10.4 billion in 2017. If those numbers are correct, her personal net worth rose by $28.6 billion in nine years. That means she grew richer by an average of $61 million a week. Or almost $9 million a day.

What does it do to an individual to have so much money? That is one of the questions I ponder as I wait to hear if Rinehart will agree to be interviewed for a profile piece. Another question: how does her outsize spending power affect the rest of us?

Recent news reports have focused on her support for One Nation, the right-wing populist party that has moved from the fringe to the mainstream of Australian politics. At the federal election in May 2025, One Nation got just 6 per cent of the vote. In a Resolve Political Monitor survey this month, its support had surged to 25 per cent, not far behind Labor on 28 per cent and ahead of the Liberal-National Coalition on 22 per cent. It did even better in a November poll by RedBridge Group and Accent Research, winning more support (28 per cent) than any other party.

In covertly recorded conversations recently reported by The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, former One Nation campaign manager Sean Black warned that Rinehart had so much influence over the party and its chief strategist, James Ashby, that she effectively dictated policies. “James’ view on policy is that the policy comes from Gina or Gina’s acolytes, and that is it,” Black said. Pauline Hanson dismissed the allegation as “absolute garbage”, but Black’s concerns were echoed by another former party staffer, Charles Swindon, who said Hanson and Ashby answered to Rinehart: “Gina tells both of them what to do.”

Closely watching the upheaval in the political landscape is Michael Yabsley, a former federal treasurer of the Liberal Party. Yabsley used to be a close friend of Rinehart. Now he is writing a book, Dark Money, in which he looks at the way the injection of private funds into politics can erode integrity and undermine democracy. “There’s no case study more fascinating than Gina and what she’s up to,” he says. It seems to Yabsley that, when it comes to Rinehart’s relationship with One Nation, “all the signs are there that she’s got pretty much a wholly owned subsidiary.”

This isn’t my first attempt to figure out Gina Rinehart: I profiled her for Good Weekend in 2012. In those days, she was a retiring figure, best known for her propensity to wage bitter legal fights against members of her family – from her father’s widow to her own kids. She refused to talk to me for the story, as did most of her associates I approached for comment. I thought I’d get help from her friend Barnaby Joyce, at that stage a National Party senator, but even the normally loquacious Joyce clammed up. “She’s a person who likes to keep to herself,” he said then. “I don’t think I’ll be saying much more than that, actually.”

Rinehart is still highly litigious – and still locked in a dispute with two of her four children – but in other respects, she has changed. Come out of her shell. At 72, she is comfortable in the spotlight, confident she knows how the country should be run and keen to start whipping the place into shape. She wants less government regulation. She wants lower taxes. She wants fewer immigrants. She wants scientists to stop banging on about climate change. She wants environmentalists who criticise the mining industry to take a leap. At a party thrown by Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, the club he owns in Florida, she wore one of his slogans – “Drill, baby, drill” – on a sign around her neck. There’s a sense that what we’re seeing is Rinehart unleashed. “I think she’s heavily influenced by the whole Trump phenomenon,” says Yabsley. “If he can do quirky things, she can do quirky things.”

But she hasn’t completely thrown caution to the wind. Her media manager, James Radford, emails to say she isn’t available for an interview. “Mrs Rinehart is very busy with a number of business projects at the moment,” Radford writes. “… Feel free to touch base in a few months.” She really is busy, I am assured by Joyce, who is now a One Nation MP and much chattier than last time. Running her business empire is an all-consuming job, he says. “If she’s awake, she’s working. Never stops.”

Rinehart owes her wealth to her iron mines in the Pilbara, a region twice the size of Victoria in the north-west of Western Australia. Her company, the privately owned Hancock Prospecting, reported a net profit of $2.8 billion last financial year, while the value of its assets climbed to $50.3 billion, up from $44 billion the previous year. Digging up and exporting iron ore is immensely lucrative but in the interest of diversification, and because she has cash to burn, Rinehart has invested in a range of companies that extract other valuable commodities from the ground. Rare earths, lithium, copper, gold, gas, oil. She is one of Australia’s leading beef producers, too. And a dairy farmer. And a clothing manufacturer (Driza-Bone coats, Rossi boots, S. Kidman apparel). “People want successful women,” says Joyce. “Well, you can’t get a more successful one than Gina Rinehart.”

As part of Elon Musk’s effort to downsize the US government, he chainsawed the US Agency for International Development, which had delivered the country’s foreign aid and humanitarian assistance. Researchers have calculated that defunding the agency has resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths. “The world’s richest man killing the world’s poorest children,” is how tech billionaire Bill Gates summed it up. Nevertheless, when Rinehart snapped up a $1.4 billion stake in Musk’s aerospace manufacturing company SpaceX in June, she called him “a truly exceptional person”.

In the video of Rinehart’s Townsville speech – which she delivered a week after buying into SpaceX – she points to a screen showing a section of the Queensland coast. Musk needs more land to build and launch satellites, she says brightly. We should offer him some Australian islands. Free of charge. Specifically, she suggests we offer “the sparsely or non-populated islands on the screen … where there aren’t high-end tourist facilities”.

I press pause and zoom in on the map. The marked islands form a chain from Orpheus Island in the north to Magnetic Island in the south. All lie within the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park. One of them, Palm Island, is home to more than 2000 Indigenous Australians.

Readers might ask: in what world does it make sense to hand part of Australia – populated or otherwise, in a marine park or not – to Elon Musk?

In Rinehartworld, evidently. Buckle up. We’re going in.

The refined accent, the genteel manner, the pearls. If you didn’t know Rinehart was a plutocrat, you could mistake her for the headmistress of a posh girls’ school – especially when she’s telling us to pull up our socks and work harder if we want to make something of ourselves. “There is no monopoly on becoming a millionaire,” she once wrote in Australian Resources & Investment magazine. “If you’re jealous of those with more money, don’t just sit there and complain; do something to make more money yourself –spend less time drinking or smoking and socialising, and more time working.”

To Michael Yabsley, who, at intervals during their 20-year friendship, was on Rinehart’s payroll as an adviser and lobbyist, there’s a familiar ring to the suggestion that if you’re not rich, you’re probably a slacker. “She would say of just about anyone, ‘Oh, they’re lazy,’” he says. When Pauline Hanson claimed in an address to the National Press Club earlier this year that industrial relations laws prevented bosses from sacking employees who “don’t work, they don’t turn up; they actually are lazy”, Yabsley suspected he knew who had been in her ear.

The princess of the Pilbara, Rinehart was sometimes called in her youth. Born in 1954, she was the only child of Lang Hancock, a pastoralist turned prospector credited with discovering enormous iron ore deposits in the rugged West Australian outback. In Man of Iron, a 1966 BBC TV documentary about Hancock, Rinehart was portrayed as an adored little rich girl who rode horses across her family’s vast landholdings. “Her parents give her everything she wants,” said the principal of St Hilda’s, her Perth boarding school. Journalist Adele Ferguson reported in her 2012 biography of Rinehart that Hancock brought 10 new cars to the school grounds in his daughter’s final year and invited her to choose one. She picked a Volvo. Yabsley tells me that getting to know Rinehart when he was a young man was an eye-opening introduction to a world of great wealth: “There were mansions and Learjets and all of that.”

When Hancock died in 1992, the 38-year-old Rinehart inherited his company, Hancock Prospecting. That year, in the Rich 200 list published by BRW magazine, her wealth was estimated at $75 million. Nevertheless, James Radford and her media team insist it is wrong to refer to her as an heiress. They say the company was in trouble when she took it over, and she built it into the huge enterprise it is now. Pauline Hanson has gone so far as to claim that Rinehart “started from virtually nothing to become the wealthy individual she is today”. The way Hanson tells it, Rinehart deserves not only our esteem but possibly our sympathy: “She’s a woman that’s done it tough.”

Millionaire. Billionaire. They’re such similar words that it’s easy to forget the big difference in their meaning. Fourteen years ago, when Rinehart was already the richest person in the country, federal Labor MP Andrew Leigh gave a speech at the Sydney Institute in which he tried to explain just how rich she was. Leigh, who was a professor of economics at the Australian National University before entering politics, asked his audience to picture a ladder on which each rung represented a million dollars of wealth. “Now imagine the Australian population spread out along this ladder,” he said, “with their distance from the ground reflecting their household wealth.” According to Leigh, the typical household would have been about halfway to the first rung. Most people in the richest 10 per cent of the population would be clustered between the first and second rungs. “Someone in the top one per cent is at least five rungs up,” he said. “Gina Rinehart is five-and-a-half kilometres off the ground.”

Since then, of course, Rinehart’s net worth has soared. Leigh, who is now assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and Treasury, has tracked her ascent from merely stonkingly rich to stratospherically so. In his 2024 book Battlers & Billionaires: The Updated Story of Inequality in Australia, he invites readers to envisage a parade of Australians in which each person’s height indicates his or her wealth. Average wealth is represented by a person of average stature, he writes. Gina Rinehart? “She is over 46 kilometres tall.”

The stories about Rinehart calling the shots at One Nation don’t surprise Michael Yabsley. As far as he can see, she’s called the shots all her life. “Is she a control freak? Absolutely,” he says. As a young woman, Rinehart could be terrific company at dinners with friends, according to Yabsley, but her intolerance of views that differed from her own meant there was an ever-present threat of her mood turning frosty and the evening ending badly. “It was always pretty tense.” A current business acquaintance of Rinehart says dissenting opinions still aren’t welcome at her table. “I’ve known her a long time and I’ve never heard her raise her voice,” he says. But Rinehart knows how to make her displeasure known: “The quiet treatment. If you’re sitting at a lunch with her and she doesn’t agree with what you said, she just goes quiet.”

Yabsley says the young Rinehart seemed to operate on the assumption that everyone was out to take advantage of her wealth. If she sensed that her dining companions expected her to pick up the bill in a restaurant, she bristled. Even if she had coffee with someone, she wanted the tab to be evenly divided. “‘Stingy’ is not a bad way of putting it,” Yabsley says. “Stingy down to the last 50 cents.”

When it comes to One Nation, though, Rinehart is Lady Bountiful. She is reported to have encouraged the party to hold fundraisers in her grand houses and her apartment on the luxury cruise ship The World. To help Pauline Hanson travel around regional Australia, one of Rinehart’s companies gave the party an aircraft – a Cirrus G7, valued at about $1.5 million. On her own plane, a Gulfstream G700, she took Hanson to stay at her Palm Beach, Florida, house, near Mar-a-Lago. She has also inspired those in her circle to dig deep. Stockbroker Angus Aitken and his wife Sarah have given $1 million. Two of Rinehart’s employees – climate-change denialist Ian Plimer, who is executive director of Hancock Energy, and former Northern Territory chief minister Adam Giles, who is chief executive of Hancock Agriculture – have kicked in $500,000 each.

“Just so you know, I’m not a sycophant,” says Barnaby Joyce, who, like Hanson, has frequently been photographed wearing Rinehart-owned clothing brands. “I’m good mates with her, right?” he says of One Nation’s benefactor-in-chief. But that doesn’t mean he has lost his independence: “I never stay so close to her orbit that I don’t have my own agency.”

He and Rinehart have disagreements, he adds with a hint of pride. “Hell, yes. We stop talking to each other for a while and then we start talking again.” He reckons Rinehart wouldn’t want him to be a pushover. “Gina likes strong personalities. If you don’t have the capacity to stand behind an opinion and fight for it, she won’t have much time for you.”

Besides taking a lively interest in politics, Rinehart is a major backer of Olympic sports – she supports swimming, artistic swimming and rowing in particular. For a decade she also sponsored Volleyball Australia, whose ex-president Craig Carracher says she wanted evidence that Hancock Prospecting signage was prominently displayed at matches. “She’d insist on me sending her photos of the umbrellas. I thought, ‘Good on her. She’s spending a lot of money. She’s certainly entitled to that.’”

Rinehart also expected results. To the players, she was unfailingly encouraging, Carracher says, but she didn’t spare the feelings of coaches and administrators if she felt a team’s performance had fallen short. He remembers her exasperation after she watched the Australian men’s team lose to the world champions, Brazil. “At the end of the match, she said, ‘Your players need to learn the very basics of the game. It’s like tennis, right? Except you don’t get a second serve! The only way to win is to get the ball in. You need to teach your players to serve in.”

He realises that Rinehart isn’t everyone’s cup of tea. “She can be dismissive. I understand why others would think she’s aloof.” But Carracher got along well with her, despite their political differences. “I think I was Gina’s little lefty mate.”

It’s interesting that he calls her Gina, I say. I’ve been struck during my research by the number of grown men and women who refer to her as “Mrs Rinehart”. Carracher replies that he, too, usually addressed her that way. Now that he thinks about it, he’d like his quotes in the story to be altered to reflect that. “I would want it to be ‘Mrs Rinehart’ for every reference to her.” A moment later, he relents. The quotes can stay as they are. “I guess everyone knows who ‘Gina’ is. There’s only one Gina, right?”

Her surname comes from her second husband, Frank Rinehart, an American lawyer who was almost four decades her senior. They married in Las Vegas in 1983, just before the death of Gina’s mother and the arrival in her father’s life of Rose Lacson, a glamorous young woman from the Philippines who answered his advertisement for a housekeeper. Lang Hancock immediately fell for Lacson, and Gina almost as swiftly decided she was a gold-digger.

Father and daughter, previously extremely close, had a terrible falling-out. In a vitriolic letter to Gina that surfaced in one of the court cases after Hancock’s death, he taunted her about the kilos she had gained, saying he was glad her mother could not see “the slothful, vindictive and devious baby elephant that you have become”.

By 1990, when Frank Rinehart died of a heart attack, leaving Gina a widow at 36, a truce had been called. That year, oral historian Stuart Reid was commissioned by the National Library of Australia to conduct a series of interviews with 81-year-old Hancock. Reid says he also got to know Gina, and was impressed by the strength of the bond between the two: “It was like a mutual admiration society. They saw one another as superior human beings.”

Hancock was a notorious racist who advocated sterilising Aboriginal people by putting chemicals into their drinking water – so they would “breed themselves out”. In the interviews with Reid, he was also callous about the plight of people who developed cancer after working in the blue asbestos mine he established at Wittenoom in the Pilbara, insinuating that they were somehow themselves to blame. Reid says Rinehart seemed unruffled by all this when she went through the transcript. “She said, ‘Reading it was like hearing my father speak. It was wonderful.’”

In massively increasing her wealth and forcefully pushing her political views, Rinehart is following an international trend. “Billionaires globally have got much richer and much louder,” says Queensland University economics professor John Quiggin.

The problem, as Quiggin sees it, is that a talent for making money doesn’t necessarily translate to cleverness at formulating public policy. Rinehart wants lower taxes, smaller budget deficits and more defence spending. How does she intend to cover the cost, Quiggin asks. Calling for the elimination of unspecified waste does not seem to him to be a serious answer. He suspects Rinehart has few people around her who are prepared to challenge her assertions: “Most of the time, anything she says is going to be greeted with approval.”

Clay Cockrell, a New York psychotherapist who specialises in treating the ultra-rich, says that’s the problem with billionaires: “They surround themselves with a lot of yes men who are not going to question them. It can lead to a very skewed world view.”

Since Rinehart won’t be interviewed, I ask James Radford to suggest people who might be willing to talk about her. I’m hoping for some names and numbers. Instead, glowing testimonials start landing in my inbox. An array of upstanding Australians, from former governor-general Peter Cosgrove and ballet star Li Cunxin to Olympic swimmer Lani Pallister, send carefully composed emails outlining Rinehart’s sterling qualities. Her acumen, her grit, her patriotism, her munificence. “Gina represents the most significant example of what can be achieved in this country,” writes pearling company chairman Nick Paspaley.

I contact David Larkin, a former chief executive of Hancock Prospecting’s agriculture division, who seizes the opportunity to sing his ex-boss’s praises. “I loved my time working with Mrs Rinehart,” Larkin says. “I think she’s a truly great Australian.”

I ask Tony Seabrook, immediate past president of the West Australian Pastoralists and Graziers Association, if Rinehart is fun. A long pause. “She’s very focused,” Seabrook says. “Whether she’s doing a deal with a big mining operation or she’s trying to work out the colour of the napkins on the table for an upcoming dinner, she is all over everything in that business. Her attention to detail is just absolutely staggering.” Another pause. “She can be fun. Don’t worry about that.”

What baffles Seabrook is the apparent coolness towards Rinehart in the general population. “You don’t hear a lot of positive stuff,” he says. “So many people seem to want to attack this remarkable lady.”

Perhaps it’s the headmistress vibe. Besides tut-tutting about our drinking and socialising, Rinehart once made Australians feel a bit guilty about insisting on decent salaries. In a speech to the Sydney Mining Club, she pointed out that Africans were willing to work for less than two dollars a day. High wages in Australia made it very expensive to operate mines here, she said. The irony is that workers at Rinehart’s mines are well compensated, says Australian Workers Union national mining organiser Shane Roulstone. “She’s the best payer in the Pilbara. Doesn’t practise what she preaches.”

Glimpses of life inside Hancock Prospecting give the impression of a corporate culture centred on cult-like reverence for executive chairman Rinehart. In a video of the 2024 Christmas party, the company choir performs a song called Drill Baby Drill while Rinehart, wearing a dainty set of reindeer antlers, bops along. To our dear Chairman, we give our thanks, the choir sings, For leading us forward through all the ranks. Your wisdom and strength light up our way, we honour you greatly on this special day. As is company tradition, the event concludes with a raffle in which randomly selected employees receive $100,000 bonuses. “Make Australia great again!” cries one of the lucky winners.

Is Rinehart Fever catching? Before I know it, I’m buying a copy of Gina Rinehart: From Red Tape to Red Carpet and Then Some, a self-published collection of her speeches, musings and poetry. Among the poems is a tribute to her friend Nick Paspaley, which includes the lines: Each Paspaley Boutique opening is an event that’s mighty fine. If your city lacks an outlet, then invest in pearls online. The book includes a long list of awards Rinehart has won, and is illustrated with 53 photographs of Rinehart.

Browsing through the images, I am reminded that in 2024, Rinehart wrote to Ryan Stokes, chairman of the National Gallery of Australia, asking him to “permanently dispose” of two portraits of her by Vincent Namatjira, the Archibald Prize-winning Indigenous artist known for his sardonic depictions of the powerful. Swimming Queensland chief executive Kevin Hasemann also wrote to the gallery, saying members of the Australian swim team were deeply concerned about the portraits because “they are offensive to Mrs Rinehart”. On that occasion, Rinehart’s will did not prevail. The pictures stayed on the wall and, after news broke of her attempt at censorship, everyone wanted to see them. The gallery reported a surge in visitor numbers.

Rinehart doesn’t care about popularity, says Barnaby Joyce. “She’s tough.” But respect is a different matter: “She demands respect.” And Joyce believes that she has earned it. “Respect for the fact that she has made Australia a better place,” he says. “Remember, Gina is the biggest individual taxpayer. By miles.”

Hancock Prospecting reports that it paid $2.3 billion in federal and state taxes last financial year. That’s a lot, but it would have been more if Rinehart hadn’t helped kill the Resources Super Profits Tax, designed to spread the benefits of Australia’s resources boom. Sixteen years ago, in her first foray into political activism, she joined fellow iron ore billionaire Andrew Forrest in leading a chant of “Axe the Tax” at a rally in Perth. Two weeks later, members of the federal Labor government ousted prime minister Kevin Rudd, the chief proponent of the proposed tax. His replacement, Julia Gillard, introduced a watered-down alternative. Ebony Bennett, deputy director of The Australia Institute, says economists at the think-tank calculate that the miners’ victory has cost the Australian people more than $100 billion to date.

Joyce is often asked by individuals and organisations hoping for financial assistance from Rinehart if he would approach her on their behalf. “I get sick of people believing that I’m the emissary to get money from Gina,” he says. “Drives me crazy.” His discomfort is due partly to his understanding of Rinehart’s attitude to such requests. “One thing she has in common with other people who are very wealthy – they hate being treated as an easy grab for money. They don’t like people thinking they’re just an ATM. They say, ‘Why don’t you go out and make your own money instead of asking for mine?’ ”

Unsolicited, James Radford sends me screeds of information about Rinehart’s philanthropic endeavours – everything from this year’s commitment to spend $200 million on accommodation for homeless military veterans to donations she has made to a cat shelter in Perth. “Philanthropy is a way of making billionaires look good,” says Carl Rhodes, professor of business and society at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) and author of the 2025 book Stinking Rich: The Four Myths of the Good Billionaire. Rhodes argues that polishing the image of the ultra-rich is especially important in an era when they make themselves so visible. “There was a time when wealthy people tried to keep a low profile so no one would be chasing them with pitchforks,” he says. Now billionaires like Rinehart are unabashedly pushing their own interests, arguing that what’s good for them is good for everyone – “the idea that you have to unleash the animal spirits of entrepreneurship in order to have economic growth”.

It seems to Rhodes that some weird alliances have been struck. “You have billionaires supporting populist politicians on the far right who claim to be speaking for the people against the elites,” he says. “You’d think this would immediately make no sense, right? I mean, it’s so illogical. But this is what’s happened.”

Unlike Andrew Forrest, fellow opponent of the super profits tax, Rinehart has never appeared on the annual list of the nation’s top philanthropists published by The Australian Financial Review Magazine. Stockbroker Angus Aitken says her benevolence is underestimated because she keeps quiet about it: “She gives an absolute shitload.” Michael Yabsley isn’t convinced. “Measured against her capacity to give, her contributions are relatively modest,” he says. “In some cases, they are also conditional.”

The limits to Rinehart’s generosity were widely discussed in 2022, when she withdrew $15 million in funding she had given to Netball Australia. The national team’s Indigenous goal-shooter, Donnell Wallam, had expressed reservations about wearing the Hancock Prospecting logo on her uniform, given Lang Hancock’s genocidal impulses. Wallam eventually bowed to pressure and agreed to wear the logo, but it was too late. Rinehart cancelled the funding and ignored calls to disavow her father’s comments.

The disappointment of the netballers echoed the letdown in Darwin after Rinehart failed to deliver on her promise in 2015 to make “the largest charitable donation in Australian history – to build a specialised cancer hospital for the people of the Northern Territory”. According to the speaker of the NT Legislative Assembly, Robyn Lambley, who was then health minister in the Country Liberal Party government led by Rinehart’s friend, Adam Giles, excitement was such when the project was on the table that Rinehart was received in Darwin like a visiting head of state. Lambley says she was reminded of an earlier visit by then-US president Barack Obama: “Her entourage was bigger than Obama’s.” After Labor won government in the Territory in 2016, Giles told the NT News the hospital would not be going ahead. “She was doing it because of me,” he was quoted as saying.

Paul McCann, who was Rinehart’s long-term lawyer, remembers being charmed by her when he met her almost 30 years ago. “She was warm and engaging,” he says. McCann is still impressed by Rinehart’s drive and business savvy but admits that, at times, she was a testing client. For a start, she was inclined to believe that she knew best, and to reject advice that didn’t chime with her thinking. “She goes into a meeting knowing precisely what outcome she wants,” he says, “and there’s no dissuading her from that course. It was her way or the highway.”

McCann wasn’t on Rinehart’s staff. He acted for her on retainer. Yet he says she called and emailed him at all hours of the day and night, and expected him to drop everything when she snapped her fingers. One year, he says, she wanted him to spend Christmas with her on the island of St Barts, in the Caribbean. She said his wife could come, but would need to bring a lot of books because he would be working the whole time. McCann declined the invitation. “I said, ‘We want to be with our family at Christmas.’” He suspects Rinehart sometimes has difficulty reading people and situations.

Her estranged son, John Hancock, believes Rinehart is driven by a desire for control – and not just over those in her immediate sphere of influence. “She would like to have some control over everyone’s destiny,” Hancock said on Gina, a podcast series released last year by Guardian Australia journalist Sarah Martin. He described his mother as indifferent to the impact of her actions on others: “She probably would have been a great soldier or something. Whatever is in her way is just obliterated without further thought.”

Elon Musk made an announcement last year. “The fundamental weakness of Western civilisation is empathy,” he said. If psychotherapist Clay Cockrell’s hunch is correct, Musk needn’t worry about being overloaded with the stuff himself. “What I’ve seen is, as your wealth increases, your empathy towards your fellow man decreases,” says Cockrell. “There’s some research to back that up.”

Many of the ultra-rich people on Cockrell’s client list have a sense of superiority. Whether they inherited their money or made it themselves, they tend to be wholly convinced that they deserve it. “‘There’s something about me that is special,’” says Cockrell, summing up their attitude. A certain detachment from reality can be heightened by actual separation from the mass of humanity, he adds. “There is an incredible amount of isolation among this population.”

Captains of industry don’t catch public transport. They don’t stand in supermarket queues. They don’t have friends who say, ‘For god’s sake, don’t publish that poem.’” The people around them are more likely to implore them to write another verse. “‘Everyone listens to me,’” says Cockrell, channelling a billionaire. “‘Everybody obeys me. I have unique knowledge and experience.’”

As he is talking, my mind drifts back to the image of Rinehart in the cowboy hat, instructing a room full of grown-ups to make bulldozer noises. Grrrrr.

Why have things started to go wrong for Manchester City under Enzo Maresca?

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 20:00:19 GMT

A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team

This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling. Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory (3-2 over Ipswich, six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. City have appealed against the ruling, saying they are “innocent of the accusations”.

Nico O’Reilly’s stop-start season (four matches missed and three very short substitute appearances) has been a definite minus for the Maresca project because here is a muscular defender who offers pace, guile via a schemer’s ability to wander infield and unpick defences (he was a No 10 as a youth) and a goal threat. City conceded two in the first half without him in their 3-1 defeat at Nottingham Forest, before he came on. As a unit the defence is vulnerable, with Rúben Dias’s lack of pace and Marc Guéhi’s erratic displays key in the concerning leaking of goals.

Gianluigi Donnarumma has also been unreliable, with mistakes against Leipzig, Aston Villa and Paris Saint-Germain costing goals and points. The goalkeeper may also feel he should have stopped Rasmus Højlund’s opener in Tuesday’s 2-2 draw with Napoli. “I’m not worried about Gigio’s performance or form, knowing he has made some mistakes,” says Maresca, who has no credible competitor to the No 1 after James Trafford’s sale to Leeds in the last window. This points to a wider worry regarding questionable squad building that might not have occurred if Txiki Begiristain were still City’s director of football. His replacement, Hugo Viana, is not proving as shrewd in the market.

The Portuguese, who worked alongside Begiristain from April 2025, before taking over that summer, has made 18 signings: Enzo Fernández (£125m), Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81.3m), Antoine Semenyo (£62.5m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Tijjani Reijnders (£46.3m), Allan (£32m), Rayan Aït-Nouri (£31m), Rayan Cherki (£30.45m), Trafford (£27m), Donnarumma (£26m), Mathys Detourbet (£21.5m), Guéhi (£20m), Sverre Nypan (£12.5m), Jeremy Monga (£10m), Pierce Charles (£3m), Marcus Bettinelli (£2m), and Gerónimo Rulli (£1m). Before any add-ons, the cost is already more than an eye-watering £700m, yet, to date, only Anderson, Cherki and Ndiaye can be counted as unadulterated successes, with the form of Guéhi, Semenyo and Fernández dipping, and Bouaddi appearing promising. This leaves 10 players who have left, disappointed or must prove their potential, plus a back-up goalkeeper.

Maresca’s engine room has Anderson, a fine player but no Rodri (is anyone?), and Fernández, who is not a No 8, more a quasi-10 without Cherki’s sorcery in the position. Fernández’s role is akin to being Maresca’s on-field enforcer, the Italian having signed him from Chelsea after their time there together. Bouaddi, the main other midfielder, has impressed but is 19 so these are very early days for him, and with O’Reilly an auxiliary option and Mateo Kovacic seemingly in a bit-part role, City’s options hardly bulge. “We are trying different solutions,” Maresca says. “Last game [against Napoli] we started with Enzo, Ayyoub and Elliot. They were quite good, especially off the ball, and no doubt we’re going to find the right balance.”

Is the team totem and goal glutton happy? He was certainly glum post-Napoli, and has been spied gesticulating angrily during games. Maresca says: “Erling is a winner. It’s normal that he’s not happy when he’s not winning games but don’t forget a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch [after the Carabao Cup win against Brighton]. Erling is upset just like I am upset.” The question, though, is more of the existential kind regarding whether the Norwegian may debate a future away from City. Haaland signed a 10-year contract in January 2025 but this will mean zero should he wish to move on. If the appeal is lost and City are demoted a division (or worse), Haaland – and others – will surely depart.

All factors cited have to be nullified/solved by Maresca. Settling on a first XI while addressing a tactical blueprint that has a prevailing sluggishness with the odd flash of directness – Haaland’s winner in September against Coventry, for example, came via a quick Fernández pass to Semenyo, whose cross was converted – would help. We have eight or nine new players, the manager is new – you need time. No panic at all. I understand we need to win games because it is a business.”

Digested week: a new forest is fine – but where’s all the fun?

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 19:54:37 GMT

The noble ambitions of carbon capture should be met with a worthy commitment to the revitalisation of ancient forest law

Happy National Tree Week, y’all! It seems an oddly timed endeavour, the week before large swathes of the populace either drag a plastic one down from the loft or in from outside one brutally cut down in its prime. But mine is not to reason why; mine is to stand in front of the news that we are getting a new forest and say, “Oh man, that’s brilliant, that is.”

Because we are, and it is. The South Downs national park authority says it’s going to fill more than 500 hectares (roughly “a big chunk”) of Hampshire and Sussex with trees over the next six years as part of a carbon-capture programme across southern England. If all goes well and none of the trees unionises and goes on strike, the new woodland will mop up the equivalent of 54,000 petrol cars’ emissions by 2050.

Now, sure – breathable air is a worthy goal and everything, but can’t we have a bit of fun with this too? Channel the spirit of everyone’s favourite conqueror, William, and put a bit of 1066 back into this thing? I want new forest law. Instead of no poaching, no phones or people I hate. Bring back pannage and agistment. Or just the words pannage and agistment. Bring back trespass against the vert and the venison but this time it means the death penalty for littering. South Downs national park authority – call me.

In remarkably unexpected news, it turns out there is something men value more than sexual prowess. In less unexpected news, that something is billions and billions of dollars, especially when it is threatening to go to an ex-wife.

Vladimir Potanin (metals oligarch, second-richest man in Russia and – it possibly hardly needs to be added – a close friend of president Putin) divorced Natalia in 2014. She is seeking more than £2bn of his estimated £30bn fortune, and part of her case hinges on her claim that in the six years prior to their split they were still at it like wolverines.

(There is actually a native Russian bird called the snowcock and I would like praise for not going there.)

Vlad countered by saying that Natalia was “exaggerating my sexual prowess” and that relations had in fact ceased by 2007. The case and hopefully more wholesale deconstruction of masculinity continues.

Look, I understand it was an opportunistic crime and everything but really – if you find yourself breaking into the home of the heir to the throne, into an actual palace (or an actual sturdy Norfolk mansion) owned by an actual prince and princess, you have GOT to do better than nicking a few cufflinks and a … a … [checks notes] clock.

Such are the charges, however, brought against the two men who shinned up a drainpipe one teatime at Anmer Hall, Will and Kate’s country pile, and were caught shortly after they left because when you shin up a drainpipe of Will and Kate’s country pile you set off motion sensors and dogs, drones and a national police air service helicopter emerge from the Sandringham grounds to chase you.

All that for some cufflinks and a clock? Even in a modest 10-bedroom Georgian royal abode, you have to do better. Even in the Norfolk reaches there’s got to be a Fabergé egg or two lying around, hasn’t there? You cannot go from Princess Margaret’s diamond-encrusted cucumber saw (oh, I do miss her estate sale reports) to cufflinks in a mere two generations. It can’t be done. I don’t know if it’s burglars or the royals who need to raise their game here, but someone needs to or else national embarrassment surely beckons.

Let us turn to a story more heartwarming and bolstering to national pride: the tale of Zeus, the four-year-old ginger shorthair (for the uninitiated, this is a cat, not a child on some kind of day release) who hopped on a train from Braintree and took a trip to London – not for the first time.

Zeus – who wears two trackers – usually likes to hang out at his local Co-op but was also keen on travelling from his old home in Stansted Mountfitchet to London Stansted airport. This week he ended up at Liverpool Street station, 37 miles away from his new Essex base.

“I’ve tried to keep him in before and he just does himself damage. He’s constantly trying to break out,” said his owner Lily Burroughs. “He’s quite a social cat. He likes to see everyone, so, yeah, without everyone else sort of looking out for him it would be a world of pain. Braintree to London is definitely the furthest he’s gone, but I think he would probably go further if he had the chance.”

Even in printed form, you can hear the weary resignation in her voice. This is what it is to be a cat owner. Or temporary custodian. Or food dispenser. Or cat-elaine. Whatever we are to them.

But this is England, so – unlike a child on day release, I suspect – Zeus was cared for throughout his journey by charmed and interested fellow passengers and eventually station staff, who then returned him safely to Lily. I only hope that on my next trip on Greater Anglia trains I get to give him my regards too.

Black Friday is here. No, the real thing. I know it’s been going on for two weeks, but this is the actual official day when you can buy all the things you want and a lot of the things you don’t, but they are pretending to be 30% off so you will.

I’ve carefully compiled my usual list after perusing the Christmas gift guides that have been dropping since, roughly, March; the more insane, the better. There’s the £4,000 pair of diamond stud earrings, of course. I chose them from a list that called them “ideal stocking stuffers”, which I presume was written by a sexually unsatisfied Russian wife. A set of cashmere bed socks is a must because imagine wearing merino wool or alpaca bed socks like a peon. A mascara that costs more than gold-plated saffron because absolutely mascara should. And some Charlie Bigham’s fish pies because only at this stage do they start to look like a reasonable choice.

Now all I have to do is find the BF deals that bring them all down to a fiver and I can look forward to a warm, sparkly and king prawn-strewn Christmas! Glad tidings, all.

Graham Thorpe’s widow takes legal action against NHS trust after inquest

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 19:52:30 GMT

Former England Test cricketer was diagnosed with anxiety and depression before he took his own life in 2024

The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care.

Thorpe died aged 55 in August 2024 in Surrey. His wife, Amanda, has lodged a personal injury claim at the high court against Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS foundation trust which was involved in his care, the Telegraph reported.

The former batsman and coach was diagnosed with anxiety and depression and had tried to kill himself in 2022, the inquest at Surrey coroner’s court in Woking heard last year. The inquest found the trust was culpable of “failings” and “shortcomings”.

Thorpe, who played 100 Tests for England, had “spiralled into depression” after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022 at the conclusion of the Ashes series in Australia, the hearing heard.

Surrey coroner’s court was told there had been a gap of more than four months in his being seen by the local NHS trust before his death despite a “crisis” call in June 2024 when he told his care coordinator that he had “given up”. Thorpe was offered a follow-up appointment by the community mental health team but no home visit was made.

Jonathan Stevens, the assistant coroner, said at the inquest: “In my judgment, someone should have been going to see him to properly monitor and assess him, to understand his care needs. Saying ‘come and see me in two weeks’ was not an appropriate response to the crisis.

“I don’t accept that when Graham was constantly asking his wife to help end his life, which was a new presentation that hadn’t been seen before, he was not at that moment in crisis. There were shortcomings in the care that should have been provided to Graham in the last four months of his life. There were failings in the provision of his care.”

Stevens did not conclude those shortcomings were negligent, adding: “I cannot say whether it would have made any difference or not.”

Amanda told the inquest her husband was constantly asking for help to end his life and that he was sure nothing would work. She also told the inquest of Thorpe’s desire to go to Switzerland to end his life, although he did also tell his care coordinator that he had “no immediate plans” to act on his suicidal thoughts. A coroner recorded a verdict of suicide.

DWP ‘cyber incident’ knocks almost all pensions and benefits systems offline

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 19:45:51 GMT

Department for Work and Pensions urges people to be alert to scams related to outage and contact helpline with urgent difficulties

Tell us: have you been affected by the DWP ‘cyber incident’

Benefits and pensions claimants have faced chaos after the system was hit by a “serious cyber incident”, fuelling concerns about the UK government’s ability to defend itself against malicious attacks.

The government took its portal down late on Thursday after detecting “unusual activity”, meaning anyone trying to check their state pension, make an application for disability benefits or claim universal credit on Friday was unable to do so.

Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said all regular benefit payments were still being made but many claimants said they were worried about delays in applying for emergency payments, had seen their appointments cancelled and were unable to access their accounts.

The incident comes days after the government issued a warning of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks in the UK, particularly against businesses supporting Ukraine.

Downing Street has not ruled out that a “malicious” actor was behind the incident, but said there was no evidence that customer data had been lost or that any other departments had been targeted.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) urged people to be alert to any scams related to the outage and stressed that the government would never ask people to confirm bank details or click a link. It also said people should contact their benefit helpline if they were having urgent difficulties and confirmed that no one would face a sanction for not meeting conditions while the system was offline.

DWP insiders said payments for Friday would already have been sent earlier in the week, but there could be a backlog of manual payments running into tens of thousands due early next week to be processed over the weekend. Internal DWP systems were restored on Friday, allowing officials to begin working again, but the public-facing portal remained offline.

The cause of the incident is not publicly known but GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre is investigating, indicating there is a suspicion it may have been malicious activity.

Senior MPs called for the government to redouble its efforts to protect its systems. Dame Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons science and technology committee, said it should be a “wake-up call” for the government and public bodies.

She said: “People rely on these systems for some of the most essential services the state provides, and they should be able to trust that the tech and data underpinning them are secure and resilient.

“My committee has repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene. Public bodies hold citizens’ data on trust, and that demands the highest standards.”

Ben Spencer, the Conservative shadow AI minister, said the cyber incident was “deeply concerning and highlights once again why the security of government systems cannot be taken for granted”.

He said: “I and colleagues have repeatedly warned about potential vulnerabilities in government technology and called for greater transparency and scrutiny of the action being taken to modernise outdated systems and strengthen cybersecurity.”

McFadden said there was a “constant effort” to ensure systems were secure. “When an incident like this happens, the most important thing is to take the system offline as early as possible to protect it, then to investigate the causes, and at the same time to make sure that payments to the public can continue as normal.”

The disruption caused concern among the public, with some reporting problems. One woman who has two young children told BBC Radio 4 that she normally received a universal credit payment on the 27th day of each month and, like others, was concerned about not having enough money to cover bills due to be paid on 1 December.

“It’s a bit scary because when I called them [the DWP] to ask, they said they couldn’t give me any other information other than the payment would definitely be made by Monday,” she said.

England target historic All Blacks treble after finally clicking into gear

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 19:00:18 GMT

Maro Itoje says the team have used morale-sapping defeats this year to reach this stage but there is ‘more to come’

Offer England’s players a choice between a cut-price “Black Friday” deal and another super soaraway All Black Saturday and this week’s answer is unanimous. This may be an opportune moment to snap up pre-Christmas bargains on the high street but Maro Itoje and his side are rather more intent on securing a priceless little chunk of history.

Never before in 121 years have England’s men beaten New Zealand in three consecutive Tests and the last time their opponents lost six times in a calendar year was back in 1949. During that distant annus horribilis the All Blacks ended up contesting simultaneous Test series against South Africa and Australia and lost them both; this time around there would be no such asterisk.

What England really, really want, though, is to round off their own eventful year in convincing fashion. They have already rebounded promisingly from the doldrums of a fifth-placed finish in the Six Nations last March and have no intention of stopping now. Another victory over New Zealand, in their Nations Championship second-v-second match, by a margin in excess of 15 points would also elevate them to second in the world rankings.

This extreme makeover is all the more remarkable given the indignities they suffered earlier this year, not least 40-point thumpings against Ireland at home and South Africa in Johannesburg. There was also an historic loss to Italy in Rome when the likelihood of them ending 2026 as fast-improving World Cup contenders felt distinctly remote.

Their defensive solidity has shown particular improvement, along with the crispness of their passing and the confidence with which they are moving the ball and manipulating defenders. As the Wallabies, Japan and the All Blacks have recently discovered, England are also increasingly expert at targeting their opponents’ strengths and eroding their momentum. New Zealand, who made it into the England 22 on just three occasions last week, have rarely been made to look more toothless.

Itoje, accordingly, was asked this week whether he felt his team have finally located the “sweet spot” where all their hard work over months and years is starting to bear fruit. “I wouldn’t say sweet spot because that implies we’ve cracked it and I still believe there is more to come,” replied Itoje, making clear his desire for England not to ease up. “But what I do feel is that this team is understanding itself better. A team that is able to apply attacking pressure with ball in hand, as well as defensive pressure … those are foundations of what a good team needs to be. Our challenge is to continue to build.”

There is certainly no doubt that, after a frustrating period of trial and error, England are exuding more collective clarity. For a long time, their relatively unambitious gameplans did not obviously suit the talent available and the senior players seemed on a different wavelength to some of their younger teammates. Now, as Eric Morecambe used to say when examining Ernie Wise’s hairline, you can’t see the join.

Itoje, who has also become a father this autumn, sounds happier, too. “I don’t think a blueprint has emerged, I think we’re just executing better.” He also believes the “tough times” have been helpful in the longer term. “They either split you or they can bind you together. No matter how good any of us think we are, if we go out on our own we’re not going to win. Or, at least, we’re not going to win consistently. So there’s a level of understanding that we also need each other. That understanding has built over time. And when you go through tricky times as we have done in the past year, it just sharpens your mind.”

Reaching the same rare emotional pitch as last week, when Lewis Moody memorably joined the team to face the pre-game haka will clearly be a challenge. But, equally, England have been talking about this week as something of a dry run for next year’s World Cup knockout stages when taking a breather will not be an option. It explains, to some degree, why Steve Borthwick has selected Freddie Steward and Greg Fisilau to start, rather than redeploying George Furbank and Ben Curry and simply asking his side to rinse and repeat last week’s effort. The head coach keeps stressing that World Cups are won with a successful squad rather than just a team, and good performances from Steward and Fisilau could well rubber-stamp their passage to Australia in 10 months’ time.

There is also a tactical suspicion that a reshuffled New Zealand side may seek to employ their aerial game more than a week ago. Whether that is the case or not, Itoje doesn’t want excessive individualism to obstruct his team’s ambitions. “We have some exciting players who have unique points of difference. For England to do well, we need all of those players to bring the very best of themselves. At the same time that needs to be in a structured sense … that’s where you see the cohesion.”

In other words, stick together and the pressure will be firmly on the All Blacks. If losing to Wales was bad enough for New Zealand morale, the manner of their subsequent 37-12 defeat at Allianz Stadium was arguably even worse. “Last weekend hurt,” their head coach, Dave Rennie, said. “We know how good we’ll need to be on Saturday.”

It could be that the Twickenham vibe will be slightly less forbidding, with an early afternoon clash between Wales and Japan also part of the package. The stadium, however, is likely to be only two-thirds full, a far cry from last Saturday’s 81,000 sellout. Such are the logistical hazards of the finals lineup only being confirmed seven days in advance, in addition to the non-Black Friday ticket prices. Itoje would nevertheless still love to see London – “Maybe Andy Burnham can add it to the EU trade talks” – remain as finals weekend hosts in 2028 ahead of another European city.

The organisers, either way, will be praying that the quality of the weekend’s rugby proves more of a talking point than the gaps in the stands. While there is every chance of France and South Africa producing another belter in Sunday’s grand final, try telling Itoje and co that their New Zealand sequel has limited significance. Reduce the once-mighty All Blacks to rubble for a second successive week and England will feel anything is possible.

Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:10:18 GMT

To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy

Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.

It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket. Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.

Plenty of people stopped being shocked by that long ago, just as they learned to shrug off most of the president’s pronouncements and posts on social media – including this week an AI-generated version of the emblematic image of a bloodied Trump raising a clenched fist after he had survived an assassination attempt in 2024, except with Huang in place of Trump, now holding up a red bra. Was that image a middle finger to Beijing, casting the CEO’s lover as accomplice to an attempt to bring down the Nvidia boss, an attempt that he had heroically survived – or was it just casual misogyny, with a woman’s underwear held aloft as a trophy of sexual conquest? Maybe both.

There are countless other angles to pursue. Should we now be speaking of Trumpian socialism, given that a supposedly conservative president obviously believes it is up to the government to decide who should be running a major US company? What is the impact of a US leader who clearly measures the health of the national economy by a single metric, namely the state of the stock market? And what are we to make of the fact that Trump constantly says the US must beat China in the race for AI supremacy, yet appears unbothered by the fact that, under Huang, Nvidia’s highest-value chips were finding their way to China via Thailand and Singapore, including by means of a company owned by the boss’s lover?

Trump was warned of the danger to US national security, in writing, by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, yet was happy to have Jensen Huang at his side as he travelled to China earlier this year. As with last week’s love-in with Xi Jinping, it shows how, for all the tough talk on trade, Trump is no China hawk. He’s a pussycat, apparently unwilling to see Beijing as anything more than an economic rival, and certainly not as a genuine strategic threat.

All of this is worth probing, but it should not divert our gaze from the heart of the matter – which is the elevation by Trump of himself, those he favours and a single industry into a realm where no law can touch them.

Consider the way he got Huang back into his job. The board needed to hear from the Trump administration that it did not regard Huang as a danger to national security and that he was not facing criminal charges. The White House duly obliged and the deal was done. But those were two assurances Trump should never have given.

The first because of the evidence that throughout her relationship with the Nvidia boss, Alice Huang was in regular contact with China’s ministry of state security, as was her business partner, the man whom she would regularly introduce as her husband. And the second, because no president should be able to say whether any citizen will or will not face criminal charges: that should be a decision of the justice system, which should stand independent of the executive. For half a century, since the Watergate scandal, US presidents have kept the department of justice (DoJ) at arm’s length, leaving that body to make its own judgments. Admittedly, Trump has long shown contempt for the principle of prosecutorial independence, brazenly urging the DoJ to pursue his personal enemies, but in his pledge to the Nvidia board, Trump trampled all over it.

He claimed his top people had been “studying” Huang’s case, which enabled him to reassure Nvidia that the ousted CEO would not be charged, either now or later, but his own attorney general was studiedly vague as to whether there had been an investigation of Huang. In effect, Trump had granted Huang immunity from future prosecution, the equivalent of a pre-emptive pardon (which, for all we know, he may have granted). Whatever Huang did or did not do to compromise US national security, whether or not he turned a blind eye to the circumvention of export laws enabling highly sensitive AI chips to reach China, whatever abuses he committed as CEO – and there is copious evidence of him not only having sexual relationships with subordinates but bullying and humiliating staff, even threatening violence and torture – he is off the hook, by order of the president.

Trump will not fear any consequences for the abuse of power he just committed. He knows that in a 2024 ruling, the supreme court granted all but blanket immunity for a president’s official actions and he is confident that, were he to be impeached, there will never be enough Senate Republicans with the courage to vote to remove him from office. And he has what he regards as the ultimate weapon, that almost monarchic power of the pardon. He can pardon himself, along with anybody who works for him or who has helped him.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, where they will start investigations and subpoena witnesses – Huang himself is due on Capitol Hill next week – but if Trump’s aides defy those subpoenas, who will prosecute them? Certainly not a DoJ controlled by Trump loyalists. And should one of his staff get unlucky, Trump will simply sign a pardon. A US president who is willing to break every convention, who has enough lapdogs in the Senate and who has no shame is functionally immune. He is above the law.

And now we know he is prepared to throw that same cloak of immunity over the AI sector on which he believes the US stock market, and therefore the US economy, depends. “We have to protect our geniuses,” the White House said of Jensen Huang. He has drunk enough of the tech bros’ Kool-Aid to believe these men are the new gods, essential and therefore subject to different rules – or rather no rules at all.

Capitalism is meant to rest on the rule of law, on the certainty that contracts will be honoured and enforced. That certainty no longer applies in the US, now that we know that a president might step in to exempt a firm he favours or an executive he regards as too big to fire. Trump has refused to regulate the AI industry, taking no action even on widely hated datacentres, and now refuses to regulate its titans. They command an industry apparently bent on making the rest of the human race dispensable and that, the US president believes, makes them indispensable – and therefore untouchable. Just like him.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:07:43 GMT

Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.

If AI can conquer mathematics’ greatest challenge, what next? Leading mathematicians fear it has broken, or is close to breaking, the encryption that safeguards global finance, communications and the privacy of billions of people. In the wake of the Riemann hypothesis proof, the Bank of England warned that unreleased models could be good enough to reverse-engineer the calculations that underpin online security. The cryptosphere is humming with rumours that its walls will be breached within two years.

Oxford University’s Marcus du Sautoy surprised his interviewer on BBC Radio 4 by wondering if such a decisive breakthrough could already have occurred without public knowledge. That is not unreasonable. It appears that the most consequential mathematical discoveries are occurring inside privately owned AI labs. Businesses are deciding what maths society can know, which governments can see them, and when breakthroughs are too dangerous to publish. Donald Trump intervened to restrain the spread of frontier models earlier this year, but most states lack sufficient independent expertise to assess the risks.

Clearly, AI does not need to become “superintelligent” to be strategically important. So far the technology has relied on human researchers to advance the models. But if AI can produce original research in the disciplines that underpin its development then humans might not be required. In a landmark 1965 paper, the British mathematician IJ Good envisaged an “ultraintelligent machine” capable of designing machines more intelligent than itself, which would in turn design even more intelligent machines. He wrote presciently: “the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control”. What was considered science fiction is now a key objective of leading AI firms.

This technology exists because humans permit it. AI doesn’t have to become conscious for the technology to produce an unprecedented concentration of economic power in a few billionaires’ hands. It doesn’t have to escape human control to give private firms the upper hand with government. It doesn’t have to become autonomously intelligent to create such competition for its ownership that international cooperation is difficult. Those choices are ones humans made. They can – and should – be unmade.

The Guardian view on the Children’s Booker prize: everyone is a winner

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 18:06:01 GMT

In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked

“Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize, as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote.

The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity.

In the wake of reports that literacy and reading for pleasure among children is at an all-time low, the prize couldn’t be more timely. It is especially welcome after the Costa and Blue Peter children’s book awards were scrapped in 2022. There is still no shortage of UK children’s book prizes, ranging from the Carnegie medal, established in 1936, to the more recent Jhalak prize for writers of colour and the Children’s Wainwright prize for conservation writing. But none has the same prestige and potential selling power of the Booker, as proven by the huge rise in sales of this year’s adult winner, The End of Everything, by the acclaimed but by no means mainstream science fiction writer M John Harrison.

Children’s fiction, which has been dominated by the same names and celebrity authors for too long, could certainly do with a sprinkling of Booker dust. Following the Guardian’s reporting of allegations against David Walliams, which he denies, the literacy charity Inclusive Books for Children has called for a greater diversity of authors in school libraries and home bookshelves.

For younger children, it is no surprise that another relative of their wart-nosed favourite has turned up for Christmas, with Gruffalo Granny, from Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler, breaking records in the book charts. With five titles from independent publishers on the Booker shortlist, the prize shines a light on works that might otherwise be overlooked. The same is true of the British Audio awards, “the Speakies”, the winners of which were also announced this week. Super Great Kids’ Stories!, which features tales from around the globe, won best audiobook for children; Margaret McDonald’s powerful debut, Glasgow Boys, about two friends who grew up in care, triumphed in the young adult category.

Both prizes reflect a shift in attitudes towards broader engagement with books. Championing the importance of storytelling in any form is also one of the goals of the National Year of Reading. Cheeringly, the latest research suggests a small but encouraging improvement in children’s reading habits. Any fears that a younger Booker might bring a whiff of literary “elitism” have proved unfounded. Perhaps we are finally catching up with other European countries in taking graphic novels and illustration more seriously.

In the run-up to Christmas, the “great eight” offer a much-needed alternative to algorithms and promotional displays. Smaller publishers, writers, teachers, librarians, and of course young readers – everyone, in fact – stands to win from a prize that celebrates the best children’s literature in all its guises. There is a whole deep, dark wood out there to discover.

The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:53:30 GMT

FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of group linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail

It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices.

The Com, crime agencies say, is a sprawling and fluid global network of online communities populated by young cybercriminals. A typical Com member is a boy or young man aged 16 to 25. They are primarily native English speakers. Their crimes are broad and may include data theft, crypto scams, bringing down IT systems and causing chaos through attacks that slow down networks.

Then there are young men such as Mensforth who targeted vulnerable young girls and encouraged them to harm themselves or sacrifice their pets.

Often the criminals coerce girls to take indecent images of themselves which they then share. They blackmail and threaten their victims with swatting and doxing, police say.

Swatting is the term used for reporting fictitious incidents at the victim’s address to the emergency services, so they turn up in numbers, sometimes armed. Doxing is threatening to put all of someone’s personal details online.

They operate on every platform, according to DCI Steve Brown of Northumbria police, who led the investigation into Mensforth. “They target people they know have vulnerabilities, people who need somebody to make them feel wanted, to feel valued,” said Brown. “They gain that trust and then they turn that trust against them by asking them to perform horrendous acts.”

In July 2025, the FBI issued its first big public alert about the Com under the headline: “Theft, extortion and violence are a rising threat to youth online”.

The FBI said the Com was a growing and evolving online threat, calling it “a primarily English-speaking, international, online ecosystem comprised of multiple interconnected networks whose members, many of whom are minors, engage in a variety of criminal violations”.

It added: “The FBI estimates thousands of individuals identify as current or recent members of the Com with varying levels of associated activity.”

The UK’s National Crime Agency has said reports of Com networks increased sixfold in the UK from 2022-2024, describing members as “usually young men who are motivated by status, power, control, misogyny, sexual gratification, or an obsession with extreme or violent material”.

The Molly Rose Foundation, a leading UK online safety charity, this year issued a stark public warning about the Com and called for a coordinated global response from governments, regulators, law enforcement and tech companies.

Andy Burrows, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The growing threat posed by Com networks is the most chilling and urgent threat to children online today and it requires a swift and comprehensive response.”

The motivations of Com members vary but, according to the FBI, often fall into one of these categories: “Financial gain, retaliation, ideology, sexual gratification and notoriety.”

They wanted to have control, said Brown. They got a kick out of getting people to do things they would never normally do.

Courts around the world are increasingly dealing with criminals linked to the Com. Sentences vary but there’s thought to be none longer than the 77-year jail term handed down in August, in Tennessee, to Kyle Spitze, 27, for abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material offences.

The US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association with an online network known for its “sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world”.

Crime agencies such as the FBI urge people “to exercise caution when posting or messaging personal information, photos or videos on social media, dating sites or other online platforms”.

For parents it can be bewildering and scary but they do need to monitor their child’s online activity, police say.

After the gruelling slog of the Mensforth case, Brown said he now checked the devices of his own children. “Personally, since this investigation, I do that to my kids,” he said. “It’s simply asking parents: talk, know and act. Talk to your children, know what they’re doing and act upon it.”
