Labour row over Rosebank deepens as dozens of MPs warn PM not to block oilfield

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:39:10 GMT

Warning of ‘lights out for Labour in Scotland’ as Burnham faces choice between warring factions over North Sea drilling project

Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could spell “lights out for Labour in Scotland”.

As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs are considering writing their own letter to Andy Burnham after nearly 100 of their colleagues called on the prime minister not to allow the project to proceed. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also reiterated his support for Rosebank, cautioning that “working-class people in vocational jobs” were threatened by the decline of the North Sea basin.

Burnham now faces having to choose between two warring factions within his own party in what is likely to be the most sensitive decision he has taken so far as prime minister.

Anti-Rosebank MPs warn about the impact on the climate. They argue that the estimated additional 254m tonnes of carbon dioxide which Rosebank will produce over its lifetime are not worth the extra £500m in tax receipts and 500 jobs it will generate.

But those in favour of the project worry that a decision not to go ahead will damage Labour’s reputation with industry and Scottish voters in general.

One MP told the Guardian: “This is very much part of Scotland’s economy and supply chain, but crucially Scotland’s identity. It has become such a totemic issue that Labour will not be forgiven in Scotland if they don’t do this.”

The person added: “Andy needs to approve Rosebank or it’s lights out for Labour in Scotland.”

Marra said he recognised that the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, had a “different” decision compared to the Jackdaw gasfield, but backed the project because of the jobs and economic activity it would support.

“The decline of the North Sea may be seen as something to celebrate by those who want us to meet our climate obligations.

“I understand that. But I ask those who call for a just transition to understand the anxiety in Aberdeen and the north-east of Scotland over a political establishment which often feels to them that it considers anything but clean energy a dirty word.

“This is people’s lives and livelihoods we are talking about. Not the millionaire shareholders of a billion-dollar multinational, but working-class people in vocational jobs,” the Scottish Labour leader said.

Several MPs have sent individual letters to Burnham urging him to allow the project to go ahead, but many are now in talks about whether to coordinate their efforts to counteract a letter against Rosebank signed by nearly 100 of their collegaues.

One Labour MP said: “The whips and the government know we have the support, we’ve made that clear behind the scenes. Conversations [over a joint letter] are ongoing over the weekend.”

Another added: “Reindustrialisation and energy jobs for young people are huge issues in Scotland, so the feeling is they need to approve it to show we’re serious about it.”

Henry Tufnell, Labour MP for mid and south Pembrokeshire said: “Failing to approve Rosebank would cost industrial communities jobs and investment, weaken our balance of payments and deny the exchequer vital tax revenues.”

Torcuil Crichton, the Labour MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar (Western Isles), said: “We need the workforce, the supply chain and the expertise of the North Sea to build our renewable future.

“There are now more jobs in renewables than in the carbon sector, but we can’t abandon the workforce like other energy communities were abandoned by the Tories.”

He told BBC Radio Scotland: “It makes far more sense from a domestic security point of view and an environmental point of view to source those carbon fuels within our own boundaries. If we don’t, we’re importing a huge carbon footprint from other places.

“So there’s no point outsourcing our environmental conscience.”

after newsletter promotion

Burnham has enjoyed early success in office by uniting his previously fractious parliamentary party and winning back voters who had defected to other leftwing parties. The Rosebank decision, however, will test his ability to keep his fragile coalitions of MPs and voters together.

While Labour has enjoyed a poll bounce since Burnham became prime minister, the improvement has been more modest in Scotland and the party remains behind the Scottish National party.

In recent months, the SNP’s stance on oil and gas drilling in the North Sea has shifted. Once strong opponents of new projects under Nicola Sturgeon, the party abandoned its “presumption against” new North Sea projects in October. John Swinney has also criticised the UK government’s energy independence bill, which aims to ban new North Sea drilling.

Polling by Survation last month found that 64% of people in Scotland say that the UK government should approve Rosebank, with 16% against.

“In Scotland, the public supports approval for Rosebank in every age group excepted 18-to-24s. But even that is very close: there’s just a 1% net difference. According to our polling, allowing the project to go ahead would make Scottish voters more likely to vote Labour. Any route to a majority for Burnham hinges on Scottish seats,” said PJ Stock, a research and data analyst with Survation.

Emma Hardy, the environment minister, acknowledged on Friday morning that her party was split over the issue.

She told Sky News: “I know from chatting to some of my friends and colleagues, some Labour MPs in Scotland feel differently to some Labour MPs elsewhere. But I know Andy [Burnham], as our prime minister, will be listening to everybody.”

While Labour went into the last election promising not to issue any more North Sea oil and gas licences, they could give the environmental approval to this project – the largest undeveloped field in UK waters – because it already has a licence.

Despite that, Fahnbulleh is understood to be leaning against granting approval on the grounds that it will emit an estimated 1m tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, but contribute relatively little to UK energy supplies.

While the decision technically lies with Fahnbulleh, most MPs believe that if Burnham signals either his approval or opposition to the scheme, she will be left with little option but to back the prime minister.

So far Burnham has said he wants to be “pragmatic” about decisions in the North Sea and won plaudits from Donald Trump after Fahnbulleh approved the smaller Jackdaw field.

Downing Street said on Friday: “The decision on Rosebank will be taken by the energy secretary through a quasi-judicial process. She will consider the relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and representations received during the consultation process, before reaching a decision.”

If the prime minister does push Fahnbulleh to approve the scheme, he could be faced with resignations from government, with more than one ministerial aide having indicated they are willing to quit over the issue.

UK man jailed for online blackmail of vulnerable girls around the world

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:27:03 GMT

Beau-Jack Mensforth, 20, part of a group known as the Com, coerced girls into self-harm, making indecent images of themselves and physically harming pets

The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children

A 20-year-old man from north-east England has been jailed for blackmailing vulnerable girls around the world, prompting a senior police officer to urge parents to regularly check their children’s devices.

Beau-Jack Mensforth admitted 17 offences of making and distributing indecent photographs of children, blackmail, and participating in the activities of an organised crime group.

Newcastle crown court heard that Mensforth coerced girls into harming themselves, making indecent photographs of themselves and physically harming their pets.

At his sentencing on Friday, victims spoke of feeling scarred for life, being deprived of a normal childhood, needing psychiatric care and attempting suicide.

Judge Bindloss jailed Mensforth for 14 and a half years, describing him as “a calculating predator who groomed and blackmailed young girls”.

Mensforth was part of a global group, known as the Com, which is involved in a broad range of cybercrime, including targeting vulnerable girls online. If the children resisted Mensforth’s wild requests they would be blackmailed, said DCI Steve Brown of Northumbria police.

The court heard that Mensforth used cyber-attack threat techniques called swatting and doxing to try to get his way. Swatting is the term used when someone falsely reports a major crime at the victim’s house so that the emergency services turn up in numbers, sometimes armed. Doxing is threatening to put all of someone’s personal details online.

Brown said Mensforth was “targeting vulnerable females across the globe in order to carry out acts at his behest. If they didn’t, he would swat and dox them.

“As he was doing this, he was also having chats in his own online forums and groups … bragging, discussing, encouraging others to do the same.”

Police say Mensforth, using the name Yuri, encouraged and incited girls to self-harm themselves by cutting his name into their body.

At his sentencing, the court heard statements from some of Mensforth’s victims around the world. All of them were given lifelong anonymity by the judge.

One teenager, from the US, said her ordeal with Mensforth had made her attempt suicide. She had become “incredibly depressed and nihilistic” and her self-worth was “ripped to shreds … I felt I was being hypnotised into believing I was nothing”.

She said she was physically scarred for life. “I can’t look at my own body without getting flashbacks to the gaping wounds he made me carve,” she said.

Another victim said Mensforth was a “psychopath” and spoke of how he had “deprived me of a normal childhood and a normal life”.

A third girl spoke of her feelings of isolation, loneliness and paranoia after her experiences with Mensforth. “I have a lot of anger towards him,” she said. “I hate him … I just want him punished for the pain he has caused me and my family.”

A girl from Australia said she was 12 when she first encountered Mensforth and he made “her believe it was OK to self-harm for your pleasure”. She said she now suffered “overwhelming anxiety” and Mensforth had ruined her ability to trust others. “My ability to feel safe was stolen from me,” she said.

In police interviews Mensforth spoke of how the group would encourage girls to kill pets “or any stray animals”. In one email exchange he suggested that a girl should be encouraged to punch a cat.

Northumbria police started investigating Mensforth, from Sunderland, in October 2023 when he was 17. Brown described it as a “very complex” investigation, with a “vast” amount of digital material recovered.

There were nine victims in the criminal case, three of them based in the UK, with others in the US, Greece, the Philippines and Australia. More than 30 other victims had been identified, but where prosecution had not been possible, Brown said. “It’s been a hard slog because there’s been a lot of gruesome and horrendous material that the investigation team had to go through. It would take its toll on anybody.”

Brown said he wanted people to be aware of what could happen online. Police are encouraging people to “support the young people in their lives by looking at their devices, monitoring and checking what they are doing online”.

Brown said warning signs that a child might be a victim could include a change in attitude or personality, wanting to just stay in their room, hiding their devices, not letting you access them, “and clearly at times people are self-harming”.

The defence counsel Robin Patton said psychiatric evaluation had revealed Mensforth had autistic spectrum disorder, which reduced his capacity to exercise appropriate judgment.

His descent into “moral squalor” started after, as a socially isolated 15-year-old, he lost his father, Patton said.

How to restore dignity to the world of work

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:25:33 GMT

Colin Montgomery suggests that expectations should be properly managed. Plus letters from Paul Hartley, Hartley Dean and Peter Thornton

John Harris’s jeremiad about what the world of work has become (A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue, 22 November) put me in mind of the old joke: “How do I get to Dublin?” “Well, I wouldn’t start from here.” Because, as he concludes, there’s almost no chance of any government being able to even begin to relieve this situation quickly, short of putting an emergency brake on 40 years of neoliberalism. As if.

I’d like to suggest a real starting point for the fightback against this seemingly interminable malaise that looks set to blight generations to come: namely, begin from somewhere grounded in properly managed expectations. Because arguably, that’s what underpins all of this: we’ve all been cynically inveigled into a bargain that can never be fulfilled.

Market forces will deliver better business and services for all? Not true. Ever greater choice in line with our individual preferences as people or consumers will free us to live more fulfilling lives? Not true. Our rights will for ever grow in an unchecked march of social progress? Not true. Accepting all of this may be hard to stomach, but stomach it we must. Only then can the real hard work begin; towards something that isn’t utopia but is still very much worth grafting for. Colin Montgomery Edinburgh

The notion of the flexible worker is do what you are told to do. If the employer wants you to stand at a till, fill shelves, pack bags etc, then that’s what you’ll do, until they want you clean windows or empty the rubbish instead. This “relationship” also now involves the rise of monitoring by electronic systems and the use of AI to “manage” workers in some areas of employment. This should give us all pause for thought, especially when our sons and daughters are entering employment.

One thing for which we all need to take some responsibility is our role as consumers. Our acceptance of fast and cheap delivery, for example, takes a heavy toll on people’s lives. Workers are left to shape their lives to the demands of companies, which often means long hours of pressurised work, monitored every minute, with targets attached.

The result of this environment gives rise to continuous anxiety, negative effects on life away from work, and exhaustion. We need campaigns which acknowledge that, as well as workers, we are also consumers. We have a responsibility to ensure that the workers who provide the goods and services we consume are treated first and foremost as human beings. Paul HartleyWitney, Oxfordshire

John Harris rightly observes that work has lost its value and dignity, but might more explicitly have considered the relationship between value and dignity. We might consider all forms of human activity as “work” – as part of our shared metabolism with nature. Its value lies in the benefit it confers upon us all.

Human dignity derives from mutual recognition of the diverse ways in which we may all be enabled to contribute. “Work” can encompass a range of vital activities beyond labour market participation: the work entailed in caring for children and more vulnerable adults; the massive amounts of everyday informal, supportive and creative activities that enhance the quality of others’ lives.

Is it not time to recognise how the substantive value generated beyond the labour market contributes to the sum of human dignity?Hartley DeanEmeritus professor of social policy, London School of Economics

John Harris writes: “Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us.” I received two brilliant pieces of advice during my career as a freelance writer. One was from the founder of The Body Shop, Anita Roddick: “You’re at work too long for it not to be fun.” The other was from my father, a toolmaker and trade unionist: “If they could pay you sixpence an hour less, they would.” Somewhere in between is what actually happens. Peter ThorntonRamsbottom, Lancashire

Psychosomatic illness diagnoses must be handled with great care

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:25:29 GMT

Willemina Rietsema, a GP, says no explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet). Carrie Eckersley thinks we need to consider the wider context in which symptoms develop

Regarding Huw Green’s article (How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?, 22 November), the body and the mind/brain have strong connections both ways. It is therefore not surprising that major psychological distress can lead to physical symptoms, and the other way around.

However, as a GP, I would recommend being extremely careful about equating “otherwise unexplained symptoms” with psychosomatic illness. No explanation doesn’t mean no physical illness, it just means we haven’t found one (yet).

We should be honest about that, to ourselves and to our patients. I have seen diagnoses of “functional” or “psychosomatic” illness being overturned by proof that patients had anything from vitamin B12 deficiency to severe neurological disorder to inflammatory bowel disease.

A recent study found that autoimmune diseases, such as thyroid disease, systemic lupus and rheumatoid arthritis were often initially misdiagnosed as psychological or functional. It could take years, and more often so in women, before the right diagnosis was found. A misdiagnosis of a psychological cause was made in the majority of women in first instance and a substantial proportion of men.

Therefore only when there is a clear connection between psychological distress and physical illness may a tentative diagnosis of psychological illness be made. Even then, we should keep on the lookout for any evidence that there is a physical disease after all. Willemina RietsemaOxford

Huw Green’s article offers a welcome challenge to the idea that unexplained physical symptoms are emotions converted into illness, but I think we need to look beyond emotional recognition.

Emotions, perception and expectations are all biological processes. Our nervous systems are constantly interpreting bodily signals, anticipating demands and adjusting physiological responses to maintain stability. When these processes become less flexible, physical symptoms can emerge, with attention, expectations and emotional responses potentially reinforcing them, but emotional distress doesn’t necessarily have to be the cause.

We need to consider the wider context in which symptoms develop, including physiological demands, environmental pressures, perceived threat and our capacity to adapt. Separating psychological and physical processes risks overlooking how closely they interact. Carrie EckersleyHolmes Chapel, Cheshire

Abusers are not ‘other’ – they are all around us

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:25:25 GMT

Male sexual violence against women is fuelled by misogyny, writes Sarah Mulholland

The courage of Joanne Young is powerful, and it could be pivotal (Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers, 20 November). The publicity given to high-profile cases such as those of Russell Brand, Jeffrey Epstein and Mohamed Al Fayed is understandable, but it runs the risk of serving as a convenient deflector, allowing us to comfort ourselves that rapists and sexual abusers are somehow “other”.

Indeed, one of the most pernicious rape myths is the belief that rape is perpetrated by men of a different social or economic status, of a different ethnicity or culture – outsiders from whom we can distance ourselves.

In fact, almost half (43%) of all reported rapes in the UK are perpetrated by either a current or a previous partner, and the vast majority are not rich and famous celebrities, but men from every socioeconomic class. In France, Gisèle Pelicot’s husband was neither rich nor famous. The men whom he facilitated to rape his wife were firefighters, office employees, manual workers; they were husbands, brothers and sons in nearby villages.

Ms Young’s now ex-husband was a businessman, apparently respected and liked by colleagues and neighbours. These men are not “other men”, they are “our men”. It is, paradoxically, their very proximity to our daily lives that protects them.

Intimate partner abuse, grooming gangs, date rape and other forms of male sexual violence against women are all iterations of the same underlying dynamic, one fuelled by misogyny. The internet enables new iterations, and new operating modes, but the underlying dynamic has not changed.

This problem is not confined to specific industries and institutions, still less to specific ethnicities, faiths or social groups. It is the expression of a deeply embedded culture in our society, and only when we confront it will we truly be able to challenge it. Sarah MulhollandSt Petry, Cornwall

Readers respond to the Saturday magazine’s list of 20 long books for short days with their suggestions

Sadly, your list of 20 long books for the short winter days (Light in the dark, 21 November), leaves no room at the inn for the Chums of Chance, the late 19th-century airship bods aboard the Inconvenience who provide lift-off for Thomas Pynchon’s 2006 Moby-Dick of a novel, Against the Day (1,085 pages – take that, Lucy Ellmann).

From page 3, when Pugnax the dog is found reading The Princess Casamassima by Henry James, thus igniting the book’s anarchical fascination and signalling its chaotic energy, the carnival of characters crossing continents and genres as conspirators and pursuers of conspirators are vivid, vital and funny. I enjoyed Chris Power’s listing of long books. It was particularly pleasing to see Stephen King mentioned, possibly the most underrated novelist of the last 50 years. Just before the bookshop shut, I got a copy of The Dead Zone by King, as I had enjoyed the films of The Shining and Carrie.

I was hooked. The late night and early morning flew by. Literate, suspenseful, dark humour – and with a buffoon in the White House!Will ReidLiverpool

I read War and Peace on a Kindle and would highly recommend it. Having abandoned a brick-sized paperback, the experience of reading it on the Kindle was to underline how relevant Tolstoy remains (as well as making it possible to continue reading it anywhere). Ann-Marie LeQuesneLondon

I expect you will be inundated with “Why didn’t you include…” letters, so I thought I’d get mine in quick: Oldest Living Confederate Widow Tells All by Allan Gurganus, first published in 1989 (718 pages).

I couldn’t begin to summarise this story of war and ancient scars, underage union and lifelong shadows told through the eyes and voice of an old, old lady, so I’ll just quote the opening line: “Died on me finally. He had to.” If that’s not enough to draw you in then you’re no reader of stamina. Lawrence ForresterDorchester

I want to throw two more titles on to the pile: The Love Songs of WEB DuBois by Honorée Fanonne Jeffers, and Hanya Yanagihara’s To Paradise. Fiery Hamilton-Leclerc lineup casts doubt on Ferrari functioning in a title fight

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:06:40 GMT

Costly on-track clashes have caused tensions to simmer and team need recent talks to tell at Sunday’s Qatar Grand Prix

There is an unmistakable air of deja vu heading into the Qatar Grand Prix and with it an intense scrutiny that might be considered unusual for a dead-rubber weekend. Yet for Ferrari, who are the subject of the attention after costly on-track incidents between the teammates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, more pertinent is how it might play out if the conflicts are not resolved and the Scuderia are in a title fight next season.

Hamilton and Leclerc clashed on track at the last round in Las Vegas, only two weeks after similarly contesting a place in Mexico cost them a potential one-two. The team principal Fred Vasseur was furious then, saying it displayed a lack of respect for the team and was unacceptable. They held talks to resolve the issue at the next round in Brazil.

Yet nothing, it appears, was resolved and after Leclerc made a clumsy effort to pass Hamilton in Vegas, Vasseur was furious, saying it displayed a lack of respect for the team and was unacceptable. He then held talks on Thursday to try to resolve the issue. Etc. Clearly having two No 1 drivers of such competitive edge and closely matched on track was never going to be easy but this has proved far more than anyone, including Vasseur it seems, expected to handle. This, however, is a season when they were never really in the title fight.

In Qatar neither Hamilton nor Leclerc would reveal what the team’s position is now on managing them or rules of engagement, which the British driver has argued in favour of for some time. Perhaps it will be shown on the track this weekend. Vasseur has been clear he believes it is impossible to legislate for every situation, which is a fair argument, but Ferrari have seemed fearful about getting involved at all.

McLaren’s “papaya rules”, employed to manage Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, may have been torturous and complex and indeed fearsomely difficult actually to manage – but they did work. They took constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and the drivers’ title last season. Norris and Piastri remain on good terms and have a clear understanding of the team’s position.

In Las Vegas, McLaren used a series of messages to both drivers about how best to deal with the complex racing there, how best to approach it and one another. Indeed, if both were given more than one entreaty it appears to be “be careful around your teammate”. It was enough that Piastri felt it was too much, admonishing his colleagues: “Stop telling me to be careful.”

Better, perhaps, too much than not enough, as Norris and Piastri took second and third, racing together line astern at times without putting a foot wrong, while Ferrari floundered. Both Hamilton and Leclerc had been expressing concern about how the other was driving but there appeared to be no stream of effective management from the Ferrari pit wall, only shock once they came together again.

Everyone involved recognises they have a problem; certainly the on-track trust between the two men appears to be paper-thin but the question now is whether Vasseur and Ferrari have the resolve to deal with it before it could cost them the title they crave.

Hamilton has been conciliatory in Qatar, saying he felt positive about the talks, but again it is impossible not to be reminded that this was exactly the sentiment expressed by all involved after Mexico. He said he and Leclerc could still work together well but noted, perhaps pointedly, that this should be a teachable moment for everyone at the team.

“We’re going to figure it out,” he said. “We’re teammates at the end of the day and I think we always learn from these experiences, whilst maybe it doesn’t necessarily look like it. You learn really through the hardest times. And these are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Charles and I.”

Kid gloves have not worked and the iron fist seems too much for the Scuderia but Ferrari cannot accept another falling-out of teammates. Whatever plan there is needs to be up to speed in Qatar, with everyone on the same page.

If not, what might ensue are even more serious questions as to whether the current lineup can even function in a title fight.

‘Genuinely emotional’: the world-conquering Chicken Shop Date’s final, eye-opening episode

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 17:00:15 GMT

After a 12-year run, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s last episode of Chicken Shop Date – a therapy session with Esther Perel – is being shown in cinemas. It’s a fittingly grand finale for a YouTube cult favourite that far outgrew its medium

The decision to screen the full final series of Chicken Shop Date in cinemas before the finale airs on YouTube is, it could be argued, overkill. The cinema is a place where you sit rapt among like-minded people, bombarded with cutting-edge sound design and world-class visuals. On the other hand, the fun interview show that is Chicken Shop Date is the thing I watch alone on my computer while I pick my toenails. It isn’t a natural fit, is what I’m trying to say.

And yet, goddamn it if the whole thing didn’t leave me slightly choked up. After 12 years of flirting and awkwardness, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s final guest is Esther Perel, the Belgian psychotherapist and relationship guru beloved by Oprah Winfrey. It is by no means a traditional episode, almost completely dismissing the tone of everything that came before it. Dimoldenberg’s well-honed persona, alternately dismissive and needy, is nowhere to be seen. Instead, Dimoldenberg does something that Perel must be deadeningly familiar with when meeting new people: she uses the episode as a free therapy session.

If you’ve been following Chicken Shop Date for any length of time, the conversation is quite revealing. Dimoldenberg explains that she has essentially outgrown the show that made her famous, and continuing to do it is sad and exhausting. Again, longtime viewers may have suspected this for a while. The scrappiness of the early days, when Dimoldenberg would almost exclusively interview musicians she fancied, has long gone. Now, Chicken Shop Date is just another stop on the promotional celebrity parlour game circuit, squeezed between chugging hot sauce and ranking scotch eggs. Dimoldenberg has had to work harder and harder to manufacture any sort of chemistry with these people. Add to this the fact that, as outlined in a piece she wrote this week for the Cut, Dimoldenberg started experiencing panic attacks towards the end of the show, and the writing was on the wall.

After a tiny – possibly ironic – bit of pushback after she notices that nobody has actually flirted with her, Perel tells Dimoldenberg to imagine she is having a conversation with Chicken Shop Date itself, and that it is time to say goodbye. What follows is a genuinely emotional monologue where the host talks about everything she has gained from Chicken Shop Date, and everything she would lose if she continued to do it. As she thanks the show and bids it farewell, she tears up. This is the part that got me.

Now, I will admit that circumstances might have heightened my response a little. I saw the finale at the premiere, in a small screening room full of people who worked on the show, with Dimoldenberg herself sitting in the row behind me. Everyone in the room was sad to see it go. There is a possibility that, without all the stifled sobbing around me, I wouldn’t have been so moved.

But who knows. Amelia Dimoldenberg has been doing this for 12 years. Chicken Shop Date is something she dreamed up at a youth club, with no idea what would come from it. This hasn’t been a case of overnight fame for her. Everything about the show has been incremental; the rise in viewers, the viral moments with Louis Theroux and Andrew Garfield, the gig at the Oscars.

When Chicken Shop Date started, online video was seen as a silly little sideshow. As it ends, the form has displaced television as the pre-eminent way of consuming entertainment. The show was one of the drivers of this change. It has been bigger than anyone’s wildest dreams.

Of course, this isn’t to say that showing the whole thing in cinemas is necessarily the best way to watch Chicken Shop Date, because the film version consists of the last six episodes, five of which have been available on YouTube for weeks. Inevitably, thanks to pure familiarity, some of it does drag a bit. But what do I know? Some of the screenings this week sold out. Maybe there is demand for recent YouTube videos to be given the cinematic experience after all.

And let’s allow Dimoldenberg her lap of honour. Chicken Shop Date has been such a wild success that she could walk into any hosting gig on the planet at the moment, so it’s impressive that she has set her sights slightly higher. She’s writing a romcom, and seems focused on becoming a movie director. The woman is already used to realising her dreams, so that should be a cinch. If any of it lands with even a fraction of the impact of Chicken Shop Date, we’ll be hearing a lot more from Amelia Dimoldenberg for years to come.

Jared Kushner’s 70-minute interview reveals naive bias in handling of Putin’s aggression

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:49:59 GMT

Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved

In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars.

During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”.

There were also many happy admissions of historical ignorance. Since taking on the Ukraine brief a year ago, Kushner said, he had to learn “the algorithm of Europe and how complicated that is”, and he had to get abreast of “the local issues with Ukraine”.

As a businessman he brought a special expertise, he claimed. “Look at what’s happening in the Middle East with sanctions, with Russia, with Iran. I think that you have to understand economics in order to understand geopolitics because the two go together very, very closely,” he said.

But the main revelation was how much he believes the Ukraine conflict is not a case of an aggressor and a victim – but is simply a series of misunderstandings and miscommunication.

Indeed, he treated Vladimir Putin as if he were a masterful corporate executive quite willing to close the deal if he were only given the right economic incentives – instead of a man ready to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of Russians to reclaim part of a historical empire.

In the process, Kushner revealed – often inadvertently – that he had largely bought into the Russian narrative of a string of postwar missteps by Europe and the US coming to a head in Nato’s expansion eastwards after 9/11.

That, in turn, has led him to adopt Moscow’s central demand to reshape the European security order to allow Russia, without opprobrium, to retain land it has gained by force. Shining through his answers was a naive bias towards the aggressor, presented as a mediator’s desire to understand both parties.

Praise veering on awe for the Russian leader flowed. “Putin – people can like what he has done, they can not like what he has done – [but] he is a grand master of politics. He is a historic figure,” he said. Any sense that Putin may have blundered escaped him.

As to the rights and wrongs of invading another country, Kushner was blasé. “After all, most lines in Europe have changed over time and they are decided through war or peace, or concessions. It’s not about fairness or who is right or wrong. It’s about ending the killing,” he said.

He understood, too, why Putin could not offer a ceasefire: “He has very little confidence that if he stops the war, that he [will] be able to get to a postwar settlement that leads to not having a future war.”

To stop the killing, the killing has to go on.

What is more, Kushner was struck by the Russian leader’s self-control. “So far Putin has shown restraint and he has agreed not to use nuclear weapons and he has reassured us that is his intention.”

Kushner denied Trump had put any pressure on Volodymyr Zelenskyy, defying his interviewer to provide evidence – at which point Döpfner recited a list of examples, including only last month when the US president suggested that Ukraine should get a new leader.

Trump was “a strong counter-puncher”, argued Kushner, implying that Zelenskyy had thrown the first punch in a conflict that began with a Russian invasion. Relations with Ukraine were cooperative, he said before pointedly saying Kyiv needed things from the US, without which “Ukraine will not be safe in the future”.

After noting that “the territorial issue is now a little bit of a deadlock”, his strategic insight was that if a future security architecture for Europe could be agreed, the answer to the land question in Donbas would eventually follow.

In essence, he proposed a revival of the Russia-Nato council, one of the bodies eviscerated by Putin’s war.

He also envisioned Ukraine inside the European Union with security guarantees akin to those offered by Nato’s article five. Though it was impossible at this stage to give “more specificity” about these guarantees in the detailed way Ukraine sought, he admitted.

So far, neither Moscow nor Kyiv have bought this plan, let alone a wary Europe.

Kushner tried to be polite about Europe, insisting it had to be at the negotiating table, but he could not stop himself characterising European military assistance to Ukraine as a “proxy war” against Russia.

As an analysis of why the Ukraine war had not ended inside the 24 hours Trump had promised when he took office again, Kushner showed an alarming belief that the answer lay in granting more concessions to Putin, and that the misunderstandings and misperceptions would then evaporate.

Watford, the Pozzos and the hottest managerial seat in the game

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:36:35 GMT

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

A few weeks ago, Alessio Dionisi was forced to deny the “fake news” he had joined Sean Dyche, Gianfranco Zola, Beppe Sannino, Óscar García, Billy McKinlay, Slavisa Jokanovic, Quique Sánchez Flores (twice), Walter Mazzarri, Marco Silva, Javi Gracia (twice), Nigel Pearson, Vladimir Ivic, Xisco Muñoz, Claudio Ranieri, Roy Hodgson, Rob Edwards, Slaven Bilic, Chris Wilder, Valérien Ismael, Tom Cleverley, Paulo Pezzolano and Edward Still in being sacked by the Pozzo family since 2012. There was no denial on Sunday, when the axe inevitably fell on the head coach following a 4-0 shellacking at Sheffield United and the Italian left after only 18 games in charge. While his reign is unlikely to live long in the memory of anyone at Vicarage Road, Dionisi can at least boast on his LinkedIn page that in terms of longevity under the Pozzos, he took charge of 18 more matches than Dyche, 17 more than García and 16 more than McKinlay. Indeed, he even outlasted Rob Edwards, who was assured he would be backed “come hell or high water” upon his 2022 appointment, only to be fired from the ejector seat 11 games later.

It’s been quite the white-knuckle ride for Watford since the Pozzos arrived, armed only with a spreadsheet, an army of Udinese cast-offs and knowledge of the loophole that there was no Football League cap on the number of players who could be brought in on loan from clubs outside the UK. And while few fans will be able to recall all 25 of the coaches who have been hired and fired by the Pozzos, they do have fond memories to take to the grave. There was that end-to-end Troy Deeney play-off semi-final goal against Leicester. There were five uninterrupted seasons in the Premier League. There was that time they ended Liverpool’s 44-match unbeaten Premier League run despite being stuck in the relegation zone. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling to watch their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?

Of course it hasn’t all been rosy in the Pozzo garden. The eight-day managerial reign of McKinlay was a source of much mirth for fans of rival clubs. A double relegation from the Premier League – the first amid allegations of a dressing-room bust-up linked to an illegal lockdown party – wasn’t great either. Playing I’m Still Standing by Elton John, the club’s honorary life president, over the Vicarage Road PA system to mark their descent into the Championship heaped further embarrassment upon the club. And what self-respecting Hornet will ever forget travelling home after watching their team play in the 2019 FA Cup final?

While it would be foolish to predict what will happen next at a club that currently sit two places above the Championship relegation zone, the one stonewall certainty is that the name “Edward Iordanescu” will be the next to be copied and pasted into the over-worked club template announcing a managerial departure. The Romanian was formally introduced this morning and with this being his 14th job in the past 16 years, he can arguably lay claim to being the most ‘Watford’ manager of the Pozzo era. “For me, I want a team that plays very good, organised football with the spirit and attitude, and the strong mentality,” he blathered, as local reporters dabbed their bingo cards. “And then, yes, regarding the organisation of the team, that takes time.” History suggests getting the time he needs is a pipe dream for Iordanescu, whose first game in charge is away at Championship basement-dwellers Derby County. Should Watford go to Pride Park and lose, he could be out of a job by Saturday night.

Join Scott Murray from 8pm for red-hot updates on Nottingham Forest 0-0 Chelsea in the Premier League.

Honey, we’ve shrunk the country! But at least the Brexiters got their wish

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:23:40 GMT

Immigration has plummeted so we’ll probably have to work until we drop – yet many still obsess about people arriving in small boats

Will the last person to leave Britain, please turn out the lights?

It was way back in 1992 that the Sun ran that headline, predicting a national exodus if its readers dared vote for that dastardly Neil Kinnock. And to be fair, it was only out by 10 prime ministers and 34 years, for now we really are a nation heading for the exits.

This week saw the crossing of two remarkable statistical streams, with immigration plummeting to its lowest level since 1997 even as the desire to have children plumbs new depths. According to the canonically authoritative Natsal sex survey, the number of childless women under 44 who say they never want children has doubled in a decade to 17%. For all that may be a heartening sign of women’s freedom to choose the lives they want, it also means deaths are somewhat demoralisingly predicted to outstrip births this year.

Meanwhile, in a less-than-glowing vote of confidence in Britain, for four years now more EU nationals have left the country than have moved here, while the number of non-EU nationals leaving rose sharply this year – especially among students. Honey, we almost shrunk the country! One more heave and we might finally get into the club of actively depopulating countries, though admittedly a lot of them are either war zones or small islands set to vanish under rising seawater.

So congratulations, Brexiters; you’ve finally got what so many of you wanted – namely a country of which people increasingly steer well clear. Shame, though, that you seem to be living in another country entirely.

Research published by King’s College Policy Institute this week shows two-thirds of Britons think immigration rose between summer 2024 and 2025 – when it actually fell by two-thirds – with only 4% aware it had significantly decreased. (Reform voters were more likely to get this wrong.) Almost half overestimated the number of people crossing the Channel in small boats, while 44% guessed Britain hosted the highest or second highest number of asylum seekers out of us, Germany, Turkey, Poland and France. (In reality, we take in fewer than any of those countries.) When asked how many new council houses go to refugee households, the median guess was 20%, 10 times the real figure. Though the researchers didn’t ask where respondents got their notions, it would be fascinating to know whether it makes a difference if you watch, say, GB News or the BBC.

If immigration was what most people think it is, you could almost understand the anxiety. But as it is, millions are panicking at figments of social media-addled imagination while ignoring the far scarier prospect that Britain is on track to becoming something like Japan; a super-ageing nation whose schools will have to be mothballed for lack of children, staggering beneath the weight of pensions it can’t afford and the challenge of generating growth without a reliable supply of mini consumers, workers and homebuyers-in-waiting. Except we’ll be attempting it without the healthy fish-based diets that keep Japanese pensioners admirably fit into old age. For Tokyo, interestingly, the answer in recent years has been letting in (albeit controversially) more foreign workers.

Maybe Britain could somehow succeed where Japan has repeatedly failed in nudging its reluctant citizens towards parenthood. But this isn’t the 2000s, when the notion of “baby hunger” – the yawning gap between the number of women saying they wanted children and the number who actually had them, blamed on the punishing struggle to combine motherhood and a career – drove investment in childcare and parental rights, helping unleash a mini baby boom. The percentage of women telling Natsal they actively don’t want children has almost converged with the 18% who end up without children, suggesting a birthrate falling less by unhappy accident than by design: either young women deciding they like their lives fine as they are, or a reluctance to bring children into a world on fire. No country in the world has yet cracked turning a falling birthrate into a sustainably rising one, which means that barring some dramatic change in the social order – and the last big baby boom came only after a world war – it may be time to brace for baby bust.

Could we thrive as a shrinking country? Green arguments about depopulation letting the planet breathe sound appealing. But they’re worth nothing unless they engage honestly with what economic degrowth actually looks like to people on the sharp end, which, barring some as-yet-unimagined grand reorganisation of society, is many more of the hard choices we’ve endured since the banking crash.

Prof Sarah Harper, director of the Oxford Institute for Population Ageing, has argued convincingly that adapting to a world where many people simply don’t want children needn’t be catastrophic; that we could smooth the transition to a top-heavy, ageing population by encouraging more people to stay healthy for longer, and getting AI to fill job vacancies. (Though until the Treasury can figure out how to tax an AI agent made in San Francisco as efficiently as it does the human worker it replaces in Sunderland, that might only further erode the tax base.) But Harper is clear on the role for what she calls the “wonderful balancing act” of migration, too.

To flourish in the modern world without new blood – just you and me, getting inexorably older and older, working until we drop – seems optimistic, to say the least. Still, at least the leavers got their country back, eh? Even if they never recognise it.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Socks, smellies, chocolates and booze: 64 ‘boring’ Christmas gifts made brilliant

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 16:19:29 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

They’re perennial favourites for a reason. But if you’re going to give diaries, toiletries, candles and more, here are the ones worth getting excited about

The best Christmas gifts for 2026

Socks? For Christmas? Groundbreaking. Perhaps, but like chocolates, candles, booze and more, perennial “boring” gifts are given for a reason: they’re universally loved, easy failsafes.

But that doesn’t mean you can’t hit the mark – you just have to know where to look. We asked seven writers who know their stuff to test and pick their favourites.

By Kate Jacobs

As a scent-lover, I’ve road-tested many fine scented candles over the years, judging the “throw” – how powerful the scent is – alongside the fragrance itself.

If you’re not sure if your recipient would enjoy a scented candle, here are a few things to consider. Do they seem to have a fair few cushions and blankets? Houseplants? And are they the kind of person who will always put on lamps rather than use the big light? If so, they’re a homebody who appreciates creature comforts and indulgent treats, and a scented candle is going to be well received. The more sustainable candles are often made with natural waxes such as soy, rapeseed and coconut and scented with pure essential oils. However, many brands, even premium ones, can opt for paraffin wax blends to maximise scent levels. Here’s my shortlist of the best candles – listed in order of preference.

Dream Catcher candle, 200g

With wafts of lavender, chamomile and patchouli, this has become one of my favourite candles, particularly great when you’re trying to set the tone for winding down and getting into sleep mode. Made in England with 100% plant-based wax.

Hedgerow candle, 120ml

Available in four sizes, I loved this hand-crafted soy-wax candle’s powerful throw – its ability to fill a room with fragrance – and pretty, but non-cloying, fresh floral scent that features neroli, rose geranium and basil essential oils.

D’Orangerie candle, 220g

With 100% natural vegetable wax, this is a lovely safe bet. It has a good, strong throw without being overpowering, with orange blossom and citrus notes. I found it brisk, uplifting and invigorating, like an old-fashioned cologne.

Baies classic candle, 190g

Seen by many as the creme de la creme of scented candles, with good reason, the candles have the most amazing paraffin-based throw and can often be smelled all around the house. The very real rose-and-berries aroma is immersive and heady, the perfect accompaniment to an indulgent bath.

Rosewood and clementine soy candle, 180ml

Bright, fresh and invigorating clementine is balanced with warm, woody notes in this 100% soy-wax candle, handmade in Dorset. It’s a scent that’s perfect at Christmas – I lit one last Christmas Day – but not in an obvious clove-and-cinnamon way, so it’s just as enjoyable throughout the year.

Sanctum candle, 200g

An intense, incense-like candle that I think is perfect for the bleak midwinter, blending rose and floral frangipani with musk and smoky sandalwood. It’s made by the Cornish candle brand Keynvor, known for its complex and unusual blends; one to pique the interest of a serious candle devotee.

St Eval sea salt candle, 227g

I found this one, from a Cornish, B Corp-certified brand, to be pleasingly reminiscent of warm, summery days by the sea, with citrus notes and the subtle coconut-cream sweetness of gorse flowers – a lovely treat!

Lit Deep Vermillion refill candle and pot, 240g

Sheffield company Lit makes its refill candles (for £22) with 100% soy wax and responsibly sourced essential oils before popping them into artisan-thrown pots. This pleasing fragrance combines zingy bergamot and ylang ylang with patchouli and black spruce.

Log Fire candle, 370ml

With a paraffin-free wax blend, this wood-smoke scent has notes of incense and leather. Rich and atmospheric, it gives me the feeling of being holed up in a country house library.

Jo Malone London lime, basil and mandarin candle, 200g

Widely considered to be a modern classic, this is another paraffin-based blend with a hefty throw. The fragrance feels warm and luxurious, with sweet citrus offset by fresh herbal notes, sure to be well received.

For more, read our guide to the best genuinely great-smelling candles

By Ellie Violet Bramley

Socks come, if not in all shapes and sizes, then certainly for all occasions. Here, there are socks for bed rotting, socks for walking and maybe the most exciting, extraordinary pairs of socks – definitely the only laminated pair – I’ve ever had the good fortune to wear. Far from feeling a twinge of boredom at receiving yet another pair of socks as a gift, anyone given one of these special pairs this Christmas should feel blessed (and sure-footed).

Colorful Standard

For the colourphile in your life, these will hit just the right wavelength. There are vivid shades – Pacific blue and red tangerine – as well as more muted ones such as faded pink. Plus, beyond the first box-fresh pop, they wear well and maintain their colour. I’ve had a few pairs in reds, greens and blues for years now and they’re yet to dull. Unisex, they’ll jazz up any outfit.

Grödo

With a cosy, homespun, Nordic energy, these are perfect for the person who would love to receive a pair of home-knitted socks – but, sorry, you can’t knit. Despite being made from 100% organic wool, they’re really soft, not scratchy, and they get even softer over time. They’re also surprisingly long-lasting: I’m entering my third winter with mine, and they’re showing no signs of hanging up their skis just yet.

Donna Wilson

For those who like to make a statement with their socks, I heartily recommend Donna Wilson’s designs that range from buzzy patterns to slogans. I bought my mum a pair emblazoned all over with “blah blah blah” (sadly no longer available) and, a few years later, they’re still adding some airiness just north of the ankle. They’re such good quality she’s bought others. Just as great with loafers to the office as on a weekend with pumps.

Finisterre

For anyone who likes to scale fells and has known the injustice of an uncomfy sock on mile six, these will be a welcome treat. Made from wool and polyamide, they’re soft but hard-wearing, and have already been cushioning several autumnal strolls this year. Made in the UK, the socks have marled wool so lovely they could be worn on non-walking days, too.

Maria La Rosa

Showstopper socks may sound like a contradiction, but this laminated pair proves otherwise. Highly unusual, in a good way, they look a bit like tinfoil but feel much more slinky and mercurial to wear. They quickly soften and, yes, lose some of their initial luminescence – but nevertheless retain charm in spades. Perfect for parties.

Community Clothing, three pairs

In stark contrast to the socks above, these from Community Clothing, available in a three-pack, are a solid, supremely comfortable gift for anyone after a more workaday but still excellent sock; in this case for sports rather than soirees. Made in the UK from a mixture of cotton, nylon and spandex, their cushioned terry loop sole pads the foot in all the right places, plus they hit at mid-calf, which should keep gen Z happy.

Pairs

Hyperbolically cosy and extravagantly soft, these are the perfect socks to give someone who likes to make a “moment” of being in bed – ie the bed rotter in your life, just maybe don’t call them that. They’ll make your feet feel like hot-water bottles, in a good way.

Made in Japan

Made in Japan using the same method since the 1950s, these socks have heritage in spades. While that won’t keep your feet warm in winter, the high-quality wool will. They’re subtly chunky and, brilliantly, they come pre-shrunk (to the correct size!) to avoid the kind of shrinking disaster that often befalls our most treasured pairs.

By Annalisa Barbieri

There are so many wonderful chocolate gifts that show originality and thought beyond just grabbing something off the supermarket shelf. There is also one excellent supermarket buy on this list, however. Here is my pick of the best chocolate offerings for Christmas gifts – they can all survive being posted.

Tosier almond cognac bonbons, 100g

Squidgy, highly boozy and delicious golf-ball-sized truffles handmade in Suffolk with the yummiest chocolate. If booze is off the menu, go for Shingle Street instead: a delicious pick ’n’ mix of chocolate-covered nut ’n’ raisins.

L’Esterre 70% dark chocolate buttons, 120g

If you know someone who is strictly “dark chocolate only”, this is a treat for them. Some of the most exquisite, smooth chocolate you will ever taste, from 70 to 85% cocoa content, in button form, which somehow elevates the experience – who doesn’t love a button? Buy early: these are made in small batches and sell out fast.

Cosmic Dealer Nut Butter chocolate discovery pack, 160g

My personal favourite and the one I buy on repeat, these individually wrapped squares are a big hit with young adults in particular – perhaps because they are slightly healthier. No crazy ingredients, sweetened with dates and a delicious mix of nut butter and chocolate. The gift boxes are super pretty.

M&S Big Mix tin, 1.2kg

Launched last year, it sold out almost immediately, and friends (pointlessly) begged me to find them one. This is miles better than any similar offering out there. Big, bright, fun and stuffed full of family favourite toffees, caramels and creams. There’s nothing craft about this tin, but it does say Christmas est arrivé when you turn up at someone’s door with it.

B Chocolates honey and sea salt caramels, box of 15

You won’t find a better chocolate caramel: in nearly a decade of testing, these always come out on top with me. The perfect consistency of chewy caramel, covered in 70% chocolate, made by a tiny chocolatier on the Suffolk coast.

Heist almond caramel filled bar, 180g

It’s hard to know what to pick from Welsh bean-to-bar maker Heist. Everything gives an Enid Blyton-style tuck-box gift-from-home vibe, but the Spanish almond and caramel-filled bar is a frontrunner as it’s crunchy, chewy and delicious. The craft bars of different cocoa content chocolate, £7.95, would also make a lovely gift. The packaging is gorgeous.

Chococo festive chocolate selection box, 250g

If you’re going to give a box of chocolates, buy these super tasty ones. There are various permutations to choose from (including a non-alcoholic version), but the festive selection of 25 is a good bet for Christmas with flavours like chocolate orange, chai spice and nutmeg praline. Handmade in Dorset.

Gabriella Cugno signature gourmet box, six filled bars

For someone who loved a “newsagent” bar as a child but now fancies something more grownup, these are an excellent gift. Made by hand by the chocolatier Gabriella Cugno (chocolate adviser on the Wonka film), the bars are covered in milk, dark or white chocolate and filled with delicious chewy nutty praline and caramels. The black sesame is a standout.

Chocolate Detective chocolate eggs, box of 12

Available in Robin and three other Christmas bird themes (turtle doves, snow goose, french hens), the boxes all contain beautiful praline/salted caramel eggs. A wonderful gift to bring to someone you’re staying with. Everyone I recommend them to orders more every year. And if praline/caramel isn’t your thing, the rose and violet creams, from £15, are a classic.

Chocolate subscription

If you’re reading this a few days before Christmas and have left it too late: tsk. A chocolate subscription bought online will still show you care. Cocoa Runners can do boxes of milk, dark, both, or 100% chocolate … Pump Street does the Rare Batch Box, which includes chocolate and baked chocolate goods.

By Kate McCusker

As someone who wakes up to the news, lives in a city notorious for its terrible public transport, and is trying desperately hard to cut down on coffee, there aren’t many things that give me hope before 9am. One constant, though, is my diary, where I jot down all the banal tasks required of the day ahead, and somehow manage to dread doing them a little less in the process. Sure, the world’s on fire, but at least I can fool myself into thinking I have some control over my own little patch of life by scrawling “olive oil” and “prescription!!” in a beautifully bound planner.

To that end, I’m willing to go to battle with anyone who calls a diary a banal gift. In a world of screaming notifications, interminable online meetings and (shudder) the shared iPhone calendar beloved of couples fruitlessly trying to make dinner plans with other couples, they’ve actually become a novelty. Maybe I’m only saying this because I’ve given many as gifts over the years, but I’ll let you make your own mind up after reading this list, which ranges from the riotously colourful to the discreetly stylish.

Liberty Faber poetry diary

This week-to-view diary contains a new selection of 40 poems from the Faber catalogue every year. And like an Advent calendar, every year I maniacally tear through them all at once rather than rationing them as their curator no doubt intended. It’s hardback, A5 and is just about the most delightful diary on the market.

Papier Desk Doodles productivity planner

I’m inherently allergic to anything marketed as a “productivity” tool – don’t we have enough sticks with which to beat ourselves? – but this planner from Papier just so happens to be a pedant’s dream. If you have a type A friend in want of a gift, this 16-week planner has luxurious, thick pages with no bleed-through, an achievement tracker and undated planning pages.

Leuchtturm1917 weekly planner

Leuchtturm1917’s notebooks and diaries are stone-cold classics for a reason. Granted, they don’t have the thickest paper (fountain pen writers, beware), but they look sleek, come in a colour selection that would satisfy even the pickiest of gift recipients (read: older teenagers) and come with embossing for an extra few quid, should you want to go truly bougie.

Papersmiths 2027 diary

Papersmiths does a limited print run of each of its diaries, meaning there will be just 150 of each colour in circulation. Each is made in a bookbindery in the south-east of England, has a hardback, cloth-bound cover and thick, fountain-pen-compatible paper. It’s at the more expensive end of the scale, granted, but I reckon it’s worth the splurge – both for the brand’s commitment to reducing waste, and its sheer gorgeousness.

Good Tuesday 2026-2027 A3 family wall planner

To all adherents to the big family planner: I salute you. Not least because it stresses me out to think about what I’m doing next week, let alone across the whole year. But just because it’s a necessity for some families doesn’t mean it has to be a grim one. This month-by-month Good Tuesday calendar is printed on recycled (and recyclable) paper and bright enough to make even the most banal after-school activities look a little nicer when pasted on the wall.

Tate 2027 desk diary planner

Whether or not you believe that life imitates art, it’s nice to be guided through the year by it. This year’s Tate diary focuses on simple depictions of gardens and nature from the Tate collection that make it a great gift for someone whose tastes you’re unsure of.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Paperian Lists To Live By undated planner

There’s something sad about the planner bought in a burst of new year’s optimism, filled in as far as February and then left to expire in a drawer. Korean brand Paperian’s undated Lists to Live by journals have 24 pages with a monthly spread, 120 pages with weekly planning, and are great for those too non-committal for a conventional diary.

Mishmash undated planner

Another undated planner for good measure – this one from Portuguese stationery brand Mishmash. I like this one for jotting a quick to-do list down on the go without sullying the pages of my “proper diary”.

Redstone Diary 2027: Living Well by Julian Rothenstein

Dubbed “the thinking man’s Pirelli calendar” by the novelist Ian Sansom in these pages, the Redstone diary continues to be as delightful as ever. This year’s edition features texts selected by the Scottish writer Andrew O’Hagan and serves as a lovely rejoinder to the dreaded productivity journal. (Though it thoughtfully guides users through cocktail-making and breaking up with people, so if anything it’s perfectly conducive to a productive life.) Despite its riot of art and advice – borrowed from everyone from Marilyn Monroe to Mark Twain – it still serves as a brilliant functional diary, with ink-friendly, week-to-view pages primed and ready for all your plans. Breaking up and otherwise.

The Completist Mixer 2027 dated pocket weekly planner book

Printed on 90gsm sheet music paper, this pocket-size A6 planner is surprisingly roomy (provided your recipient has neat handwriting). It’s better for weekly planning, but the monthly overview is helpful during those “how many more weeks can I reasonably procrastinate this task” moments.

By Joanne Gould

A thoughtful bottle of something delicious, exciting or unusual is always welcome in my house. Fine wine, artisanal spirits, luxury labels and this year’s must-try tipple all make easy-yet-personal gifts for friends, family and beyond – particularly during party season. With a wide range of drinks out there, you can choose whether to spend a little or a lot.

Schug Carneros pinot noir 2024, 75cl

Waitrose says it saw a 34% sales increase in American reds this year. I tried this California number at its autumn wine showcase and thought it very good for giving as a gift; accessible price, fresh fruit flavours plus some oak ageing. Something for everyone.

Fortnum & Mason chablis, Louis Michel, 75cl

Christmas calls for the classics, and a quality chablis never disappoints, particularly when it comes bearing the traditional Fortnum’s label. Unoaked, with apples and flinty minerality; ideal with oysters and fish.

Nyetimber classic cuvée multi-vintage and bauble duo, 75cl

English sparkling is lovely at Christmas, and this is one of the most decorated. Fresh yet creamy and elegant, it goes with almost anything. And how cute is the hot air balloon bottle bauble with it?

No 3 Organic London Dry Gin and martini glasses gift set, 70cl

I’m very into the grapefruit-y crispness of No 3 London Dry right now, plus the mini martini glasses have pushed this to the top of my list. Makes a ferociously silky ice-cold gin martini.

For more, read our guide to the best gin for G&Ts, martinis and negronis

Johnnie Walker Blue Label, 70cl

If in doubt, this whisky always impresses. A smooth, honeyed scotch with a prestigious reputation but well-balanced enough to be appreciated whatever whisky style your recipient prefers. Get it engraved for extra points.

For more, read our guide to the best whisky

Isle of Raasay, the Draam, 70cl

If you suspect your whisky recipient would be open to something a little less mainstream, however, this single malt from the Hebrides does a sterling job of balancing notes of peat smoke, salt, spice and dried fruit with layers of complexity for a pretty approachable price.

Altamura Distilleries vodka, 70cl

Off the beaten track, this premium Puglian vodka is made from prized durum wheat, resulting in a cereal-sweet, clean vodka that many of my favourite hotel bars pick as their house vodka, and so should you.

For more, read our guide to the best vodkas

St-Germain spritz kit

The Hugo spritz is gen Z’s number one cocktail. Make it a stylish one with this sweet spritzing set of all-important St-Germain elderflower liqueur, Martini prosecco and art-deco-inspired glassware.

Cointreau Spicy triple sec orange liqueur, 70cl

The spicy marg is going nowhere; save yourself the chilli muddling with a triple sec ready-infused with warming bird’s eye and jalapeno for a cocktail with a kick. Great with Dwayne Johnson’s Teremana (which I recommended here) and fresh lime.

Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Clemencello, 50cl

This was a big hit at Sainsbury’s Christmas preview (M&S has one too, which I haven’t tried). Deliciously seasonal, off-sweet and zingy, I love it straight like limoncello, or try a fresher Aperol upgrade.

Shogun sake gift set, 700ml

This Peckham-brewed sake makes a thoughtful gift for curious culinary enthusiasts. Not just for Japanese cuisine, serve chilled and enjoy fresh orchard flavours and umami, or warm as a novel digestif.

By Sarah Matthews and Peter Bevan

We’ve all received them: body washes and creams in some heinous festive scent; Christmas-themed bath bombs you feel weird about using in the new year; that Lynx Africa set your well-meaning relative gifts, forgetting you’re decades past wanting to smell like a secondary-school changing room.

Gifts like these have earned their cliched reputation because they often feel like an afterthought. At their core, “smellies” are personal care products, so they should feel just that: personal. Instead of picking a random gift set from the shelves of your local chemist, choose something more unique from the options below.

Aromatherapy Associates bath and shower oil gift box

These bath and shower oils contain ingredients that are said to help alleviate common ailments, like a racing mind, aching muscles or lethargy. The 10 bestsellers inside act like a chocolate box for bath time; I keep a full-size bottle of de-stress mind on hand to help unwind during busy periods like Christmas, but this set allows you to discover which ones work for you. Each bottle includes enough for three baths in this set, but there’s also a smaller set available, in which each bottle contains one bath’s worth. SM

Verden Nocturne sleep mist, 60ml

This sleep mist from natural fragrance brand Verden is formulated with lavender and other sleep-inducing herbs. Unlike cheaper sleep mists, this comes in a glass bottle, which looks and feels luxurious. I keep one on my bedside ready to use whenever I struggle to drift off; it works like a charm. SM

Phlur vanilla skin body oil, 118ml

More interesting than a moisturiser and packaged in a weighty glass pump, the Phlur vanilla skin body oil has a cocooning, woody vanilla scent that lingers on the skin. It also has squalane, jojoba and rosehip oils, all of which leave you feeling nourished and glowy. SM

Satisfaction eau de parfum, 100ml

The Rolling Stones worked with fragrance maker Nirvana Brands to launch Subversive Scents, a line of punchy unisex fragrances. Satisfaction is the most intimate of the lot, blending spiced pineapple with tobacco and a grounding base of cedar and tonka bean. It leaves a subtle trail of scent behind you as you move, has amazing longevity, and its locking lid means you can take it rockin’ and rollin’ wherever you please. SM

No 98 beauty Hydra Bond hair masque, 175ml

This is the best-smelling hair care I’ve ever used. Hydra Bond is designed to restore hair’s elasticity, leaving it feeling soft, and its sophisticated spiced woody scent lingers on the hair for days after use. Apply it to damp strands for at least 20 minutes before a shower or wear overnight for a deeper hydration hit. SM

For more, read our guide to the best hair masks

Ritual of Sakura whipped body cream, 220ml

Rituals has stepped up its refillable body care game. Now, one of the best rich, indulgent moisturising creams comes in a weighty glass jar that looks and feels high-end. When it’s empty, pop out the recyclable insert and refill it. SM

For more, read our guide to the best body moisturisers

Lush massage oil bar, 65g

Unlike traditional massage oils that run all over the place, these massage bars melt on to the skin exactly where you want a bit of slip. Deep Sleep is my favourite from the range – it has a relaxing lavender, chamomile and neroli fragrance and contains magnesium to help soothe aching muscles. SM

Salt & Stone body wash & lotion duo, 450ml

Leaping Bunny certified cruelty-free, Salt & Stone uses vitamin C, niacinamide and humectants in this body care set. The soothing seaweed-infused body lotion absorbs quickly, while the body wash lathers up generously, leaving skin soft and resilient. Its santal and vetiver scent is glorious. SM

Bob the Bob Starter Plan body wash kit, gift purchase

Bob is a fresh take on men’s body wash. Solid soap bars slot into a sleek refillable applicator that lathers generously while exfoliating your skin, ditching the need for plastic bottles and throwaway bath accessories such as puffs or loofas. The sulfate-free, vitamin E-enriched formula is gentle on the skin. In the “starter plan” you receive a wall mount for your shower and three bars, each with a different fragrance, to try – my favourite is sandalwood and geranium. PB

Mircea cedar and rosemary hand & body wash, 400ml

Mircea makes shower gel feel like a proper present. It comes in a weighty glass bottle they’ll want on display, which you can top up with plastic-free refills (a sachet of concentrated crystals which mix with water). It’s sulfate-free, vegan, 99% natural and scented with perfumes from Grasse, France’s perfume capital – which explains why it smells more expensive than anything you can buy at the supermarket. There are three scents on offer, but my favourite is cedar and rosemary. PB

&Horace eau de parfum, 50ml

Finding a lasting fragrance that’s relatively affordable isn’t easy. One that delivers every time for me, though, is Horace. My favourite is &Horace – it opens with fresh, zesty bergamot before settling into a crowd-pleasing creamy sandalwood – but, if you think he’d prefer something cosier, Vintage Vanilla is also a strong choice for the season. PB

Aesop Arrival travel kit

This is the kind of present I love to receive at Christmas because there’s always a long weekend on the horizon. Aesop’s Arrival kit packs shampoo, conditioner, its cult geranium leaf body cleanser (one of my favourites) and rind concentrate body balm into 50ml bottles. When you order online with Aesop you can select complimentary gift wrap at checkout in one of the brand’s signature scented muslin bags (each is spritzed with a fragrance when it’s packed). Aesop is a vegan B Corp, too. PB

Cowshed the Powder Room hand care caddy

I’ve tried a lot of hand washes, but Cowshed’s Restore is one that’s earned a regular spot in my rotation. The exfoliating wash easily handles dirt – even after potting plants – without leaving my hands feeling dry, and the lotion soaks in fast for a nice, soft finish. It smells like a British herb garden – think minty, thymey goodness – so it’s perfect for the keen gardeners in your life. It also comes with a smart black caddy, making it feel special next to the sink. PB

Malin+Goetz tomato home spray, 147ml

Every friendship group has them: the one who talks about their tomato plants the way most people talk about their children. This is the gift for them, and, actually, for everyone else, too. It’s the freshest room spray I’ve ever used and impossible not to like. A quick spritz before guests arrive and the house smells better than it would after a day of cleaning – and it even looks good on the sideboard. PB

Grown Alchemist polishing exfoliator, 75ml

A great gift for women, too, but most men I know love a face scrub – there’s something about that gritty texture that makes it feel like it’s doing a proper job – but many rely on abrasive ingredients that leave the skin feeling raw. Grown Alchemist uses finely milled bamboo, which buffs away dead skin and dullness without the harshness. The camellia seed and rosehip oils also make your face feel nourished rather than tight afterwards, and the scent – orange zest and grapefruit – takes you to the spa every time you shower. Just make sure he sticks to twice a week: overdoing it with a scrub risks damaging the skin’s protective barrier. PB

For more, read our guide to the best Christmas gifts for 2026 and Sali Hughes’s best beauty gifts

Christmas shopping can be tough, but the Filter is here to help. We’ve been testing Christmas presents all year to help you find thoughtful, creative and genuinely brilliant gifts for everyone on your list. Browse our other gift guides for hundreds more tried-and-tested ideas, from the best gifts for mums and dads to teens and tweens.

Parents urged to vaccinate children for flu as hospital cases surge in England

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:52:57 GMT

Pharmacies being asked to administer jabs to children for first time amid NHS pre-Christmas vaccination push

Parents are being urged to make sure their children are vaccinated against flu before Christmas amid a surge in hospitalisations, with pharmacies being asked to administer them for the first time.

The NHS in England is pushing to vaccinate thousands of children who missed out when jabs were administered at schools. More than 6,000 high street pharmacies are offering appointments, with bookings opening on Monday through the NHS app or the NHS find a pharmacy webpage, with appointments from Tuesday.

Dr Suzanna McDonald, the flu vaccination programme lead at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said: “Vaccinating schoolchildren against flu not only helps protect them, but crucially helps protect younger siblings and other more vulnerable family members at greater risk, like grandparents.

“Ensuring all children from age two receive a flu vaccine every winter is so important to help prevent the thousands of unnecessary hospitalisations we see among unvaccinated children.

“Please don’t dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children. It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives. Don’t put your child needlessly at risk; book that appointment with your GP surgery or at some community pharmacies offering the vaccine.”

Pharmacies are also offering nasal spray flu vaccinations for two- and three-year-olds. Children can fall very ill with flu and can spread it to more vulnerable people. More than 3.5 million children from reception to year 11 have already had their vaccine.

The rate of flu admissions in England stood at 9 in 100,000 people last week; up from 5 in 100,000 in the previous seven days, according to the UKHSA. Admissions stood at 4.9 in 100,000 in the equivalent week in 2025.

UKHSA data shows the rate has not been at such a high level at this point in November in any previous year this decade. It confirmed the number of attendances at hospital emergency departments for flu-like illnesses was “above seasonally expected levels”.

The NHS England national medical director, Prof Frankie Swords, said: “The run-up to Christmas can be such a busy time for parents, so it’s great news that for the first time, it’s now really easy to book your child’s flu vaccine at your local high street pharmacy if they missed it in school.”
