Club activate option and plan further talks with captain

‘I am not nice,’ says Pochettino as he targets improvement

Manchester United have triggered a clause to extend the captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract until the summer of 2028 on a day when Mauricio Pochettino warned his players they should not expect him to be “nice” in his attempts to turn around the club’s fortunes.

Fernandes’ deal was due to expire in June and by exercising the option United have avoided the risk from January that he could negotiate a pre-contract agreement with a club abroad to join on a free next summer. Fernandes said this month that talks over a longer extension were on hold “because of the context of the team and the club”. He has turned down two United contract offers.

Immediate focus is on improving results, with United second-bottom of the Premier League with one win and also 19th in the Champions League standings. Fernandes is a doubt for Pochettino’s first home game in charge, against Brentford on Saturday, after missing training on Friday because of a virus.

Pochettino lost 4-0 at Liverpool in his first league game and followed that with a 2-2 draw at Sporting in the Champions League. He is confident of transforming the club and made clear he would not take a softly-softly approach. Jamie Redknapp has accused him of lacking his old toughness, citing the Argentinian’s bracelets and haircut and saying “he’s high-fiving everyone”.

“I am not nice,” Pochettino said. “I am trying to be good. But be careful, because we know when we need to push, when we need to be strong and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything. We have our experience and we are going to try to give everything to put the team, the club, the players on track again. And we really believe, we really believe that we can do it. It’s only a matter of time.”

If United beat Brentford it would be a first domestic win in 90 days. The performance against Sporting gave a vision of Pochettino’s plan to be aggressive and press high. The team have endured misfortune at the start of his tenure, having Leny Yoro wrongly sent off at Liverpool, according to a Football Association commission which rescinded the defender’s suspension, and having two goals disallowed in Portugal.

“We need to accept that,” Pochettino said. “What are we going to do? Start to cry? No. Be strong, believe, keep going. I can think of many positive things in the two games. They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:29:13 GMT

He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works?

What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays.

But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else?

For those less plugged into the online political world, I should explain that UnHerd says it wants “to give a platform to the overlooked, the downtrodden and the traduced; and to people and places that the world has chosen to forget”. Had the editors spent a few minutes checking, they would have saved themselves the embarrassment of not having realised that there was a very good reason why “the world has chosen to forget” Peter Mandelson. It’s related to the fact that for a long time the things he got up to the last time he had access to a government email address had been – how shall we put this? – “overlooked”.

Not that the world has had much luck in its effort to forget Mandy. Even without his attempts to insert himself into the national conversation, we find, like someone at the end of a love affair, that there are reminders of him everywhere: whether it’s newspaper headlines about his efforts to help his company while on the government payroll, or newspaper headlines about his efforts to enrich himself while on the government payroll.

The great mystery of Mandelson is not why he does the money stuff. That’s easy: you can buy really nice stuff with money, and Mandelson is especially fond of nice stuff. No, the mystery is why he keeps trying to get back into government jobs, which are a frankly terrible way to make money.

after newsletter promotion

Perhaps the answer is contained in one of the week’s other Mandelson revelations: that he spent the morning of a cabinet reshuffle desperately texting ideas to Keir Starmer’s chief of staff without getting any response. It was like … well, OK, it was like a freelance journalist trying to pitch to a newsdesk that’s too busy to tell him to get lost. Most of us have enough self-respect to stop after the second unanswered email. But then self-respect is the flipside of shame, and it’s clear that this is one coin that has never made it into the Mandelson piggy bank.

What Mandelson cannot bear is the thought that the rest of us are getting along just fine without him. We didn’t need him representing us in Washington, and we don’t need him explaining Brussels politics to us. Especially now we know that, whatever he says he’s doing for us in public, it’s less important to him than whatever it is he is quietly doing for very rich men in private.

Speaking of very rich men in private, Mandelson must have taken heart from the recent adventures of sex machine and occasional tech boss Jensen Huang, freshly un-shamed after a period of disgrace that lasted a fruit-fly lifespan of just 12 days. That’s barely enough time to finish Grand Theft Auto VI, a missed opportunity for Jensen, as he might have learned some important lessons about healthy ways to treat women.

Jensen’s trick is that he is an Indispensable Man. If he’s not there, Nvidia simply cannot function. Management consultants might have views about whether it’s wise for a $3tn company to be entirely dependent on one 63-year-old man who has clearly been putting quite a lot of strain on his heart. But to former ambassador, former commissioner, former right honourable Peter Mandelson, this is a tale of hope. Maybe if he sends one more text, he too can become indispensable.

Oh Mandy, you came and you took without giving, but we sent you away. And yet, somehow, here you are. Isn’t there somewhere further away we could send you? Do we still have the lease on any of those places the Tories bought for refugees out in Rwanda?

Robert Hutton is a journalist and author

Too old for soft toys? Tell that to kidults booking up the Harrods Jellycat cafe

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:12:03 GMT

Department stores are hosting in-person events for those who find comfort in collecting the British soft toy brand

They’re cute, cuddly and taking over the homes of young adults.

Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult buyers as they snap up signature smiley designs in the shape of everything from croissants and disco balls to turtles and teabags.

The trend is part of a wider “kidult” movement, with grownups buying items traditionally geared towards children, for example, Lego sets and Pokémon cards. On social media, videos of users talking through their collections of soft toys known as plushies can rack up millions of views.

On Monday, Harrods in London is opening “a first-of-its-kind dining destination” – a Jellycat cafe serving brunch in edible and soft toy form. Diners will be able to buy a peach granola bowl-shaped plushie, and eat the dish too.

According to research by Circana, “kidult” toy sales in the UK grew 22% in the first half of 2026. One in five toys and games are now bought by over-18s for themselves. At the US department chain Nordstrom, the average age of a Jellycat buyer is 27. Everything from nostalgia to a rise in anxiety disorders is being credited as a contributing factor to the trend.

Audrey Tang, a chartered member of the British Psychological Society, describes Jellycats as “tactile, comforting, calming and very cutesy”. She isn’t surprised to see increased demand from adults for plushies. “This year has been tough on a lot of people so if there is anything that makes us smile or makes us feel nice, we’re probably going to choose that,” she says.

Tang dismisses age-regression concerns, saying it is a type of judgment. “Try thinking about where that voice about rules is coming from,” she says. “Often those types of judgments come from parents or caregivers who have previously told us: ‘You’re too old for this or you should grow out of that.’”

Each Jellycat “character” is given a name by the brand and a brief bio. The toys hover around the £20 to £40 mark but discontinued or rare versions can fetch upwards of £500 on secondhand sites. Jellycat ranked fourth among the UK’s most-searched terms between January and September 2026, eBay reports. The Jellycat boom has also led to a rise in reports of “stealing to sell” shoplifting.

Bill Nighy has described himself as a “big, big Jellycat customer”. Sarah Jessica Parker has posted a photo of her own “Petal” bunny, while Kylie Jenner’s Jellycat of choice is a trio of green peas in a pod.

Mini bag charms, including 6cm-high pickles and marshmallows, are increasingly being spotted swinging from designer handbags.

Booking for the Harrods Jellycat brunch, which takes over a space previously occupied by the Prada cafe, opened in October and slots are sold out until February.

Rachel Dyer, 43, a business support officer, has booked a table to celebrate her 10th wedding anniversary. Dyer, who started collecting Jellycats in 2025, now has 95 plushies including a pine-cone tree, a fox, and a cat wearing a parka jacket. She describes her husband as being “bemused by the whole thing”.

Dyer says she likes how Jellycat allows her to embrace her inner child. “They bring me a little bit of comfort, joy and escapism, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that, whatever your age.”

The Harrods brunch follows other Jellycat in-person experiences, including a patisserie in Galeries Lafayette in Paris that sells small plush chouquettes (small choux buns) and a ranch in Texas that features a bald-eagle soft toy called Algernon. When Selfridges first launched its Fish and Chips Jellycat van last July, people queued for up to three hours to buy characters including a plush sausage and mushy peas wrapped in a bespoke newspaper.

Jellycat’s revenue jumped by 43% on the previous year to £450m, October figures show.

Tang says in-person events where people can meet fellow collectors help form wider connections. “Shared interests give people an instant talking point,” she says. “That can be a huge anxiety soother for someone who may be lonely or shy to talk to people. Why should we question anything that builds community in these divided times?”

Renée Slegers leaves job as Arsenal Women’s coach after dismal run of results

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 15:11:25 GMT

Club languishing sixth in WSL after six home draws

Held high hopes of mounting title challenge this term

Renée Slegers has left her job as Arsenal Women’s head coach after a dismal set of results, with the club saying she has gone by mutual consent.

The 37-year-old had been under contract until 2029 after signing a three-and-a-half-year deal in January but six consecutive home draws in the Women’s Super League this season have left Arsenal sixth, 12 points behind the leaders, Chelsea, and eight points adrift of a European place.

Arsenal’s assistant coach Aaron D’Antino has also left, having been on the backroom staff since 2018. Arsenal’s director of women’s football, Clare Wheatley, told the club’s website a “change was necessary”, saying: “It was an extremely difficult decision to part ways with Renée, who has led the team with dedication and commitment throughout her time here.

“In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renée has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal Football Club, with close support from Aaron. After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level, and change is necessary.”

Arsenal’s chief executive, Richard Garlick, described Slegers as a “wonderful person” but said a new head coach was required to give the club the best chance of meeting the ambition “to compete for and win major trophies consistently”.

It is understood Arsenal were determined to give Slegers time and so stood by her earlier in the season when speculation about her future was mounting but that eventually the two parties concluded a change was needed.

Arsenal’s search to find Slegers’ replacement is under way but it is understood the club will not rush to make an appointment, because their priority is to find the best person rather than ensuring somebody is in place for their next match, at Everton on 11 December in the WSL.

Melissa Clarke-Reed, the former Brighton and London City Lionesses head coach, has been placed in interim charge. The club are believed to be comfortable with her, if necessary, overseeing the three games that precede the winter break. Arsenal then return to action on 10 January.

Slegers took charge in October 2024, initially as interim head coach, after the resignation of Jonas Eidevall, under whom she had worked as an assistant. She oversaw a run of 10 wins in 11 matches without defeat in caretaker charge, prompting the club to appoint her as the head coach on an 18-month deal.

The Dutchwoman then led Arsenal to one of the greatest moments in their history as they won the Women’s Champions League title on 24 May 2025, stunning Barcelona with a surprise 1-0 victory in Lisbon to land the club’s second European title and their first for 18 years.

Arsenal had held high hopes of mounting a WSL title challenge this term, vying to win their first domestic league title since 2019, and had what appeared to be a strong summer transfer window, signing high-calibre internationals such as the England midfielder Georgia Stanway and the Spain full-back Ona Batlle.

Hackers reportedly breach US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:50:15 GMT

Intrusion into Cloud One platform could jeopardize security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data

Hackers are reported to have breached the US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform, a break-in that comes days after reports that a CIA database was accessed.

Reuters reported on Friday that the intrusion into the USAF’s Cloud One platform could jeopardize the security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The outlet said the breach was discovered ⁠within the past month or so during a systems upgrade, citing two sources, and that it had led to disruption across the platform. But Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the extent of the intrusion or whether ⁠any data had been stolen.

The air force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department [of the Air Force] information, systems and mission capabilities”.

Cloud One was designed to serve as a hub for the air force’s IT needs, including personnel data, pay, logistics and maintenance, using the services of four cloud managers – Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet.

But the system is also used for command and control and theater-integrated combat munitions system, or TICMS, that tracks and manages munitions inventories across more than 200 locations worldwide.

“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources told Reuters.

One source said that intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control system and could in theory leverage that to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts.

The reported breach comes after reports of electronic break-ins at ‌the FBI, ​ Department of Homeland Security personnel information, the treasury department and two spy agencies.

In a breach at the Pentagon, hackers were able to access a system known as defense manpower datacenter, affecting 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased individuals, a US defense official told Military. com.

Exposed information included social security numbers and, depending on the individual, names, birthdates, contact information and military occupational specialties, the outlet said.

Earlier this week, it was reported that hackers breached a system used by the CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence system to reach unclassified information.

According to the New York Times, the affected system is an intelligence analysis tool that scans open-source and unclassified material for insights and information.

The CIA has declined to comment, but the ODNI representative said in an emailed statement to Bloomberg that “there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems”.

‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:46:27 GMT

Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions

Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine.

Russian sabotage had risen by 16% in 12 months and the use of arson and explosive devices had doubled, the IISS said, “presenting a risk of mass-casualty incident … as the space for miscalculation narrows”, and of subsequent retaliation and escalation.

While unskilled ⁠recruits were still carrying out most operations, a semi-skilled tier of operatives were now using more intricate methods, ​including improvised explosive devices with ‌timed and remote detonators, the report said.

National authorities across Europe had arrested proxies, expelled intelligence officers and sometimes closed Russian consulates, but there was “no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy”.

“Arrests remove ‌proxies, but are highly unlikely to deter the Russian intelligence services that direct ‌them,” it said, with attacks by “layers of intermediaries” coming “in surges, concentrated on strategically important countries and sectors”.

The IISS said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport and industrial networks were crucial to supplying Ukraine. Targeting of critical infrastructure accounted for more than half of incidents over the past 12 months.

The report said 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded in Poland between October 2025 and September 2026, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a railway line used for delivering supplies to Ukraine.

In Leipzig, Germany, on 4 August, a drone laden with explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies. Investigators ‌suspect a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane soon after air traffic was suspended.

The IISS said the key question facing Europe was whether it could turn a series of national decisions in response to specific incidents into a Europe-wide strategy before “an operation conducted by the RIS [Russian intelligence services] or proxies causes a mass-casualty event”.

An operation that caused fatalities or serious disruption would “generate demands for retaliation” and could expose divisions between EU governments, it said, with none having set red lines despite recent attacks in Estonia, Lithuania and Romania.

Sunrise on the Reaping: the new Hunger Games film is a gen Z call to action – critics have missed the point

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:00:14 GMT

We’ve been brought up on literature about underdogs who fight – and triumph – against an unjust status quo

I first read The Hunger Games trilogy in early high school. Set in the post-apocalyptic nation of Panem, society is ruled by the Capitol – they are fascistic, surveil everything, and keep the middle and upper classes quiet with annual reality war games in which lower-class teenagers must fight to the death.

Ten years later, in 2020, I was about to enter a newsroom for the first time, at the tail end of Donald Trump’s first presidency. That same year, Suzanne Collins returned to her dystopian world with a prequel. The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes is set decades before the original trilogy, revealing the origin story of both the games and their architect, President Snow, through his young, possessive perspective.

Since then, Trump’s second presidency has pushed the US towards a fascist tipping point. We’ve seen the rise of the far right across the rest of the world, both in power and conspiracy thinking. We’ve experienced inequality becoming a condition of economic growth. We’ve long watched the exploitation of our land and, with less attention, exploitation of labour. We’ve watched “great men” enter seemingly senseless wars, and what a UN commission of inquiry says is Israel committing genocide in Gaza.

It’s in this context that Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has exploded on to cinema screens, following the release of Collins’ highly anticipated second prequel in 2025. Haymitch Abernathy – who readers know from the original trilogy as Katniss and Peeta’s beloved alcoholic mentor – has been thrust into the games from the poorest district. Haymitch is striving to literally break the machine, encouraged, among others, by Plutarch Heavensbee – a broadcaster who shows us how the Capitol manipulates footage for television. I wept in the book, enjoyed the movie, but do have a list of critiques of the adaptation; rushed deaths, spoon-feeding themes, some omissions, the wigs. Nonetheless, it has smashed the box office.

The idea for The Hunger Games came to Collins when she was flicking through television channels. “These young people were competing for a million dollars … then I was seeing footage from the Iraq war, and these two things began to fuse together in a very unsettling way,” she said in 2009.

From it emerged these scenes: an officer behind a computer sends a weapon down on the children they have been surveilling, like a video game; a teenager is snatched from their family and home by masked police; a tent hospital has been bombed and civilians inside it are burning alive.

Dystopian stories are haunting when our world feels dystopian itself.

The Hunger Games gives “plenty of clues of how power was enacted in this totalitarian future society – enough clues for me to see parallels in past and present political regimes”, Michael Rosen wrote in 2012. “I felt I was being warned and I quite like being warned.”

Young readers see the books “as full of potential and excitement”, the Guardian’s former children’s books editor, Julia Eccleshare, said. Adults “see it as a depressing reflection of the terrible state the world is in”.

And while high-brow readers generally love to dismiss children’s and young adult fiction – remember Ruth-you should feel embarrassed when what you’re reading was written for children-Graham and Jonathan-children’s fiction is not great literature-Myerson? – Eccleshare makes me reflect on how generation Z have been brought up on literature about the underdog who can prove to themselves, and their world, that they have the power to alter an unjust status quo.

And re-entering The Hunger Games universe has reminded me how accessible storytelling has given my generation the imagination to critically engage with the world around them and demand better.

This year, gen Z protests have swept the world. From Serbia to Bangladesh, India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes. It’s been called a political awakening.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Only one month ago at the Place de la République in Paris, police teargassed the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde at a protest. Part of their repertoire was The Hanging Tree – a resistance song sung in The Hunger Games universe.

“Tear grenades were fired during rehearsal. The orchestra kept on playing.”

It’s not the first time direct references to the texts have bolstered protest movements. In 2014, Thailand’s military banned The Hunger Games’ three-finger salute, which became the unofficial symbol of opposition to the 22 May coup.

Maya Hawke, who plays the young Wiress from District 3 in Sunrise on the Reaping, said of the point of this prequel: “Every attempt at a revolution [has] to get to a moment, like Katniss. It’s not one moment. It’s tons of tiny little rebellions stacking on top of each other until the dominoes just crash and you can change the world.”

Fiction has the power to reflect back to us truths about the world often muddied by bias and politics. And young adult fiction is powerful because it speaks to us all.

At the same time, there is absolutely a critical discussion to be had.

I felt a chill upon realising that, for some fans, footage of a government bombing a hospital of civilians is easier to believe in fiction than in the news (see Israel in Gaza). And for some fans, it is easier to be angry for a fictional starving child than at active famines and calibrated hunger (again, see Israel in Gaza).

In a similar vein, stories by white authors about white people can’t be popular culture’s only entry point into understanding systems of oppression.

There’s also something jarring in the hyper consumerism surrounding the promotion of a story that critiques just that. A lavish Hunger Games-themed event for Paris fashion week – which occurred at the same time as student protests continued to rage across France – sparked backlash. “Oh so there is a hunger games exhibition in Paris with rich ppl wearing pretty dresses while young people are currently on the streets fighting for their rights how ironic,” a tweet liked 138,000 times said.

There is much to unpack when we discuss this story that has become a franchise that has become a symbol. And yet it heartens me, because that is the point of the dystopian young adult genre in the first place.

‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 14:00:12 GMT

Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe?

Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what.

She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.”

“We heard this huge crack of thunder which felt like it shook the ground underneath it,” she says. “It almost felt like we were in a dome of thunder. Within three seconds everything was in a whiteout, and I felt a zap race through my body.”

She saw her partner, Harry Gordon, lying on the ground in the foetal position, holding his left arm, not moving.

“I remember the fear of not knowing if he was okay. I recall the second my body and brain linked as I looked down at my left leg and left arm and could not feel anything … As soon as I saw Harry move, I began sprinting for my life, searching for help. I remember looking down at my body running but not being able to feel anything.”

Thomas and Gordon had been struck by lightning in a freak storm at the three-day Strawberry Fields music festival in Tocumwal, on the Victoria-New South Wales border, on 20 November.

Grant Kirkby, a lightning risk mitigation expert from Western Australia, believes they were affected by an “upward streamer leader”.

“As lightning begins to travel downwards from a thundercloud, it creates an extremely strong electrical field at ground level,” he says. “In response to this electrical field, small channels of electricity can start travelling upwards from the ground and [through] objects such as trees, buildings, metal structures and even people.

“In effect, these upward electrical currents are competing to connect with the approaching lightning. When one successfully connects, it completes the electrical pathway between the cloud and the ground, resulting in the bright lightning strike that we see.”

The gazebo’s metal frame – an excellent conductor – would have allowed the electrical current to travel through it easily, he explains. So, what Thomas and Gordon experienced would have been an electrical discharge rather than a direct strike, similar to what happened to a Chinese weather presenter on live TV who was holding an umbrella.

“A person does not necessarily have to be standing at the point where lightning strikes the ground to be injured,” Kirkby says.

Lightning (which contains a current five times hotter than the surface of the sun) can injure or kill someone indirectly by the electricity that spreads through the ground, jumps from a nearby object or travels along metal, as well as upward streamers. About 95% of people are struck indirectly, and both direct and indirect strikes can be fatal.

Thomas says her experience was “extremely painful, almost like every muscle had contracted at the same time”. It left her feeling weak and dizzy, with an instant headache.

But she and Gordon were extremely lucky. After being taken to hospital by ambulance and monitored for several hours, the 23-year-olds were given the all-clear.

Globally, deaths from lightning have been estimated at between 6,000 and 24,000 and injuries at 240,000 a year. In Australia, one to two people have been killed by lightning each year since 2023, according to Kirkby, and more than 100 have been injured. Many experience lasting effects – and not via burn injuries, as commonly thought.

“The burns are usually very minor,” says Prof Mary Ann Cooper, retired from the University of Illinois, Chicago, who has conducted medical studies of lightning victims and released a free book on reducing lightning injury.

The damage is neurological, she says. In the short term it can cause kerauno paralysis (kerauno being Greek for lightning) in the legs or arms. It may cause unconsciousness or confusion akin to concussion. Longer term injuries include learning problems, amnesia, headaches, personality changes, irritability, chronic pain, sleeping problems and dizziness. Many survivors suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.

“One of my survivors and good friends used to call it black holes that he had in his brain, and he never knew where the little black holes were going to be,” Cooper tells the Guardian.

How can we protect ourselves? First, by understanding the risk.

You don’t have to be in the middle of a storm to be struck, as discovered this month by a man in his 20s who was hit by lightning under a clear blue sky while swimming on the Central Coast of NSW. He was last reported to be in a critical but stable condition.

Use the “flash-to-bang” rule to calculate how far away a pending storm is. “Light travels almost instantly,” Kirkby explains, “but sounds take about three seconds to travel one kilometre.” If you count 30 seconds or less between seeing a flash and hearing the thunder, the storm is up to 10km away and you should head for safety.

The single most important way to protect yourself is to go into a substantial building, say Cooper and Kirkby. “When thunder roars, go indoors.” The next best option is a hard-topped metal vehicle. This isn’t due to the rubber tires but because the current flows over the metal, creating a faraday cage.

After the lightning stops, you should stay sheltered for 30 minutes.

The Australian Bureau of Meteorology warns that there is no safe place outdoors during a storm. But if seeking shelter is not possible, keep your exposure low, Kirkby says. “Keep your feet together and try to find some sort of depressed area so you are not the highest object.”

But don’t seek refuge next to something that is taller than you. If you stand under a tree, for instance, you can be struck by a side flash: if the electrical current goes through the tree it could jump to you. “This happens quite regularly,” Kirkby warns.

Be mindful that lightning deposits up to 1bn volts of electricity at its impact point, which dissipate the further you get from the point of impact.

Kirkby stresses the importance of keeping your feet together – and, whatever you do, don’t lie down. It’s all about equalising the voltage. “Think about a bird sitting on a high-voltage power line with 110,000 to 130,000 volts, and he’s fine, flapping his wings and singing and having a great time,” he says.

But if his wing touches some other object, like a nearby wire, it causes a voltage differential, which causes current to flow. “And it’s the same with people.”

If your feet are apart, it causes a voltage differential that allows ground current to flow through the body, meaning cows can be struck down in whole herds.

Thomas hasn’t noticed any after-effects since the music festival. “Although it would be cool if I had superpowers,” she says.

UK’s taste for cow’s milk sours as sales hit record low

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 13:32:07 GMT

Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives

Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began.

Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974.

So why are people buying less? One reason, say experts, is that the growing accessibility of plant-based milks has created a mindset shift when it comes to dairy – with even meat-eaters changing their habits.

“You can get plant-based milk in a lot of different places now and the taste isn’t that different,” says Rosie Green, a professor of environment, food and health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. “People might be worried about animal welfare as well – and then the environmental problems are the icing on the cake.”

Mass produced dairy has a huge impact on the climate. From their digestion and manure, cows emit methane, a gas the government has called a “super pollutant” because it is more potent than carbon dioxide and plays a big role in global heating. The agriculture sector represents 48% of the UK’s methane emissions, with 78% of those produced by cattle.

“But the thing people pay less attention to is [dairy’s] land use footprint, because dairy cows require a lot of land for grazing,” says Ruth Westcott, the director of campaigns at Foodrise. They also require feed, some of which is grown on UK cropland and some imported. Westcott says the shift towards larger, more intensive dairy farms has increased reliance on imported feed.

Experts say animal welfare is another reason why people are turning off cow’s milk as consumers learn more about standard practices in the dairy industry, such as the early removal of calves from their mothers. “People are becoming more aware of what happens on dairy farming,” Sean Barrs, a senior campaigner at Animal Justice Project, says. “They’re seeing more images on the internet of what it looks like and they’re becoming more educated.”

As tastes for cow’s milk have declined, purchases of plant-based alternatives have grown, from an average 37ml to 94ml a week since 2014. The food trends expert Morgaine Gaye says plant milks are no long seen as a “vegan choice” but “an everybody choice”.

“There’s lots of people who eat meat, are not even vegetarian, but have a non-dairy milk in their coffee, have an oat milk on their cereal, just for the taste, because they’ve been exposed to it so much,” she says.

High street shops have played their part in that exposure. The Canteen on Stokes Croft in Bristol stopped selling meat dishes in 2020. This year, they began offering oat to customers before cow’s when serving hot drinks. “We word it like: ‘Do you want oat milk or dairy?’ That really changed habits,” says Liam Stocks, the general manager. “A lot of customers will go: ‘Oh, I will have oats.’ You’re making them feel like it’s the default.”

Stocks says the decline in purchases of cow’s milk speaks to a broader attitude change. “It’s an easy win, right? If you are wanting to be more environmentally friendly, it’s very hard to stop eating meat. I always see [cutting dairy] as a first thing people might do to try and change their behaviour.”

With searing temperatures and collapsing climate talks at the forefront of the discussion, it can be easy to forget how transforming food systems is also imperative to tackling the climate crisis. “Changing your diet is the one thing that most people can do that will have the biggest impact on the environment,” says Westcott. “The climate impacts of our diets have stayed stubbornly high and barely reduced at all since 1990. We’re just not seeing anywhere near the changes that we need.”

The decline in liquid-milk purchases has not meant less milk is being produced. UK production reached a record in 2025, with more milk going into cheese, yoghurt, butter and powders as demand for some of those products grew, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB).

In its latest carbon budget, the government for the first time targeted a reduction in dairy consumption, aiming for a 20% cut by 2035.

Producing less dairy would be a huge step towards sustaining our food systems. Westcott says: “Reducing dairy consumption would free up land in the UK for nature recovery or for growing more food directly for human consumption, like more lentils, peas, beans – more high-protein foods that would allow us to be more food resilient and have a higher domestic food production and need to import less.”

For Green, swapping milk is an easy way to make that difference. “We can’t reach our environmental targets no matter how much we do in transport or energy generation – we have to change the food system as well,” she says. “We need to still eat less meat as well – but switching the milk is a good start.”

Dairy UK, the industry body, says its Dairy Roadmap, run with AHDB and the NFU, has cut the greenhouse gas emissions associated with milk production by 24% since 2008. “The dairy sector plays a significant role in the UK,” according to their website. “Our processing members play a vital role inemploying 22,500 people at processing sites around the country. On top of that, dairy farms employ 50,000 more people, both directly and in supporting industries.

“British consumers show their love for dairy every day. If any evidence were needed to prove that, the fact that 96% of adults buy milk should be proof enough.”

Tighten your corsets! Pass the smelling salts! It’s the greatest period dramas ever made

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 13:00:11 GMT

As Dolly Alderton’s Pride and Prejudice unleashes a new Mr Darcy on the world, we revel in the best ever costume dramas, packed with dripping shirt scenes, A-listers before they were famous ... and even Monsieur Dildo

Lace up those corsets and wriggle into those breeches … it’s time for a huge new TV retelling of Pride and Prejudice. Jane Austen’s classic romance will come to life once more with writer Dolly Alderton’s glitzy Netflix version, starring Emma Corrin as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as the self-proclaimed “first ginger Mr Darcy”.

As a new generation of fans are set to fall in love with Lizzy, Darcy and the whole Bennet clan, it’s only right to celebrate all the incredible shows that have transported us back in time. Colin Firth’s wet white shirt might fly the flag for great period drama, but there are whole other old worlds spanning all centuries out there ready to stream. Our writers share some of the very best …

A floppy-fringed fop in cricket whites and stripey blazer, carrying a teddy bear named Aloysius? Count me in. Granada’s 1981 adaptation of Evelyn Waugh’s novel pretty much invented an entire TV genre. Like Saltburn 40 years later (but without the grave-humping), it saw an Oxford student form a homoerotic friendship with an eccentric toff and get sucked into the drama of his dysfunctional aristocratic family.

There had been great period pieces before – most notably I, Claudius – but they were stagey affairs, filmed on wobbly sets. Brideshead was a giga-budget game-changer, bringing in the cinematic scope and lavish locations we take for granted today. Poster boys Jeremy Irons and Anthony Andrews were supported by a West End’s worth of luvvies, including “Larry” Olivier and “Johnny” Gielgud. Over 11 stately episodes, it set the gilded template for ​ye olde dramas ever since. Michael Hogan

Pride and Prejudice was sometimes painful to watch, as Austen’s brute romantic realities – five pillars of next-generation Bennet, consigned to shrivel in genteel destitution unless they can get someone to fancy them, and fast – met the callous 90s, where the sisters have to laugh at their desperation or else they’re a killjoy. Andrew Davies’s script was fabulous but not kind. The great houses of the English aristocracy brought an elegantly tense, here’s-what-you-could-win atmosphere; like Location, Location, Location meets Squid Game.

Consequently, there was much more riding on Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle than a plain will-they-won’t-they: their unbearably slow though entirely predictable passion (even if you’d never met the book!) had to rescue the family, the society, the viewer, the very blades of grass all around, from the stress of a world in which the stakes were both impossibly high and pitiably trivial. And they really, really delivered: Ehle’s expression, as she’s almost winded by genuine feeling, is exquisitely evocative. Firth, of course, was never able to erase the cultural mark he made by jumping into a lake with his shirt on. The pair had a brief fling during and after filming, almost (one imagines) as a courtesy to the cultural fervour they created. It didn’t last, but it would have been rude not to. Zoe Williams

Technically, it can’t be done. You cannot take over a 1,000 pages of the most luminous, intricately woven prose ever written, put them on screen and lose nothing in translation – or at least nothing you don’t gain back tenfold elsewhere.

But that is what writer Peter Straughan and director Peter Kosminsky, plus a handful of actors at the top of their game, did when they adapted the first two volumes of Hilary Mantel’s trilogy about the rise and fall of Thomas Cromwell, and how he oversaw Henry VIII’s split from Rome, marriage to Anne Boleyn and eventually resolved on a scaffold at dawn the king’s Great Matter once and for all. There’s simply nothing like it – for beauty, for delicacy, for horror, for heartbreak. Every line, every frame, every fleeting expression on an actor’s face does double, triple duty as an engine of story and creator of an experience that allows you to watch the past unspool as if for the first time and stands as a testament to human creativity and the power and refuge of art. Lucy Mangan

Bleak House is the celestial moment when BBC period drama, the baronet of its adaptation for the screen Andrew Davies, the enormous cast of characters, and Charles Dickens himself were all at their very best. The outcome is 15 exquisitely taut, tense, addictive, fog-ridden half-hour episodes (except the first one which was an entire glorious hour), restoring Dickens to the serial format that made him so famous, broadcast twice weekly with cliffhanger endings so finely judged even the Victorians would have approved. Anna Maxwell Martin, in her first lead role, delivers an astonishing performance as Esther Summerson. Gillian Anderson’s haunting (and haunted) Lady Dedlock is unforgettably sombre and devastatingly sad. Charles Dance’s Tulkinghorn is the most terrifyingly serpent-like family lawyer known to the profession, all hooded eyes and hissed threats. And there will never be a more comically spot-on Mr Guppy in televisual history than Burn Gorman. Millions tuned in every week to see how Jarndyce and Jarndyce would pan out (badly, of course). I still rewatch it every single year, hanging on every perfectly-paced word. The benchmark of grip-the-nation British period drama, then and now. Chitra Ramaswamy

Period dramas are so firmly associated with bonnets and windswept moors that suggesting anything that doesn’t fit that description feels faintly sacrilegious. But despite depicting an era maybe even your mum can just about remember, and being [drops monocle into snifter in horror] American to boot, Mad Men is a proper period drama. And not just because the costumes are on point – though they are, with every last Sterling Cooper employee’s pocket square positioned just so.

No, what makes Matt Weiner’s ad industry saga so great is its ability to make its chosen age – buttoned-down late 50s giving way to the charged, chaotic 60s – both alien and achingly close to home. After all, nostalgia, as Don Draper reminded us in the show’s most memorable sales pitch, translates as “the pain from an old wound”. It’s a show that both seduces and repels you with its vision of the not-so-distant past – capitalism starting to curdle, sexism and racism both casual and deeply ingrained. But like an appealing if inadvisable Old Fashioned, you can’t help yourself from drinking it down. Gwilym Mumford

In truth, I have always struggled with period dramas, since it’s as if all the fun stuff – the characters, the plot, the identifiable human behaviour – is obscured behind a thick screen of frills and waffle. But Lucinda Coxon’s 2011 adaptation of Michel Faber’s novel cuts straight through all that. It’s a queasy, bilious four-parter that heaves with fury from the outset. Romola Garai plays Sugar, a sex worker fuelled by hatred for all the men who casually abused her and her friends. Chris O’Dowd plays William Rackham, an ineffectual rich kid who wants to be a writer but has no talent for it. He falls for her, despite having a mentally ill wife at home, and invites her to become the governess to his daughter. Sugar gets to see all the opportunities afforded to the upper classes and maximises upon them, while William stumbles into a trap of his own making. The Crimson Petal and the White represents period dramas at their nastiest. If only more would follow suit. Stuart Heritage

Any Brontë fan who has walked around the tiny, rickety rooms of the sisters’ Haworth home will have spent hours imagining the young women huddled together, scratching away with pens to tell their stories. Leave it to Sally Wainwright to put her ideas of them on screen in this exquisite feature drama about Charlotte, Emily and Anne – and their brother Branwell, whose alcoholism deeply affected their lives and works. It shows not just their fight to get published, using pseudonyms, but their increasingly desperate need to earn money as unmarried women. Filmed in a replica of the Brontë parsonage and on the surrounding Penistone Hill Country Park, it’s like living daily life and walking the moors with the sisters – played almost precisely how I picture them by Finn Atkins, Chloe Pirrie and Charlie Murphy. Forget Margot Robbie in red latex! This is the real Brontë experience. Hollie Richardson

It has been almost 25 years since it aired on BBC Two, and in many ways, Andrew Davies’ adaptation of Sarah Waters’ debut novel does look and feel of its time. It told the story of fictional Victorian music hall star and male impersonator Nan Astley, whose lesbian awakening dragged her through the highs and lows of London’s bohemian society. It was raucous, camp and surprisingly sexually frank. It may have cast pretty, overtly feminine women in roles that would, today, demand a more butch presence, but in the early 00s, it was a rare case of a period drama, or any drama for that matter, that did not skirt around its queerness. As such, it deserves its place in TV history. Also fun to spot Benedict Cumberbatch and Sally Hawkins and Monica Dolan in early roles, and to wonder how “Monsieur Dildo” ever made it on to the screen in 2002. Rebecca Nicholson

We tend to think of period drama as telling stories from a century or more before and coming from a dead writer’s book. Peter Flannery’s nine-parter was adapted from his own stage play with a narrative starting 32 years before the transmission date and ending just one year before. Yet all other qualifications of the genre are met: the popularisation of distant history (in this case, civic corruption in the north east), spectacular work by the costume and wig departments, characters of Dickensian richness that four young actors – Gina McKee, Daniel Craig, Mark Strong, Christopher Eccleston – made glorious calling cards: the show’s alumnae include a James Bond (Craig) and a Doctor Who (Eccleston) and the four share a heavy shelf of Bafta, Emmy, Olivier and Tony wins and nominations. Mark Lawson

“To the North. Where we do what we want!” In period terms, this three-part adaptation of David Peace’s titular trilogy is riveted tightly to Britain in the 1970s. The original novels were loosely inspired (if that’s the right word for the ambient horror they conjure) by the hunt for the Yorkshire Ripper. These dramas pick up that deadly trail and run with it, into purgatory and beyond. The police station resembles the inside of a smoker’s lung. Straight-dealers end up in metaphorical and sometimes literal ditches. And around every corner, there’s a moral dead end waiting. The cast – which includes Andrew Garfield, Rebecca Hall, Sean Harris, Daniel Mays, Maxine Peake and Paddy Considine – is extraordinary and taken as a whole, Red Riding represents a relentlessly claustrophobic suite of desolation and corruption. Bodices and frilly frock coats are conspicuous by their absence. Phil Harrison

Parade’s End, a sumptuous adaptation of Ford Madox Ford’s quartet of novels of the same name, aired on BBC Two when I was 16, just at the point when my TV tastes were becoming refined enough for meaty, sexy fare. I was blown away by Tom Stoppard’s expert take on Ford’s twisty story, which follows righteous aristocrat Christopher Tietjens as he serves in the first world war. And what a cracking cast: Benedict Cumberbatch plays Tietjens, Adelaide Clemens is excellent as Valentine Wannop, the young suffragette for whom he develops feelings, while Anne-Marie Duff and Stephen Graham appear in supporting roles. It’s Rebecca Hall, though, as Sylvia, Tietjens’s mesmerising and manipulative – but ultimately miserable – wife, who steals the show. Being closeted at the time, I put my teenage obsession with the show down to a crush on Cumberbatch, but I knew deep down it was actually Hall I fancied, with her long tailored coats and ability to express five emotions with the smallest raise of an eyebrow. I defy anyone watching Parade’s End not to fall in love with her. Lucy Knight

“It’s 1973, almost dinner time. I’m havin’ ‘oops!” growls DCI Gene Hunt (Philip Glenister) as he pins bewildered noughties metrosexual DI Sam Tyler (John Simm) against a filing cabinet in the first episode of the BBC’s still mindblowing police procedural Life on Mars. I generally find costume drama a bit too much like homework. For Life on Mars, I make an exception. That’s mainly because it’s a show about suspension of disbelief. Has Simm’s detective really time-travelled from 2006 or is he comatose, dreaming? Could his subconscious have cobbled together a vision of the past this credible? This is a show that encourages you to question every little detail of the seductive 1970s setting – a deconstruction of the period drama that reflects on nostalgia, the nature of reality and the strangeness of the past. Now, 20 years on, it’s technically a relic itself – but this postmodern masterpiece is far from dusty. Rachel Aroesti

Pride and Prejudice is on Netflix from Thursday 3 December

Meta whistleblower calls on Burnham to go further with ban on NDAs

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:30:08 GMT

Sarah Wynn-Williams says tech insiders with concerns about AI are being silenced in system reminiscent of George Orwell’s 1984

The Meta whistleblower who made allegations about the social media company’s treatment of teenagers has urged Andy Burnham to go further in banning non-disclosure agreements, warning that tech insiders with concerns about AI development need to be protected.

Sarah Wynn-Williams, who served as the director of global public policy at Meta, then called Facebook, has been unable to talk about a series of allegations made in her memoir as a result of restrictions secured by the company.

The restrictions, which stem from a severance agreement Wynn-Williams signed after leaving Meta, mean she could face significant legal penalties for speaking about the company.

Giving the annual Orwell lecture in London, Wynn-Williams said she could not discuss her own case. However, she said NDAs had become a key weapon used by the powerful to keep “control over narrative”.

“The aim is not to win the argument,” she said. “The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures.”

She noted that NDAs appeared to have been used in the cases of both David Walliams, who faces allegations of sexual misconduct by several women, and Russell Brand, who was recently convicted of rape and sexual assault. Walliams denies the allegations against him.

“In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women to ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed,” she said. “It may, allegedly, still be being suppressed.”

She welcomed the prime minister’s commitment to restrict the use of NDAs. Burnham said earlier this week that he was bringing forward changes to ensure victims of crimes or workplace harassment will have complete freedom over whom they can speak to, even if they have signed an NDA.

However, Wynn-Williams called on Burnham to go further by making the changes retrospective. She also called on the public to lobby for stronger action. “Change like this is hard,” she said. “And it is meaningful. It is an achievement that will impact people’s lives. But as the prime minister said, it is just the start.

“Tell your MP, your politically connected friend, your neighbour, it needs to go further. Make it retrospective, ban NDAs, allow people to speak. Even with this announcement, there will still be many with information that the public needs to know who are silenced.”

Wynn-Williams compared NDAs to the “memory hole” that George Orwell envisaged in his novel 1984 – a slot into which inconvenient documents are dispatched and destroyed.

She said action on NDAs was needed in relation to the rapid development of AI, to ensure insiders felt able to sound the alarm. “Parliaments, the press, the law – they’re all outside the building,” she said. “The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say, ‘I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn’.

“They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place they needed to sign away their rights to speak.

“The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the contract, and we are relying on those silenced by contract to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.”

Wynn-Williams made her allegations against Meta in a memoir, Careless People. However, under an interim arbitration ruling secured by Meta she is unable to speak about the book, which contains claims about Meta working with the Chinese government on censorship tools, and its negative impacts on teenagers.

She sat in silence on stage at the Hay literary festival in Wales earlier this year after taking legal advice, and is suing Meta over the restrictions it secured over her.

Meta strongly disputes Wynn-Williams’s book, saying it contains several false claims, and describes her legal case as a ploy to shift more copies.

“An NDA agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car,” Wynn-Williams said.

“It is signed by all types – from the C suite to the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips.”

Labour backs bill to stop lawsuits used to silence journalists and whistleblowers

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:15:44 GMT

Anti-Slapps campaigners criticise draft bill, saying process of dismissing claims will be challenging and costly

The government is to back legislation aimed at preventing wealthy and powerful individuals using the courts to silence critics and curb free speech.

The justice minister Sarah Sackman told parliament on Friday that Labour would support a private member’s bill sponsored by the Conservative MP John Whittingdale, who is spearheading the latest attempt to bring in anti-Slapp measures in England and Wales.

She told the Guardian: “Our legal system should be a route to justice, not a weapon of intimidation, used to evade scrutiny, suppress reporting or discourage people from speaking the truth.”

The bill attempts to define abusive cases, often referred to as strategic litigation against public participation, or Slapps, so that they can be dismissed early before defendants incur unaffordable legal costs.

However, campaigners have criticised the draft legislation, saying it will not work in its current form because the process of dismissing claims will be too challenging and costly for defendants.

The government’s decision marks the latest acknowledgment by Labour of the need to rebalance a legal system that too often favours powerful individuals or organisations over those who seek to hold them to account, be they victims of abuse, whistleblowers, journalists or academics.

“Speaking out against wrongdoing takes courage, whether you’re a journalist exposing corruption, a whistleblower or a victim finding the strength to talk about abuse,” said Sackman, who announced the government’s support after the bill’s second reading on Friday.

“Too often, wealthy or powerful individuals use the threat of expensive legal action to silence people. Not because they expect to win, but because they know the process itself can be punishing.”

Her intervention follows an announcement by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, earlier this week that the government would bring forward changes to non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to ensure they cannot be used to hide crimes.

The debate around the use of legal threats against victims has been reopened in the wake of allegations against David Walliams of improper behaviour – which he denies – and the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault.

Labour’s support means Whittingdale’s bill now has a better chance of passing into law, but success is not guaranteed – most private members’ bills are defeated or struggle to secure the time and attention needed.

Even if it passes, campaigners say the bill risks sitting on the statute books unused.

The UK Anti-Slapp Coalition has not endorsed the bill, saying last week it had concerns about the early dismissal mechanism.

“The legislation has the potential to make a significant difference in people’s lives, but it will only live up to this potential if the mechanism contained in the law works in practice,” the coalition said. “Crucially, as currently drafted the early dismissal mechanism is too complicated, imposes too high a bar to be used, and creates financial risk for Slapp targets which will prevent it from being used.”

The bill sets out three tests for identifying Slapps. Defendants have to show the dispute relates to a matter of public interest, the claimant’s behaviour is restraining their right to freedom of speech, and is intended to cause them harm beyond what would normally be encountered in litigation.

Proving a claimant’s intentions is notoriously difficult, and defendants may in effect be forced to undergo a mini-trial in order to have the case dismissed. The coalition said it was ready to work with ministers to improve the wording.

The Labour MP Apsana Begum, herself a survivor of financial abuse, said the bill needed to go further. During Friday’s debate in parliament, she called for stronger protection on costs, and for judges to have powers to identify and dismiss Slapps themselves.

“This bill could be our only and best opportunity to finally outlaw Slapps and in a way that does justice to survivors of abuse,” said Begum.

However, it is understood the government supports the current draft, believing it strikes a balance between tackling abusive litigation and ensuring legitimate access to the courts.

An earlier private member’s bill sponsored by the Labour MP Wayne David received cross-party support and the backing of the last Conservative government, but it did not complete its passage through parliament before the 2024 general election. Later that year, the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, promised legislation, but the government never put forward its own bill.

Some protection exists, thanks to legislation introduced in 2023, but it applies only in cases where litigants are accused of economic crime. The new bill widens the scope to cover sexual abuse, corruption and other wrongdoing.

Whittingdale said he was “delighted to work with the minister on a cross-party basis in order to achieve the widest level of support to stop this abuse”.

You Can See Everything: what to know before watching this year’s ‘must-see’ film

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:04:41 GMT

Documentary focuses on disgraced biotech billionaire Elizabeth Holmes – but who was she and what did she do?

It is the documentary everyone seems to be talking about. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s three-hour film about Elizabeth Holmes has become a box-office sensation on both sides of the Atlantic, grossing more than $100m ($76m) worldwide.

But what do you need to know before you watch it? Here’s a spoiler-free rundown.

Holmes is the disgraced founder of Theranos, a Silicon Valley biotech company once valued at $9bn.

In 2003, aged 19, she dropped out of Stanford University to launch the business. She claimed her invention – a machine she called the Edison – could carry out hundreds of blood tests using just a few drops of blood taken from a finger prick. It was, she said, “the most important thing humanity has ever built”.

At 30, Holmes was named the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire by Forbes. The magazine’s portrait of her, wearing a black polo neck and looking directly at the camera while holding a small vial of blood, was a huge cultural moment. She attracted wealthy investors and prominent supporters, including the Walton family, Rupert Murdoch and Larry Ellison. Theranos also formed partnerships with major retailers including Walgreens to make its blood-testing services more accessible.

But the technology was not delivering on its extraordinary promises. It was found to have relied on conventional blood-testing machines for many of its tests, while misleading investors about the capabilities of its own technology. Patients were receiving misleading and sometimes dangerous results.

After intense media scrutiny, led by a Wall Street Journal investigation, regulatory investigations and growing doubts among investors and business partners, Theranos eventually shut down in 2018. Holmes and her former business partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, were subsequently charged with fraud.

Holmes was found guilty in January 2022 of four counts of fraud relating to investors: one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and three counts of wire fraud. She was acquitted of four charges relating to patients, while the jury failed to reach a verdict on three further investor-related charges.

A significant part of her defence centred on her relationship with Balwani, Theranos’s former president and chief operating officer, who was also her romantic partner for more than a decade.

Holmes alleged that Balwani had been emotionally, psychologically and sexually abusive, and that he had exerted considerable control over her life and the company. Her lawyers argued that the relationship was relevant to whether she had knowingly intended to defraud investors. Balwani denied the allegations.

In November 2022, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and three months in federal prison, and began serving her sentence in April 2023. Balwani was convicted of all 12 fraud charges in a separate trial and sentenced to 12 years and 11 months in prison.

You Can See Everything was made in secret over several years and produced by A24.

The film is co-directed by the Canadian comedian and film-maker Nathan Fielder and the American documentary-maker Lance Oppenheim.

Fielder is best known for his deadpan and deeply awkward comedy which deliberately blurs the line between reality and fiction. He first built a cult following with his TV series Nathan for You, in which he played an exaggerated version of himself offering outlandish business advice to unsuspecting small-business owners.

He went on to create HBO’s The Rehearsal, in which he staged elaborate simulations to help people prepare for difficult moments in their lives, and co-created The Curse, a dark comedy starring Emma Stone and Benny Safdie.

Oppenheim is best known for Primetime (2026), a drama starring Robert Pattinson as the To Catch a Predator presenter Chris Hansen, which was a commercial and critical success when it was released in September. He has previously directed the documentaries Some Kind of Heaven (2020), about residents of a Florida retirement community, and Spermworld (2024), which explores the world of sperm donation.

Billy Evans is Elizabeth Holmes’s partner and the father of their two children. He comes from a wealthy San Diego hotel-owning family – his grandparents founded the Evans Hotels group – and graduated from MIT with a degree in economics in 2015.

The couple met at a party in San Francisco in 2017, after Theranos had begun to unravel, and became romantically involved the following year.

Holmes’s first pregnancy delayed the start of her trial in 2021, and she gave birth to their son shortly before it began. She was pregnant with their second child when she was sentenced in November 2022, giving birth in February 2023, just months before she reported to prison.

The story has been dramatised in the Hulu miniseries The Dropout (2022), starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Balwani. Seyfried won an Emmy for her performance.

The series was based on ABC News’s investigative podcast of the same name, presented by Rebecca Jarvis.

Other notable accounts include Bad Blood (2018), the bestselling book by the former Wall Street Journal journalist John Carreyrou, whose reporting helped expose the scandal, and Alex Gibney’s documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley (2019).

Phoebe Bridgers review – phone-free arena show is a cosmic, communal revelation

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 12:00:51 GMT

Co-op Live, ManchesterBridgers caused some controversy by banning phones on her Lost Weekend tour, but the intimacy and attention it forces feels as much a gift to fans as it does to her

The giant white dome that hangs over Phoebe Bridgers’ stage looks like Disney World’s Epcot, Walt’s “experimental prototype community of tomorrow” envisioning how we might live better. Bridgers’ tour is its own utopia: everyone’s phones are locked away, an edict that caused some controversy among younger fans who have never experienced a gig any other way. Down our aisle, none of us know the time and two teenage fans wearing skeleton outfits (Bridgers’ old stagewear staple) faux-complain that they’ve actually had to talk to each other.

It’s so unusual not to see a speckle of screens at an arena show that, from the seats looking down on the standing area, it feels as if there’s been some kind of power cut, or we’re in a protected natural dark reserve. The decision seemed made to protect the sanctity of the pain in Bridgers’ third album. Lost Weekend swims in her conflicted feelings over her sometimes-estranged father’s death, given his abuse of her mother, and the end of Bridgers’ fairytale engagement, after she realised she wanted something different.

The dome lifts to reveal a black-clad Bridgers and her nine-piece band, led by Melina Duterte of Jay Som, who play beautifully orchestrated, faithful versions of these songs. They tap into the Sufjan/National school of ornate crescendo, but nothing is being unduly dressed up here, or inflated to mirror Bridgers’ stature as a generational, Grammy-winning songwriter and conspicuous influence on pop stars from Taylor Swift to Gracie Abrams.

What’s miraculous is how Bridgers has transformed melancholy, silvery alt-rock into something that hits on the level of pop music, yielding feral screams from the crowd for Elliott Smith-worthy interiority. The production is the only pop thing about the show: later tilted high above the band’s heads, the dome’s concave insides turn into a sort of crystal ball, showing hazy visions of Bridgers, planets and black holes – maybe the alien, cosmic hugeness of a complicated and irreconcilable grief.

Bridgers’ restraint in not trying to fill the 23,000-capacity room means that when she and the band really lock in, it takes your hair clean off. Kill Me goes from a stunned wisp to furious, slamming drums, prompting the dome to rise up, beaming spaceship-style lights from its rim. She moves to the B-stage for Lost Weekend’s title track, sitting cross-legged on the floor at a small organ. When the bass floods and then breaks, the lights strobe Bridgers in white as she howls to the rafters: one minute she’s there, then she’s not, a faltering ghost. Glitter rains down for the belting climax of As Above, which feels something like being flayed.

With the exception of new-love anthem Bobby, these are not particularly cheerful songs (in case you couldn’t tell by the pearlescent tears painted on Bridgers’ face). You can imagine how she might have anguished about reliving their griefs and disappointments night after night. She’s talked about her discomfort at being reduced to a sad-girl meme; some fans thought it was OK to harass her in the airport en route to her dad’s funeral. She would have been well within her rights to put her guard up for life. Notably, she’s given no interviews about this album.

But aside from the lasers and dry ice, the most striking element of the show is how purely happy Bridgers looks, more so than on any previous tour. She looks genuinely pumped at the huge singalong to Motion Sickness: given recent events, hearing 23,000 young people roaring along to a song denouncing emotional abuse by an older man, is worth getting pumped over. She legs it across the main stage, beaming at the nosebleeds. The phone ban seems as much about preserving the sanctity of her happiness from commodification.

Sign up to Sleeve Notes

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

Part of Bridgers’ USP is that, for all her emotionally annihilating songs, she’s extremely funny. When she asks who has conservative parents, she gets a fairly muted response. “That’s much more universal in the US,” she says, then nods to the gig’s Manchester soil. “You guys have Morrissey. He’s everyone’s conservative parent.” She says she’s happy her UK tour means she can dodge Thanksgiving – “celebrating the genocide of people we stole the country from” – and says that for all her differences with her dad, she’s grateful they shared those values. “I never had to teach myself critical thinking.”

Alone on acoustic guitar, she plays Still Standing, her complex memorial to him, and the widespread sobbing is audible. It’s manifestly a devastating song, but something about the lack of phones seems to heighten the response. Taking away fans’ ability to turn away from hard feelings feels like a gift that forces a quality of attention: maybe the space theme hints at how disquietingly alien it feels to have nowhere to run, to see what comes up when you stare discomfort in the face. Bridgers has made her career doing it.

After the communal scream-fest I Know the End, she returns to the B-stage for an encore. Now dressed in white, she sings Scott Street sitting on the floor, and the house lights come on as everyone sways, arms in the air, looking giddily at one another after two hours of being locked in. The lack of video emerging from these gigs protects Bridgers’ privacy, but if you’re down to submit to the terms of her magic kingdom, you can see everything.

At OVO Hydro, Glasgow, on 27 November, then touring the UK until 2 December

Overton’s fiery five-wicket haul helps England to flip Gabba script against Australia

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 11:43:16 GMT

No ground in Australia is more associated with ritual guttings of English cricket teams than the so-called Gabbatoir. They usually leave in a state of disarray, beaten up on the field and with ears still ringing from abuse on the boundary’s edge.

Yet on a muggy Friday night on Vulture Street, the locals had precious little material to work with and the traditional script was flipped on its head. Driven by Jamie Overton’s fiery five-wicket haul, England wiped the floor with their hosts for the second match in a row to claim a 2-1 lead with two to play.

The pockets of England supporters inside the Gabba would sooner this scoreline had come during that ill-fated Ashes tour 12 months earlier, clearly, not a low-key T20 affair against a barely semi-skimmed Australian XI. For all the sandpaper-related schadenfreude, this tour is not proving a great return on their investment.

Still, they got to watch an English fast bowler release the handbrake as Overton’s five for 12 rolled the hosts for a sorry 108 all out in 16.5 overs. A few brief rain showers were pretty much the only thing stopping England’s march from there and an adjusted 93-run target from 16 overs was wiped out with 43 balls to spare.

The initial source of the runs was again Aneurin Donald, with the self-professed slogger following Tuesday’s fireworks display on the Gold Coast by cracking 32 from 13 balls.

But this match was settled by Overton’s remarkable first innings, claiming two catches inside the ­powerplay and then unleashing with ball in hand for the best T20 figures by an Englishman against Australia. Only Sam ­Curran – five for 10 against Afghanistan in Perth four years ago – has ­better overall.

“It has actually been a frustrating tour,” said Overton afterwards, revealing some back-to-basics drills with the bowling coach, Tim Southee, were behind his personal turnaround. “It’s funny how quickly things can change. And T20 can be a funny game. Obviously it’s nice to get five but I feel like I’ve bowled better at times previously.”

The daft thing was, Australia had actually started reasonably well after being inserted. Despite being pegged back twice by the wily Liam Dawson en route to personal figures of three for 16, the hosts had put 64 runs on the board after six overs and so were tracking for a 200-run total that looked like par.

Enter Overton. With Adil Rashid spinning a thrifty web at the other end, Surrey’s giant Devonian struck in each of his first three overs and then finished off with a double-wicket maiden. As is the way with T20, these were not classical dismissals but still owed plenty to classical pace on a typically rapid Gabba surface.

Jake Fraser-McGurk sent one down the throat of long on, while Tim David was cracked flush on the elbow before top-edging his next ball to deep fine leg. Joel Davies wafted tamely to midwicket and while Nikhil Chaudhary scrapped his way to 19 – wearing one nasty blow to the grille – he eventually went the same way as Fraser-McGurk.

Chaudhary middling one straight back into Overton’s left thumb the ball before could easily have ended his night early. But much like an ­earlier near-miss with the one of flamethrowers on the boundary’s edge, the 32-year-old shrugged it off and made Ben Dwarshuis his fifth via a ­regulation outside edge behind.

With the remainder soon mopped up – including one farcical run out that snuffed out the last recognised batter Mitch Owen – Australia had conspired to lose eight wickets for 43 runs and were staring at their lowest T20 total on home soil.

Even with the slippery Riley ­Meredith then unleashing with three wickets in the reply, and big Billy Stanlake flooring Harry Brook with a brutish delivery that the England captain did well to evade, the match was long since over as a contest.

After Donald’s eventual demise the most eye-catching strokeplay in between the stoppages for rain came from Jordan Cox and an unbeaten 33 from just 14 balls.

An anticlimax in some regards overall, not that Overton – or any previous English visitors to the Gabbatoir – had too much cause for complaint.

Leicestershire all-rounder Rehan Ahmed and Glamorgan uncapped opener Asa Tribe will join the tour in Sydney as cover for the final two matches. Harry Brook and Jordan Cox will play in Sunday’s fourth T20I in Sydney before departing for the Test tour of South Africa.
