‘I am scared’: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order - and why it’s time to speak out against big tech

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 10:00:01 GMT

Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she talks about corporate lawfare, and the growing backlash against NDAs

George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.

The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”

Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine. Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.

In 2011, Sarah Wynn-Williams was appointed director of global public policy at Facebook (now Meta). Over seven years, she brokered meetings with world leaders and contributed to public policy strategy in developing nations across three continents.

She left the company in 2017 and in March 2025 published a book about her time at Meta. Careless People: A Story of Where I Used to Work describes a journey of disillusionment with a company that she was sure would change the world for the better to one “helping some of the worst people in the world do terrible things”. It contains allegations of a toxic internal culture, including sexual harassment and gender-based discriminatory practices.

Meta has described the book as a “mix of out-of-date and previously reported claims about the company and false accusations about our executives”. On publication, it sought an emergency order preventing Wynn-Williams from promoting Careless People, on the basis that she had signed a severance agreement that included arbitration and non-disparagement clauses. It has not sought damages for defamation. Instead, Meta is claiming damages of $50,000 for every alleged violation of a provision of her severance agreement. Each book sold is alleged to be a separate violation.

Careless People was a No 1 bestseller in the UK and the US. In May, Wynn-Williams sat in silence on a stage at Hay literary festival on legal advice, while the academic Tim Wu and journalist Carole Cadwalladr discussed censorship and corporate overreach. Despite this, Meta sought to impose additional sanctions based on her appearance.

A month later, Wynn-Williams filed a lawsuit against Meta in California federal court, requesting the removal of the temporary gag order, accusing the company of “coercive surveillance” and first amendment violations. In a statement, Meta said: “This former employee is trying to use the legal process to sell books, which an arbitrator already ruled broke the agreement she signed with the company when she accepted a large financial settlement years ago.” It argued that Wynn-Williams “has long waived any objection to arbitration by actively participating in it, seeking relief, filing a counterclaim, and insisting that the arbitrator should decide the issues she raised”.

Ravi Naik, the legal director of AWO Legal and Wynn-Williams’s UK lawyer, said Meta had used a private arbitrator to “silence” the whistleblower. “No judge, no trial and no finding that she said anything untrue. Just a secret proceeding between an arbitrator and one of the most powerful corporations in the world.” He concluded: “Meta’s campaign to silence Ms Wynn-Williams must now end.”

Knowledge matters. People need to know what actually happened. But in 2026 the language of tech has taken on a quality of manifest destiny: the men in charge have determined how it should be, as though there could be no other way, even though none of us voted for any of it.

Control of the prevailing narrative is held tacitly: the only time this authority is given voice is when it acts, decisively, to silence an alternative account. Control over narrative is becoming the real power battle in technology. The aim is not to win the argument. The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures. Without memory or evidence, dissent has nothing to stand on. That is why memory matters. Why evidence matters. Why books matter.

You don’t need a Ministry of Truth to make a memory hole. An employment contract will do. An NDA will do. A court order will do. A legal bill – large enough, frightening enough, open-ended enough – will do very nicely. The modern memory hole does not smell of smoke. It smells of printer toner, fresh paper and billable hours.

In libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.

The agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, still reeling from an “incident” while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car. It is signed by the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips. In a justice system based broadly on the principle that sunlight is the best disinfectant, NDAs grip the elbow of truth and stay it. This is a private form of censorship, enforced by private arbitration and the public courts.

Anyone targeted by an institution with a formidable legal department is, by definition, very vulnerable. It is one person against a building full of lawyers who seek only to protect the interests of the company, truth be damned. Some businesses are more powerful than states.

They have mastered corporate lawfare, letting slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against these attacks brought on by trying to defy the memory hole. The word “brave” gets bandied around if you speak out despite all this. But “brave” should be for haircuts, not for telling the truth.

You do not have to silence everyone. You could never afford to. You only have to silence one person loudly enough that everyone else does the maths for themselves. These contracts seek to mute the truth, and they carry a big stick. The result is a society that has censored itself far more thoroughly than any Ministry of Truth ever could. No furnace required. Just fear, doing its patient and persistent work in the dark.

Recently, in the realm of entertainment, some big names have faced accountability or at least the prospect of it, because of women speaking out. Russell Brand was convicted, and David Walliams faces allegations. (Walliams has denied any wrongdoing in response to the allegations that he preyed on young women for sex.) In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women. To ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed.

And while we should celebrate the courage and fortitude of the women who spoke out at unimaginable cost, and the media organisations, including the Guardian, whose investigations were instrumental in ensuring this information became public, I can’t help but notice that this accountability occurred at a time when the professional standing of these figures was already significantly diminished.

For a long time now it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity. I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.

Whoever you are, whatever you believe, with an ever-more powerful elite there will come a day when you need to say something the powerful would rather you didn’t. And on that day, you will want three things: a place to say it that they do not own, a law that will not let them constrict you in grinding legal processes before bankrupting you for saying it, and people who will remember that you said it. The protections you are willing to fight for are the only ones that will be there when you need them.

Silencing the person who speaks is only half the job. The other half is making sure no one is paying attention. There is a detail in Nineteen Eighty-Four I used to skim past. Julia works in the Fiction Department of the Ministry of Truth. She services the novel-writing machines. These mass-produce literature as a commodity without any human creativity or critical thought. They use the same six stories, recombined endlessly to churn out formulaic slop for the proles.

The purpose of the novel-writing machines is to keep the proles distracted, passive and incurious. And it works. The proles never notice. The fiction machine has much in common with the feed: an endless scroll engineered by the brightest minds of a generation to keep your attention indefinitely. Nineteen Eighty-Four also gave us the Two Minutes Hate. A daily ritual of collective rage aimed at an enemy of the state. We have improved on it. Ours is continuous. Personalised. Delivered by push notification. And now with AI we have, literally, machines that write and humans that service them.

Orwell imagined the novel-writing machine as satire. We have built it. It was trained on the work of writers who were never asked. And sold back to them on a subscription. The Fiction Department of Nineteen Eighty-Four is now an industry. And it is the fastest growing one on earth. The memory hole removes what is true, and the fiction machine fills the space.

So much for what the machines do. The harder question is who owns them, and Orwell had a view on that too, though he was writing about a different technology. In October 1945, weeks after the atomic bomb was dropped, Orwell wrote a short essay exploring the deep connection between weapons technology and political power, observing that the shape of power in any age follows the shape of its decisive weapon. When weapons are cheap and simple – like the rifle – it empowers democracy and and gives “claws to the weak”, meaning ordinary people who can get hold of it have a fighting chance. When it is expensive and complex, like nuclear weapons, it concentrates power in the hands of a few and gives rise to oligarchic empires. And Orwell warned that these oligarchs might use the fear of the bomb to keep their populations suppressed, afraid to revolt.

Now think about the decisive technology of our own age. One that offers tremendous promise but also tremendous peril. The most advanced artificial intelligence takes investment measured in tens of billions. Chips made by a tiny number of firms, in a tiny number of places. Nobody builds this in a shed. Most governments do not have the resources to build it. A handful of companies can, mostly in just two countries.

Facing this, the most powerful technology in the world concentrated in a few hands, what would Orwell observe? Would he notice the democratic deficit around the technology? Would he worry about who can warn us today? Parliaments, the press, the law. They’re all outside the building. The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say “I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn.” They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place, they needed to sign away their rights to speak.

Two years ago, current and former employees of the leading AI companies including OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter asking for a right to warn. They asked for a prohibition on non-disparagement clauses and restrictive confidentiality clauses, anonymous reporting channels and no retaliation against employees. The letter said that the employees feared various forms of retaliation, given the history of cases across the industry. The fear was so pronounced some signed the letter anonymously.

The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the sale, and we are relying on the silenced to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.

I have spent the most recent chapter of my career on what happens when this technology meets the weapons Orwell warned us about. Because it is happening. Artificial intelligence is rapidly being integrated into weapons, including command and control for nuclear weapons. Concentrated power all around.

Anyone who has worked closely with new technology will tell you the same thing. It is buggy. It does things you don’t expect and don’t understand. Now connect this technology to nuclear command and control. The question we need to ask: if someone on the inside saw something going wrong, would they be free to say so? Would they be free to warn?

We have spent the last two decades reacting. Responding to each harm long after it arrives. Arguing about what to ban, but never about what to build. That is not a vision. It is damage control. We have not yet tried, in any meaningful way, to create a vision for technology that serves our society. That delivers growth and opportunity. That chooses to mitigate harm as it builds a society with massive advances in health, in education, in science, and in the dignity of ordinary work.

We are living in an era that will be defined by technology. By removing what we can know, by creating a memory hole, the technology companies have controlled our knowledge, our common ground of facts and what we can imagine. But it doesn’t have to be this way. We can choose a different future. One that builds on the positive, the ineffable possibility technology offers while meaningfully grappling with its harm. But you cannot choose a different future if you are not allowed to describe the present one. Choosing requires knowing. And knowing requires that people are free to speak.

It is hard to explain what it is like to try to live under a gag order. Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty. You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out. You start to rehearse sentences before you say them. You worry which word will produce the next legal letter. You begin, without ever meaning to, to censor yourself. So many times I go to say something and just … stop.

But even silence is no protection.

I want to acknowledge, here, that I am scared. If I am ultimately crushed and bankrupted, everyone will agree that it’s terrible, that NDAs are bad, that someone should have given her a voice, that someone should have supported her. And then they will forget. And the powerful will continue as normal.

But the thing about a memory hole: it only works if nobody outside it remembers what went in.

You are outside. You see. Please remember.

The silence is mine. It does not have to be yours.

Sarah Wynn-Williams is the author of Careless People. She delivered the Orwell Lecture 2026: The Modern Memory Hole at the Southbank Centre’s Queen Elizabeth Hall, London on 26 November. To support the Guardian order Careless People at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 09:53:11 GMT

Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.

Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate established with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.

Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.

“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”

However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.

“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”

He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.

Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations.

“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”

Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online. Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.

From toddler tantrums to teenage strops – how to manage your kids’ meltdowns

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 08:01:00 GMT

We asked the experts – all parents themselves – for practical tips on dialling down the conflict

From toddlerhood to teenage years, kids’ meltdowns and mood swings are a given. In fact, they are reassuring markers of child development. But for parents, they can also be minefields. So, what do experts do in the face of dysregulation and defiance? We asked development specialists (who are also parents) for their hacks, tips and tried and tested scripts.

Clinical psychologist Dr Emma Svanberg, author of Parenting for Humans, advises us to distinguish between a mood swing, a tantrum and a meltdown because a child’s receptiveness to our help will differ depending on which state they are in. “A mood swing is an emotional shift that a child or teenager still has some capacity to think their way through. A tantrum is more of a protest, so they may still have one eye on your response. A meltdown is a child or teen who has gone past the point of overwhelm, the ability to reason has largely switched off – that’s where soothing can really help them,” she says. “The mistake is treating a meltdown like a tantrum; someone in meltdown can’t be negotiated with – they need help getting back to a state of calm before anything else can happen.”

Whatever the scenario, says family therapist Deena Margolin, of parenting duo Big Little Feelings: “Don’t join the chaos!”

The first thing experts caution against is punishments. Dr Siggie Cohen, author of You Are the Parent, says threats, ultimatums and raising your voice are “a big mistake. Don’t go there with punishments – you’re wasting your time,” she says. “If you say, ‘You talk to me this way, no phone,’ you’re not on solid ground. Then it’s war.”

Dr Ross Greene, author of The Explosive Child, confirms this: “Traditional parenting – reward the behaviours you like and punish the behaviours you don’t – is often going to blow up in your face.”

“Before you go near one of your sons who’s just thrown a chair across the room, ask yourself: ‘How am I in this moment?’” recommends Dr Billy Garvey, author of 10 Things to Know About Your Child’s Mental Health and 10 Things to Know About Raising Boys. “If you go, ‘I’m really pissed off because I’m exhausted, trying to get out of the house and that’s the 15th time he’s done that today’ – take a beat.” This might mean ensuring your child isn’t in danger, then explaining you need a moment in another room and only returning once you have the energy to regulate yourself as well as them. As Cohen says: “The pauses we take, the ability to not jump in, is one of our best tools.”

For Svanberg, regulating yourself first is a win-win: “Imagine you are lending your child your calm, steady nervous system; that can help bring the temperature down. With a baby, that’s holding, shushing and soothing while steadying yourself. With a toddler or child, that might be slow voice, physical presence, contact if they want, few words. For a teenager, it might be less about presence (they may want space), more just letting them know you’re there.”

Once you’re ready, intonation is key, says Cohen: “Not, ‘We need to talk’ as a finger wag; instead, it’s a calm, ‘We need to talk.’”

She advocates empathy over pity: “‘I hear you, I see you’ is still the most effective thing you can say. Don’t throw in too many questions or suggestions. That means avoiding, ‘What’s the matter?’ or ‘What’s going on?’ while their stress response is firing.”

Garvey adds that if your child is growing tense, back off .“You might say: ‘It seems I’m making things worse right now, but I’m here, I’m going to be in the next room.’ Simple language, minimal words, slow and low tone.”

Margolin says parents should face meltdowns like “calm, confident CEOs of the home. Start by validating the feeling: ‘I see you’re upset. I know you’re really angry. It’s OK to feel that way.’ Then, we can hold a boundary. If they’re a toddler, we might say: ‘It’s OK to feel really angry about this and we don’t hit when we’re angry.’” You can then step in to separate or move kids. This is better than begging a child to listen to the boundary, such as “I’m asking you not to hit. Please stop, you’re not listening” – which feels optional.

This can be especially hard with teenagers: “A lot of us sometimes want to say things such as: ‘You’re acting this way after everything I do. You’re ungrateful,’” observes Margolin. “‘I hate you’ is going to come out of their mouth. Don’t treat those words as an emergency and don’t treat them as truth.”

Cohen advises: “They can intimidate us, they can hurt us, they use foul language, disrespect you. You can say, ‘Hey, that’s way too much,’ or, ‘You can be angry, but not this way.’ The same as when they’re three and they try to bite you.”

“Whether it’s the play mat, sports pitch or the arcade where they’re having a meltdown, you can just say: ‘Hey, this is too much for you right now, so let’s go,’” says Garvey, and then help them to leave.

Margolin agrees that reduced stimulation away from the scene can help, but warns: “Some kids absolutely don’t want to be touched.” Either way, she says: “You can totally stay present, be that anchor as they go through their big feelings. You know your kid best and what they need to feel safe and steady.”

after newsletter promotion

When leaving is the cause of tantrums, Margolin recommends offering a choice: “‘I know leaving the park is really hard. It’s OK to feel sad. We’ll come back soon. Do you want to walk or do you want me to carry you?’ Something that gives them power can shift them into a collaborative state.” It won’t always work, but that’s OK, she says: “The main point here is boundaries. When it’s time to leave, it’s time to leave. The grownup holds the boundary, and the kid is allowed to feel upset about it.”

Svanberg adds: “Some children might push back on boundaries. Sometimes this is about temperament, sometimes due to neurodivergence. You know your child. It’s important to remember that if they struggle with change it is not a sign you are doing something wrong. They may just need a different approach.”

“Don’t give a dressing down in the moment,” says Garvey. “They’re flooded, stressed. They can hear you, but they can’t understand you.”

Cohen explains that a reflective conversation can follow “in an hour or after three days. Then it’s not you telling them what they did wrong. Start by calmly revisiting the moment, or pattern, you want to discuss. So: ‘Yesterday, you and I were having a hard time.’ Ask: ‘Do you think we run into this problem often?’ Then try: ‘I have some thoughts about it – do you? I’d love for us to put our minds together and think how we can each make it better for both of us.’”

Garvey recommends taking a walk or drive together. Talking in less forced settings can “open up a safe space” to discuss feelings, particularly if you can make it a regular sanctuary.

“It can’t be that they’ve just punched their brother and you drag them over by the arm and say apologise,” says Garvey. “They’re just being conditioned to say sorry.” Modelling is better: “It’s a real strength if you can say sorry to your children. It can be a hugely disarming, powerful thing.”

Margolin advocates being reflective with little ones. “You can say: ‘You got frustrated. How does she look right now – really sad, huh? Hitting is not the way we handle stuff. What can we do right now? We can go say sorry. I’ll come with you.’” Then later, says Margolin: “Go back to it with your kid and identify how to do things differently in future. You could even use dolls to teach and practise the phrases and skills they might need next time.”

And with teens: “We can model repair when we mess up. Those moments make so much impact, when we say: ‘I didn’t handle that the way I wanted.’”

It’s OK to display your emotions too, says Garvey, just keep it “developmentally appropriate”. So don’t tell a three-year-old, “‘I’m worried we’re going to default on the mortgage,’ but ‘Mummy’s really frustrated and you just told me the dinner I made was yuk and threw it across the room,’ is fine, and also teaches children not to suppress emotion.”

Food tantrums and feeling hangry are real, says paediatric dietician Malina Malkani (AKA Healthy Mom Healthy Kids). “Sometimes a meltdown is a fuel gauge, not necessarily a character flaw, particularly in teenagers notorious for skipping meals.” Meals and snacks at reliable, regular intervals help, and when moods are swinging, avoid difficult dinner table conversations: “Much better to have these while cleaning up or driving. Keep mealtimes positive and judgment-free for teenagers.”

Meanwhile, to stop younger kids’ tantrums sending mealtimes sideways, Malkani advises: “Avoid pressure tactics – cajoling, begging, bribing. Anxiety ratchets up.” Her top tip? “Instead of saying ‘Just take one bite,’ try ‘It’s OK, you don’t have to eat it.’ Then it’s case closed. The child will look at you like: ‘Wait, I thought we were going to do the thing.’ Instead, you cut the battle off at the knees.”

Even if this feels hard, it will pay off, promises Malkani: “You can’t let the desperation seep through in your delivery. Nine times out of 10, if they believe you mean it, they will take a bite. Meal times are a learned skill for children; they need to have their nervous system in a calm place in order to feel enough trust to take that bite. So, when we remove that anxiety and that battle, they’re often calm enough to be able to try the food.”

Never mind EU student fees – it’s time to rethink the entire UK higher education system

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 08:00:59 GMT

The last shake-up, in the 1960s, was based on pure anti-technological snobbery. Let’s put vocational learning back in the heart of our cities

What is it about the EU student fees debate that means it has almost derailed Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset? Can the issue be that important? The answer is simple – and, I am sure, personal. Before Brexit, the EU’s citizens, among them its diplomats, were paying the same as UK citizens to have their children’s English perfected at a UK university. Now, some pay up to three times that figure. To put it mildly, they have an interest in persuading the UK government to slash fees. As of now, the issue is still deadlocked.

The total cost of meeting the EU’s demand and reducing EU student fees to the new British rate of £9,790 a year has been put at an astronomical £570m a year for Russell group universities alone. Burnham has declined to answer the question of who would foot the bill. Indeed, it is difficult to understand why British taxpayers should subsidise the education of wealthy Europeans. But the cost would then fall on individual universities. The University of St Andrews estimates it would lose a devastating £12m annually.

This could not have come at a worse time for higher education in the UK. Its finances are now chaotic. Student fees have barely risen since 2017 and will not reach £10,000 until next year. As a result, the House of Commons was told in May that 45% of higher education institutions in England were currently running deficits, with 24 facing bankruptcy this year. The University of Nottingham posted an £85m budget deficit last year. Queen’s University Belfast, Cardiff University, Sheffield University and even the University of Cambridge face multimillion pound obstacles. From Exeter to Edinburgh, courses are being dropped and staff laid off.

MPs debated at length earlier this year whether universities could continue teaching when effectively unable to trade, or whether they would fragment like an upmarket Poundland. Meanwhile, private equity operators such as Arden, London Churchill and Regent College are flourishing at the bottom of the stack, largely using so-called franchise university teaching. Work-from-home courses are outsourced to anonymous tutors, so that mostly overseas students can gain a British degree.

Universities are already starting to head for the lifeboats. Greenwich and Kent have merged, as have London’s King’s College and Cranfield. Humanities courses – supposedly delivering poorer job prospects – are closing down. A few universities, such as Buckingham and Royal Holloway, are at last offering two-year courses.

This is all the legacy of one of the greatest restructuring blunders inflicted by central government on any British public service. Just as in the 1960s secondary education supposedly “went comprehensive”, a similar approach was inflicted on higher education. First to go were the colleges of advanced technology, followed by the polytechnics in the 1990s. All were to become universities. The reason was pure, anti-technological snobbery.

The consequence was a mass demotion of the idea of vocational learning in favour of academic. Many British cities now have two universities, two student bodies, two headquarters and two claims for research grants. I once heard a Taiwanese professor say that he was baffled at why the British “arrest your youths for three years in the prime of life, lock them in a monastery and make them drunk”.

Local colleges that had been attuned to local business and commerce were reoriented as national academies. They donned gowns and mortar boards. Every subject was awarded the same three-year degree course, with actual teaching taking place barely half of each year. No evidence was sought on whether this was necessary or efficient. Holidays remained medieval, dictated by the church calendar and the harvest. Cities became dotted with student housing blocks standing empty half the year.

The university must be the only British institution (other than parliament) immune to productivity or reform. I served for two years in a senior common room and was always baffled as to what it was we were all trying to do, given that no one ever asked us or checked. In return, students are now forced to take out loans involving debts of inexplicable magnitude. It is hardly surprising that, as the so-called graduate premium in the jobs market declines, many school-leavers are having second thoughts.

This is surely the moment to re-examine the entirety of higher education in the UK, much as the Robbins report did in the 1960s. What does it really purport to do? For a start, according to the conservative thinktank Policy Exchange, there need be no more than 20-30 national research universities; many of them can be merged with specialist centres. Of the remainder, universities should surely revert to teaching what will most help students in later life, from engineering and computing to social studies and business. We may treasure and appreciate the humanities, but their place in the curriculum desperately needs redefinition.

As for the former polytechnics, they must be reintegrated with their localities. For more than a century, a city’s institutions of technical and vocational education were features of the local economy, a true source of pride. Perhaps that is a job for Burnham’s new regional mayors.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:00:57 GMT

Human rights groups report increasing attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers

Yousef Diriyeh and his son Hadi, both paramedics in the occupied West Bank, were lifting a wounded young woman into their ambulance when they heard shots crack and bullets whistle past their heads.

Less than an hour earlier, armed Israeli settlers had attacked the village of Qusra, killing three Palestinians and wounding several more. They were now shooting at the paramedics who had come to help.

Diriyeh urged his son to hurry as bullets struck the windscreen. It was the first time he and Hadi had come under attack.

As he sped to a hospital in Nablus, Diriyeh, now 50, remembers thinking to himself that the events of that day – 11 October 2023, shortly after Hamas launched the attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war – would mark the beginning of a series of attacks on emergency responders such as him and his son.

Since 7 October 2023, Israeli soldiers and militant settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian paramedics and blocked them from reaching the wounded in the West Bank. Violence against healthcare workers rose by more than 350% between 2022 and 2024, according to Physicians for Human Rights Israel, a non-profit organisation which documents human rights abuse affecting the right to health in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Insecurity Insight, a Geneva-based nonprofit humanitarian research organisation, recorded 1,020 attacks on health workers in the region from 7 October 2023 to 15 September 2026.

Physicians for Human Rights Israel shared dozens of videos with the Guardian, including of the incident shown above in October 2023 in Huwara, showing militant Israeli settlers throwing stones at ambulances, using cars to block their passage, and, in some cases, shooting at them. The footage also shows damaged ambulances, bloodstains on drivers’ seats and injured paramedics. It does not include the attack on Diriyeh and his son, which was not filmed.

The Guardian joined a team of paramedics near Nablus and spent a day in their ambulance, with Diriyeh at the wheel as he recalled that moment.

“That day I realised the militant settlers had fired directly at us with the intent to kill,” said Diriyeh, a tall, broad man with a thick, greying beard, driving along Route 60 towards villages recently targetted by settlers.

Israel has retained effective control over the occupied West Bank, including its borders and the movement of people, despite the Palestinian Authority’s nominal autonomy. As an occupying power, Israel is obliged to keep civilian medical services running, yet Israeli forces and settlers systematically subject emergency workers to abuse and violence.

“Over the last two years, [attacks] have increased at an insane rate – meaning there are attacks taking place every single day,” said Diriyeh. He has been based for the last 15 years in Aqraba, a village near Nablus for the last 15 years. “Sometimes there might be three, five or even six separate attacks taking place simultaneously.”

Heading south from Nablus, the village of al-Sawiya comes into view.“It was near here that settlers killed my colleague and friend, Mohammed,” Diriyeh said, pointing towards the houses. Mohammed Awad Allah Musa, an ambulance driver for the Palestine Red Crescent Society, was killed on 20 April 2024 taking wounded Palestinians to hospital.

He was one of 13 West Bank health workers killed since 7 October 2023, according to Insecurity Insight.

In news reports of recent settler attacks, reports have regularly suggested that ambulances have been prevented from reaching injured people in the region.

Ambulance crews in the occupied West Bank depend on Israeli military approval, passing through checkpoints to reach patients and take them to hospital. By December 2025, the UN had recorded 925 obstacles in place in the occupied West Bank, including checkpoints, road gates and roadblocks.

Militant settlers have also obstructed ambulances, Diriyeh said.

“They try to prevent us from passing by driving very slowly in front of us. Sometimes, when a settler’s vehicle is ahead, I might attempt to overtake, only for another settler to block the way to stop me,” he said.

In some West Bank villages, militant settlers have locked the gates, leaving ambulances stuck at their stations and unable to answer emergency calls. Since first occupying the West Bank in 1967, Israeli forces have continued to install road gates at the entrances to some Palestinian villages.

“Sometimes they come and lock the gates in and out of Aqraba – you’d practically need a helicopter to get past them,” Diriyeh added. “Some women have even given birth inside the ambulance itself when these gates are blocked.”

Omar, a 34-year-old emergency medical worker from Nablus, told Physicians for Human Rights Israel that soldiers at a checkpoint in Awarta stopped an ambulance carrying a woman in labour.

“Traffic was backed up, and the soldiers were refusing to let anyone through,” he said. “By the time they finally let us through, there was even more traffic ahead. In the end, while we were still on the way, the woman gave birth.”

The Pulitzer prize-winning book A Day in the Life of Abed Salama follows a father’s search for his son after a school bus crash in 2012 near Jerusalem. The writer, Nathan Thrall, who is based in Jerusalem, said more than a decade later that restrictions on Palestinian movement in the West Bank had become far worse.

“For many, they are the most severe they have experienced since the occupation began,” he said. “The goal, as ever, is to constrict Palestinians into ever-tightening spaces so that their land may be taken over for Israeli settlement and de facto annexation, a project that is not only steadily succeeding but accelerating rapidly.”

Imran Anati, a researcher for Physicians for Human Rights Israel, said: “These are not isolated incidents, but a systematic assault on Palestinian emergency medical care for which Israel bears responsibility.”

The Israeli military denied allegations that it had obstructed the work of Palestinian paramedics or prevented them from reaching the wounded, saying it “enables freedom of movement for medical teams” throughout the Palestinian territory. It said it condemned all acts of violence against medical teams and ambulances.

Diriyeh’s job has become one of the most dangerous in the occupied West Bank, as settler attacks become ever more frequent. The Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism”, while the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called the actions “ethnic cleansing”.

Diriyeh said he had made the “difficult decision” to ask his 20-year-old son to stop working with him.

He said on his first day of training as an ambulance driver in late 2013, the first case he had to handle involved a settler’s vehicle which had overturned on the road to Jericho.

He said Israeli emergency services couldn’t locate the vehicle, so Palestinian paramedics arrived and provided medical aid to the settlers on-site.

“In my career, I have provided medical aid to Israeli soldiers, too,” he said. “Whether they are Palestinian, Israeli, Christian, Muslim, Druze, or Jewish – it is of no concern to me. My mission is simply to provide humanitarian aid to anyone who needs it. That is my job.

“And it’s painful to think that today, a Palestinian life is worth less than an Israeli one.”

Additional reporting by Jamal Risheq.

The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 06:00:56 GMT

‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs?

Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning.

Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar.

Yet it would be a mistake to see Burnham as simply a charming procrastinator. He also has another speed: not slower than expected, but faster. He officially opened No 10 North – an unprecedented, potentially major redistribution of power – on the fifth day of his premiership. Since then he has rapidly reopened a succession of supposedly closed political topics, from reforming social care and the electoral system to rejoining the EU and ending the pensions triple lock. Meanwhile, his government has launched waves of micro-policies, sometimes responding within days to public controversies or the latest developments in the cost of living crisis, and invited dozens of social media influencers into No 10, before he distanced himself from “an inappropriate video” posted by one of them. Critics who claim he is doing too little, such as the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, often find themselves switching awkwardly to arguing he is trying to do too much.

For more than a decade, since the twin jolts of the Scottish and Brexit referendums, much of British politics has happened at an accelerated but fairly regular tempo, with brief premierships, almost annual reshuffles, consistently rushed policies and a steady stream of scandals, splits, defections, early general elections and leadership contests. For media made even hungrier and more competitive by digital technology, this has all been good content. Yet before Downing Street, Burnham spent most of this period in the less feverish environment of municipal politics, where he was a steadily reforming mayor for nine years, watching events in Westminster from a distance, as a cautionary tale.

In his first speech outside No 10, he said, “I am acutely conscious that I am … the seventh prime minister since 2016.” In Head North, the 2024 book he co-authored with his close ally Steve Rotheram, mayor of the Liverpool city region, Burnham criticises “the culture of the ministerial merry-go-round” and “constant chopping and changing of national policies”, which cause “delay and complexity and … spiralling costs”. “By contrast,” he continues, England’s regional governments take a “long-term” approach. At times in the book, and in his statements as premier, this reverence for incremental but fundamental reform risks turning into an argument for change endlessly widened, qualified and deferred. “Step by step, it is possible to see a roadmap taking shape,” he writes, “for how Britain could be converted into a more functional, modern democracy.” The book approvingly describes political projects as a “work in progress”, or a “journey”.

To some journalists, Burnham’s measured style is just maddening. “We were promised a speech from Burnham before Christmas on the options and then a decision about which to pursue,” wrote Tim Shipman of the rightwing Spectator magazine about the UK-EU summit in Brussels last week. “Instead, today fired the starting gun on talks about talks about talks. The prime minister promised a year-long ‘informal brainstorming’ with the EU. Ye gods, shoot me now.”

The constant announcements from the Conservatives and Reform UK, promising instant solutions to pressing national emergencies, frequently get more favourable media coverage. Yet Labour’s seemingly solid poll lead over both parties suggests many voters understand that manic rightwing politics hasn’t exactly improved the country, while a more considered, left-of-centre alternative might.

In parliament, Burnham often speaks slowly for a modern politician, with ruminative pauses and regular changes of tone. All this could be more performative than profound – people skills rather than deep thought. But he has had a longer, more varied political career than most of his peers and opponents: before his mayoralty, a wide range of ministerial jobs under both Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, and then senior shadow cabinet posts under Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn. This experience of very different versions of Labour politics, and of long stretches in both opposition and government, successful and not, may have made him more reflective and flexible. The unchanging ideological trajectories of Badenoch and Nigel Farage are one-dimensional by comparison: little more than extended political rants in career form.

A better criticism than theirs of Burnham’s sometimes patient, sometimes rapid-reaction premiership is that neither of these modes suits some of our deepest crises. This week, the UK Health Security Agency revealed that 5,258 deaths in England alone were connected to this summer’s record heat – many more than in all political violence in Northern Ireland since the 1960s, usually considered one of this country’s worst modern public safety emergencies. Yet so far the Burnham government’s climate-crisis strategy has been “pragmatic”, as he always puts it, which seems to mean trying to find a middle way between the well-funded but scientifically bankrupt fossil fuel lobby and the longer term needs of everyone else, both helping finance new windfarms and allowing more North Sea drilling – the latter to growing alarm among his MPs.

Even if such a compromise exists – and the fossil fuel lobby’s ferocity suggests not – finding it is going to take too long. As with the latest price hike from the highly profitable privatised energy utilities, the government’s challenge is not just to approach the problem at the right pace but to pick a side.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Burnham talks a lot about hope. That’s welcome, after so much self-fulfilling declinism from the right. His premiership could be the beginning of a new Downing Street model, with less deference towards an insatiably impatient, professionally hostile rightwing media.

But talking about hope can also be a way of perpetually pushing problems and their difficult solutions into the future. The country can’t afford that, and nor can Labour. The left-leaning, climate-conscious voters that Burnham won back from the Greens, who are largely responsible for his party’s poll lead, will drift away again if “Andy time” goes on too long.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power

The Guardian Fri, 27 Nov 2026 05:00:55 GMT

Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent

It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP).

The perpetually dour Abascal may lack the charisma of Trump or Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, but Vox is projected to increase its vote share from 12.4% in 2023 to close to 20%. It has achieved this surge not by moderating its rhetoric as it draws closer to power, but by embracing some of the most radical positions on immigration from across the European far right. A place in government for the party could, in turn, embolden its allies across Europe, as France, Italy and Poland prepare to go to the polls next year.

Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past. Yet since its disappointing showing at the 2023 general election, Abascal has purged much of the party’s original leadership and overseen an ideological renewal.

In looking to update its messaging, Vox has blended elements of Marine Le Pen’s welfare chauvinism, such as the concept of “national priority”, with ideas coming from the pan-European, white nationalist identitarian movement. Virtually absent from Spanish political debate a year ago, national priority would give Spaniards preferential access to social housing, public services and welfare benefits, with Vox already securing PP backing for the principle in regional coalition deals. In September, however, the European Commission warned that even the residence-based criteria used at a regional level could discriminate against citizens of other EU member states. Vox’s general election manifesto goes further, pledging to exclude all non-Spanish citizens from the country’s minimum-income benefit.

The party was also the only major far-right party to send a member of its leadership to the extremist identitarian conference on “remigration” in Porto in May, whose organisers openly advocate for mass deportations as a means to defend “a white and Christian Europe”. It has since made remigration a central plank of its election campaign, pledging the immediate deportation of all those who remain from July’s border surge in Ceuta, while also promising to “repatriate” immigrants who are in Spain illegally or “live off welfare benefits”.

In pairing that nativist agenda with a push for sweeping deregulation and tax cuts, Vox has expanded its electoral coalition in two directions: by winning over PP voters concerned about immigration levels, and by gaining significant ground among younger and economically discontented voters. It is now the largest party among voters aged 18-24 (backed by 23% of that age bracket) while its vote share has nearly doubled since 2023 among those who describe their financial situation as “poor” or “very poor”.

As the political scientist Mario Ríos told me recently, these cohorts are backing Vox as “a protest vote against the status quo, not out of nostalgia”. Despite Spain’s strong headline economic growth, average real wages have stagnated since the pandemic, and prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s progressive minority coalition has struggled to respond to soaring rents and the latest inflationary spike since the Iran war. Abascal has sought to channel that frustration, accusing the left of putting migrants first and claiming that its national priority and remigration policies would leave more homes and public resources for Spaniards. Similarly, its Doge-style deregulation agenda is framed as a revolt against a “bureaucratic hell that blocks Spaniards’ prosperity”.

Despite doubts over the feasibility of key parts of its manifesto, it is clear Vox has moved the national debate on irregular migration to the right, with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the PP, now backing five EU states’ plans for migrant deportation centres in Rwanda. There is also clear overlap between the PP and Vox’s plans to partially privatise Spain’s public pension system. If the polls are right, Feijóo could become prime minister on a lower vote share than the PP secured in the last election. He would then owe his majority to Vox’s surge and support in coalition, and Abascal would have both the leverage and the incentive to show his voters what the party can deliver in office.

A coalition formed on those terms could also foreshadow a closer alliance between conservatives and the far right at a European level. A Le Pen victory in the French presidential election next spring would put the nationalist right at the head of one of the EU’s two most influential states, shifting the political centre of gravity in Brussels and opening the way for a durable governing bloc to the right of the EU’s traditional grand coalition.

It was not by chance that Vox opened its election campaign with a rally displaying video messages of support from Le Pen, Meloni and AfD’s Alice Weidel. Having drawn on its far-right European allies to reinvent itself, Vox could now in turn strengthen their hand if it is successful in becoming the PP’s kingmaker after Sunday’s vote. Sánchez’s defeat would also deprive the centre left of its strongest counterweight in the European Council, where he is the only social democrat to represent one of the EU’s major powers. Speaking to the Vox rally, Weidel proclaimed: “All of Europe is waiting for a political change in Madrid.” All of Europe may not be waiting for such a change, but it is certainly watching.

Eoghan Gilmartin is a freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast

‘You’re Not Dying Fast Enough’: When Medicare Hospice Caps Cut Off a Patient

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Critics say the payment limits to companies penalize patients who are not dying on the government’s timetable.

By Christopher Rowland

Amy Lynn Birmingham couldn’t believe she was being cut off from hospice care. Nurses who came to her home in Sandpoint, Idaho, had gotten her pain under control, managed her supply of oxygen and stabilized some symptoms from blood clots, stroke and heart failure.

But after 15 months, the for-profit hospice company in charge of her care decided last year she no longer qualified. Ms. Birmingham said a sympathetic nurse had schooled her in the reality of hospice economics: “You’re not dying fast enough.”

More than a year later, Ms. Birmingham, 64, is alive yet still dying, with a cascade of issues relating to blood clots and severe vascular disease that she is navigating outside hospice. Her case highlights what critics say are flaws in the way hospice care is delivered in the United States, a concern that is growing in urgency as boomers live longer and swell the ranks of people needing end-of-life care.

Citing fraudulent practices in the industry, the Trump administration this month extended a moratorium on registering new hospice agencies with Medicare to deliver service. But even absent wrongdoing, financial incentives frequently result in harm to patients, according to critics of the current system.

Comfort care for elderly patients and people with disabilities, typically delivered at home, has been covered by government Medicare insurance since the early 1980s. It began mostly for patients at the end of their battles with cancer. Qualifying for hospice requires a doctor to predict that a patient will die within six months.

That six-month survival benchmark influences an average per-patient cap of about $36,000 that a hospice agency can receive from Medicare, which paid an estimated $27.5 billion for end-of-life services in 2024. Patients and some experts say the cap acts as an incentive for hospice agencies to remove people who are dying on their own timetable, not the schedule baked into the regulations.

Recent evidence raises questions about whether the cap makes sense, medically or economically. Former President Jimmy Carter died in 2024 after 22 months in hospice. A study last year led by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist found that hospice care saved Medicare $29,000 for every patient with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia by keeping those patients out of nursing homes.

“The big picture is there is almost nothing else in health care that we can think of that makes people better off and saves money,” said the paper’s author, Jonathan Gruber, who was a central architect of a groundbreaking Massachusetts health reform that served as a model for the Affordable Care Act.

The restriction on hospice services adopted by Medicare nearly a half a century ago should be re-examined, Mr. Gruber and his colleagues wrote, because it “distorts care” and, when people are thrown off, denies vital services to people at the end of life. The researchers said their findings suggested that “expanding hospice access would reduce Medicare costs, even if it meant admitting patients who could potentially live longer than six months.”

The concept of raising or eliminating payment caps in hospice has not gained traction in Washington. Instead, hospice for years has been marked by fraud investigations, with the focal point often on whether hospice patients are truly dying. High rates of “live discharges” are a sign that hospice companies may be accepting patients who are not sick enough to qualify, according to federal officials. The number of people whose hospice care ends without their dying is rising, according to federal data — to 19 percent, or 270,000 people, in 2024 from 16 percent in 2020.

Industry representatives, while acknowledging fraud and condemning bad actors, say that hospices are balancing regulations and the threat of fines with the delicate task of estimating how long someone will live.

“It’s not an exact science,” said Patrick Harrison, vice president for policy and legislative affairs of the National Alliance for Care at Home, a trade group. “I have seen patients myself where you would not be surprised if they passed away the next day, yet they have lived for nine months or a year.”

“From a hospice perspective, there is some risk there” of having to return money to Medicare as a penalty for excessive payments, he said.

The Trump administration decided this year that hospice fraud had become such a problem that it placed a six-month moratorium on certifying new providers. This month, it extended the moratorium for another six months.

“Fraud in hospice and home health persists, and our work isn’t finished,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in announcing the extension.

The continuing moratorium drew mixed reactions from industry. “Program integrity and access to care should not be competing priorities,” said Katie Smith Sloan, president of LeadingAge, the association that represents nonprofit hospice agencies and nursing homes.

The vast majority of hospice care takes place in a person’s home, in an assisted living facility or in a nursing home, according to federal data. A limited number of patients, less than 2 percent, receive care at inpatient hospice units. Four states have been targeted by various authorities as rife with hospice fraud: California, Arizona, Nevada and Texas.

A report by the state auditor in California in 2022 found high indicators of fraud in Los Angeles County, including long stays in hospice and unusually high numbers of people being discharged alive.

Hospice agencies have been accused of cherry-picking people with dementia, who live longer and require fewer nurse visits than someone dying of cancer. Legislation has been introduced in Congress that would change some of the economic incentives to better reflect the types of patients needing care.

Patient advocates point out that being discharged from hospice doesn’t mean a patient isn’t dying and won’t still need help, as Ms. Birmingham learned. Patients are allowed to re-enroll with a different hospice agency, but that is not always possible in rural areas with few providers, like Sandpoint.

Ms. Birmingham is a former flight engineer and aviation expert who moved from Bend, Ore., where she owned a llama ranch, to Sandpoint to be closer to her son after she had a stroke in 2022.

She was declared disabled, qualifying her for Medicare insurance, soon before she entered hospice in February 2024. Her removal from hospice, called a discharge, in May 2025 meant she was suddenly cut off from comfort care. The discharge form, which she shared with The New York Times, had a single line of justification: “Patient is no longer hospice appropriate.” She had to find a doctor in Sandpoint who would manage her complex needs, including prescribing fentanyl patches for severe pain.

“These hospice nurses cried because I got discharged,” she said. “It’s about the money.”

Auburn Crest Hospice, the for-profit provider that determined Ms. Birmingham was no longer eligible for care, did not respond to requests for comment.

Medicare reimburses hospice companies at a flat daily rate that starts above $236 for the first 60 days and then drops to $186 a day. The per-patient cap of $36,000 is applied to the average for a hospice provider’s patients. That provides an incentive for operators to remove patients from hospice once their care significantly exceeds the cap, because it will push up the company’s per-patient average and could result in financial penalties from Medicare, according to Mr. Gruber and other experts.

A study published this month in the medical journal Health Affairs found that after private equity owners purchased a for-profit hospice provider, billings increased an average of nearly 6 percent. Discharges of people who were still alive rose 11 percent.

“If a person is discharged alive from hospice, for any number of reasons, the hospice wasn’t used completely as intended,” said Dr. Sneha Kannan, an author of the analysis.

Ms. Birmingham contacted Stephanie Wladkowski, a professor at Bowling Green State University, about the cutoff to her care.

It’s disruptive for patients to be summarily removed from hospice without careful planning, said Ms. Wladkowski, who studies the effects on patients when hospice benefits end.

The problem is worse in rural areas, where patients cannot find an alternative hospice to re-enroll. Losing access to narcotic pain medications is common. So is the removal from the home of equipment, like medical-grade beds and specialized wheelchairs, Ms. Wladkowski said.

Having worked as a hospice social worker, she said, she has seen how the caps influence decision-making to the detriment of patients. Hospice providers hesitate to admit some terminally ill patients, worried they will not die soon enough, she said, or they sometimes discharge someone whose decline has slowed or even reversed.

Hospice typically requires that lifesaving measures be curtailed. Chemotherapy and radiation are typically stopped for cancer patients, for instance.

But palliative care continues. Debilitating pain can be reduced with the use of narcotic drugs, relieving emotional and physical stress. Insomnia, nausea and agitation can also be brought under control. Bathing, skin care and repositioning in bed reduces bedsores, infection and sepsis. Social workers and chaplains offer counseling.

There is some evidence those measures prolong life for patients with certain diseases, including congestive heart failure and lung cancer.

Ms. Birmingham believes hospice extended her life. Since she was dropped from hospice in May 2025, she has been paying out of her own pocket for in-home care because she realized the benefit to her well-being.

“Imagine my surprise when I lasted,” she said. “And here I am, still.”

Christopher Rowland is a reporter for The Times covering the health care economy.

Thanksgiving Storm Leaves 375,000 Without Power on the East Coast

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The storm brought heavy rain and strong winds from Virginia to New York, disrupting travel during the holiday season. Conditions were gradually improving on Friday.

By Qasim NaumanFrancesca Regalado and Ishani Desai

Crews from Virginia to New York worked through the night and into Friday to restore power to hundreds of thousands of people after a Thanksgiving storm lashed the East Coast with heavy rain and strong winds.

The storm had moved north into New England by Friday morning after disrupting flights, trains and highways.

It dumped heavy rain — one to four inches in some areas — on Thursday afternoon in Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Virginia before moving into New Jersey and New York in the evening. Some parts of North and South Carolina were walloped with more than nine inches of rain.

In New York City, Central Park received a little over two inches of rain, its wettest Thanksgiving on record, according to preliminary data from the National Weather Service. The severe weather downed trees and damaged power lines in many areas. At one stage on Thursday evening, more than 750,000 customers were without power on the East Coast, according to PowerOutage. us.

By Friday afternoon, about 375,000 customers remained without power from North Carolina to New Hampshire, with the most in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

Nationwide, more than 480,000 were without power in states hit by bad weather, including more than 70,000 in eastern Missouri, where forecasters said as much as 15 inches of snow fell on Thursday.

Utility companies said their crews would work through the holiday weekend to restore power as long as conditions were safe.

Hundreds of flights were canceled, many to airports in the Northeast, and more than 2,000 others were delayed in the middle of the busy holiday travel season.

Some disruption spilled into Friday, with more than 600 canceled flights and 2,000 delays as of 3 p. m., according to the tracking service FlightAware.

Videos on social media showed some people in New York City struggling to hold on to their umbrellas as they were buffeted by wind and rain. Traffic was disrupted on several roads and bridges in New York, while parts of the Jersey Shore were inundated as strong winds pushed seawater inland.

The storm forced the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City to be postponed to Saturday — the first time in the event’s 100-year history that it was moved to another date. The parade is now scheduled to begin at 8:30 a. m. on Saturday.

Conditions were gradually improving on Friday for much of the Eastern United States.

Forecasters said though that there would continue to be “widespread inclement weather” from the sprawling low-pressure system behind the storm, from wet snow in the Tennessee Valley and central Appalachians, to freezing rain in northern New England.

“This huge system will take some time to weaken and move away into the Canadian Maritimes on Saturday,” an early-morning note from the Weather Prediction Center said on Friday.

Rain was falling in New York on Friday, with winds of up to 30 miles an hour.

Sopan Deb contributed reporting.

Qasim Nauman is a Times editor in Seoul, covering breaking news from around the world.

Francesca Regalado is a Times reporter covering breaking news.

Supreme Court Rulings Cheered by Republicans Wound Up Hurting Them

The New York Times November 27, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Decisions on voting rights, immigration and corruption generated a backlash that helped spur turnout that drove the Democratic sweep of Congress.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from Washington

Republicans celebrated last April when the Supreme Court held that a Louisiana House district drawn to give Black voters more say in who represented them was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.

The decision freed legislatures across the South to reconfigure maps to their party’s advantage, providing what Republicans thought would be an edge for them in the midterm congressional elections.

“I don’t think it’s a controversial notion,” Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisianian, said of the ruling at the time. “All states who have unconstitutional maps should look at that very carefully, and I think they should do it before the midterms.”

As it turned out, it was a controversial notion — very controversial, in fact. The decision enraged and energized Black voters in a region where the history of past attempts to restrict minority voting rights still runs deep. It spurred a backlash that amped up turnout, helping propel Democrats to big new majorities in the House and Senate.

“I went into 14 states, and it was everywhere,” Representative James E. Clyburn, Democrat of South Carolina, said of the deep resentment to the ruling seen as a final step in the court’s dismantling of the Voting Rights Act, a premiere achievement of the civil rights movement. “Even in states that were not necessarily what you might call targets.”

“The Supreme Court was absolutely the motivator in all of this,” added Mr. Clyburn, a civil rights activist first elected in 1992 when the court initially opened the door to “majority-minority” congressional districts to offset an ugly history of voter suppression.

It wasn’t just on voting rights where the court’s influence was felt. In taking up cases on immigration enforcement, presidential spending and more, the high court delivered a series of decisions that at first appeared to benefit the president and his party, but ultimately may have had the opposite effect.

Many voters didn’t like what they were seeing. They concluded that the Trump administration needed a check that the court under the stewardship of Chief Justice John Roberts, a longtime critic of the Voting Rights Act, was not providing, and that the court might need a check of its own.

“John Roberts, perhaps unwittingly, undercut the Republican cause as much as anyone else except for Donald Trump,” said Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, who served as a Supreme Court clerk in the mid-1970s. “He has tried to function as a politician in robes completely unsuccessfully because he has no intuitive grasp or experience in the political world.”

Rahm Emanuel, the former House Democratic strategist who ran his party’s successful effort to capture the majority in 2006, said a trio of court decisions reverberated for Democrats. He pointed to the voting rights outcome; the grant of immunity from prosecution to President Trump that helped fuel a narrative of runaway corruption; and a decision by the court that allowed ethnicity to be used as justification for stops and searches by immigration agents.

Together, he said, the rulings alienated Black Americans, Hispanics, more moderate Republicans and independents — all groups that had been crucial to the success of Mr. Trump and congressional Republicans in the last election.

“It broke up their 2024 coalition,” Mr. Emanuel said.

Even Mr. Trump seemed to concede the point on immigration enforcement, saying after his party’s midterm drubbing that his federal crackdown might have been “too tough.”

Other Supreme Court rulings influenced the election as well, including a decision allowing construction of the White House ballroom to continue. It fueled Democratic ads that argued the president was prioritizing luxurious vanity projects for himself over making life more affordable for Americans.

The court also allowed the national parties to spend in direct coordination with candidates — an outcome seen as favoring Republicans — and agreed to let the Department of Homeland Security screen state voter rolls for noncitizens. But in at least one significant case, a result played to Democrats’ advantage, as the court refused to restrict mail-in balloting despite an aggressive push by the president.

The flurry of election-related jurisprudence led Justice Elena Kagan to lament in a speech just before the midterms that “the court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works.”

It could be the voting rights decision that had the greatest impact. Mr. Clyburn and others said it clearly rallied voters to deliver a series of stunning victories in states including Mississippi, South Carolina, North Carolina and Georgia.

Voting data still being compiled by The New York Times showed a significant uptick in the Black share of the electorate across the South from 2024 to 2026, while the national share remained unchanged.

The gains included an increase from 30 to 34 percent of the electorate in Mississippi, which elected its first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first ever since the popular election of senators began. In South Carolina, where a Democrat won a Senate seat for the first time in almost three decades, the share increased from 21 to 24 percent.

“What happened in my part of the country — we witnessed again the assault on the franchise, and we don’t take kindly to that,” said Senator Raphael Warnock, Democrat of Georgia. “We know it when we see it. We’ve seen it time and time again.”

The results reached from Congress into the state legislatures. In South Carolina, 10 statehouse seats flipped from Republican to Democrat. Activists attributed some of those defeats to the legislature’s unsuccessful effort to redraw the congressional map and put Mr. Clyburn’s seat at risk.

“Eight of the folks who lost their seats voted in favor of a rigged map,” Jace Woodrum, executive director of the ACLU of South Carolina, said on a media conference call exploring the 2026 results. “And Black and brown South Carolinians said, ‘Absolutely not. You cannot rig our maps.’”

Mr. Clyburn noted that the conservative-dominated court had been steadily chipping away at the Voting Rights Act and that he and others needed to drive home in the election what was at risk.

“A few of us around here have got enough intelligence to explain that to people,” Mr. Clyburn said. “It was the center part of my campaign.”

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom got considerable attention for a political ad lampooning his Republican opponent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, for her suggestion that her constituents could pick another protein if they could no longer afford beef.

“I’d rather pick another senator,” voters shown in the widely circulated ad retorted.

But one piece of Mr. Colom’s closing message in his stunning upset win that did not attract as much national attention was a tribute to Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader whose assassination in Jackson, Miss., in 1963 drove support for the 1964 Voting Rights Act that was weakened by the high court.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Mr. Colom said in the video as Election Day loomed. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.
