Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Is Rich-Guy Propaganda

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By David Colman

Mr. Colman is a critic and a former writer of the Possessed column for The Times.

After years of having their greedy exploits valorized in popular culture and rewarded at the ballot box, rich people are feeling misunderstood these days: The socialist haters have taken over the culture. Fortunately for them, these oligarchs also happen to own big media companies — which means they could, if they wanted, greenlight films and TV shows that are sympathetic to their plush predicament.

Take “Ebenezer,” the latest version of Charles Dickens’s “A Christmas Carol,” now in theaters. Johnny Depp’s Scrooge, the horrible miserly capitalist lacking in empathy and Christmas cheer, is, as it turns out, also the victim of a resentful, grasping society that preys on rich, hard-working men like him.

Reimagined as the son of a cruel drunkard who gets bullied at school, the embittered grown-up Scrooge can see what foolish Christmas revelers do not. In the movie’s very first scene, Scrooge discovers that the half-blind man begging for coins is a fake. In a pair of scenes that bookend the present and future, two men who visit Scrooge collecting for charity — charity being the central theme of Dickens’s story, mind you — turn out to be lowlifes who try to steal his fortune.

Directed by Ti West (who is best known for “MaXXXine”) and starring Mr. Depp in his own attempt at redemption after long, ugly lawsuits against and by his ex-wife the actress Amber Heard, “Ebenezer” is among the first films greenlighted and produced by Paramount after its acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance.

Call it billionaires-are-people-too propaganda.

Most of the film is a perfunctory retelling of the tale we all know well: ghosts, Tiny Tim and all. And. yes — spoiler alert — by the end, Scrooge has seen the Christmas light, loosened his heart and purse strings enough to make Bob Cratchit a partner, help save Tiny Tim and bring his affluent nephew (rather than the poor Cratchits) a goose for dinner.

But give to charity? The movie has already established that in this Scroogiverse, charity and fraud are two sides of the same ha’penny. That’s enough to dangerously warp the hundreds of years of Christmas culture that animated Dickens’s 1843 novella and helped crystallize it into such a powerful emblem of the season.

For centuries before the Industrial Revolution, Christmas was celebrated not as the foremost Christian holiday but as an occasion for far more secular, populist revelry, with a sometimes rowdy spirit, that was closer to today’s New Year’s Eve or Halloween. It also had a special emphasis on class reversal: The custom of wassailing involved groups of people (a-caroling or not) knocking on the wealthy’s doors and demanding food, drink or even money, sometimes under an implicit threat of vandalism. The carousing got so out of hand that Christmas celebrations were occasionally banned, as they were in 17th-century Massachusetts.

By the 1840s in London, industrialization and commercialization were in full swing. This was the time and place that both Marx’s “Communist Manifesto” and Thackeray’s “Vanity Fair” were published and that saw the birth of the commercially printed Christmas card, the chocolate candy bar and Harrods department store. At the same time, nostalgia for simple, charming and rustic Christmas customs swept into vogue. An engraving of Queen Victoria with her husband, the German-born Prince Albert, and their children gathered around a Christmas tree was widely reproduced, probably doing more than any other image to turn the German custom into the holiday’s crowning symbol.

The rowdy shakedown of wassailing was transformed into family-friendly carol singing, and the public sentiment that the haves had a charitable obligation to the have-nots took hold. This iteration of Christmas also sanctified a mercantile boom in Christmas presents, by implicitly stressing a moral counterweight. Simply put: You can have what you want if they have what they need.

Into this era arrived “A Christmas Carol,” the first edition of which sold out in days and helped codify the Christmas spirit of giving freely. But now, by trying to update and humanize Scrooge by making him a 19th-century libertarian, “Ebenezer” ends up echoing today’s Silicon Valley-centered anti-charity entitlement (see: Thiel, Peter) and stingy reluctance to offer fair pay (see: Bezos, Jeff). “I will not apologize for my well-earned success,” Scrooge tells the Ghost of Christmas Present, sounding awfully similar to the victimhood expressed by tech investors like Marc Andreessen and Kevin O’Leary. You almost expect Mr. Depp’s Scrooge to sneer, “Fake news!” instead of “Humbug!”

While minor, the changes feel major — and rather on point at a time when the very rich (including Elon Musk) are feeling and acting in a decidedly uncharitable manner. The Scrooge of “Ebenezer” gets into “giving” minus the “freely,” explicitly adding exceptions to the social contract. This Scrooge will be generous to his family and employees, but that’s not exactly the major worldview transformation Dickens wrote about. It’s a pointed reminder of how our culture has come to interpret selfish motives as virtuous and selfless ones as suspicious or woke.

As adaptations go, far more creative interpretations, like “It’s a Wonderful Life” and “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” express Dickens’s original spirit better. Toward the end of “Ebenezer,” when Scrooge, repenting his ways, cries, “Allow me my redemption!” before falling into his grave, I did not find myself charitable enough to oblige him. The lesson here is that, as it turns out, salvation is a lot like money. You have to earn it.

David Colman is a critic and a former writer of the Possessed column for The Times.

Canada’s Top Court Lets Quebec Use Controversial Measure for Secularism Law

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Quebec had used the measure to pass a law barring certain public workers, like schoolteachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols on duty, which critics called discriminatory.

By Norimitsu Onishi

Reporting from Montreal

Canada’s top court ruled on Friday that Quebec could use a legal provision of the Constitution to pass a secularism law that overrides some rights, a landmark decision that likely averts an immediate political crisis for the country.

The Supreme Court said Quebec was within its rights to use the so-called notwithstanding clause to pass legislation in 2019 that reinforced secularism in the French-speaking province. That law prohibited certain public workers, like public schoolteachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols while on duty — leading some linguistic and religious minorities to call it discriminatory and a violation of the Canadian Constitution.

But the long-anticipated ruling was not a total victory for Quebec and other provinces that had fiercely defended using the clause to set aside parts of the Constitution. The court also ruled that, even as such legislation was allowed to stand, courts can still declare that they violate Constitutional rights.

That could open up such legislation to legal challenges in the future, and raise the political costs for governments using the provision.

But the Supreme Court on Friday made no judgment on whether Quebec’s 2019 law itself had violated the Canadian Constitution, mitigating any strong pushback from the province.

For now, Friday’s ruling seemed unlikely to cause problems for Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has emphasized Canadian unity against threats from the United States and amid separatist sentiments in Quebec and Alberta.

Yves-François Blanchet, the leader of the Bloc Québécois, a party that holds seats in the federal Parliament but supports independence for Quebec, described the ruling as a victory for the province.

“Unequivocally,’’ he said, “the highest court in Canada told Quebec: You have the right, and it is crucial to resort to the notwithstanding clause to protect who you are.”

In Quebec, some separatists had hoped that a strong ruling against the 2019 law would help stir nationalist sentiments in the province. In October, the separatist Parti Québécois returned to power for the first time in 12 years, promising to hold a referendum on separation from the rest of Canada after 2029.

Quebec’s new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has focused his first weeks in power on asserting the province’s authority against the federal government. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has pledged to push Quebec secularism further, for example by barring students at public primary schools from wearing religious clothing or symbols.

Joe Ortona, the chairman of the English Montreal School Board, a lead plaintiff against the Quebec government, told reporters that the board was “obviously very disappointed with the decision,” adding that “the sun comes up tomorrow.”

At the heart of the case is a provision of Canada’s Constitution known as the notwithstanding clause. It allows governments to pass legislation that overrides some of the rights in the country’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and protects it from legal challenges. The override is valid for five years and can be renewed. Provinces have used it pre-emptively, trying to shield a law before anyone could challenge it in court.

Provinces have increasingly used the clause in recent years to pass laws geared toward local interests.

Alberta and Saskatchewan have used it to protect laws barring children under 16 from changing their names or pronouns at school without parental consent, laws that could otherwise conflict with the rights to free expression and equality. Ontario used it to protect a law limiting election advertising and another that ended a strike by education workers, shielding them from claims that they violated free speech and the right to organize.

Stephen Brown, the chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said the ruling reinforces the increasingly casual use of the notwithstanding clause.

“It was intended to be an instrument of last resort, and now it has become an ordinary instrument of government,” he said.

The use of the clause grew after Quebec passed the 2019 secularism law, known as Bill 21, that overrode the Charter’s protections for religions, conscience and expression. Quebec’s nationalist, right-leaning government argued that the law was crucial to protecting secularism in Quebec. The Roman Catholic Church once held enormous political influence and control in the province, including over public education. Religious symbols worn by some public employees, the government said, would undermine the neutrality of the state, as well as the separation of state and religions.

In its ruling Friday, the Supreme Court said that Quebec’s 2019 law “is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society.” Laicity is a term used in Quebec and in France to refer to secularism.

But some minority groups — including the English Montreal School Board, as well as Muslim and Sikh organizations — sued the Quebec government, arguing the law was discriminatory and that it violated their rights to religious freedom and equal treatment under the Canadian Constitution. The law was upheld by two lower courts, ultimately reaching the Supreme Court. In a sign of the case’s significance, the Supreme Court last spring devoted four days to hearings on the case, one of the longest in its history.

At the hearings, plaintiffs pressed the court to strike down the 2019 law and restrict the use of the notwithstanding clause. Quebec and other provinces opposed any changes to the clause. The Canadian government asked the Supreme Court to restrict its use and let courts declare a law enacted under the clause to be a violation of rights.

Beyond its implications in Quebec, the use of the notwithstanding clause touches upon a historically sensitive issue in Canada, the balance of power in its federation.

In the early 1980s, Canada updated its Constitution by ending Britain’s remaining control over it. Canada adopted its current Constitution — and a newly created Charter of Rights — in 1982 but only after a political compromise: the inclusion of the notwithstanding clause, which pacified provincial leaders who feared handing too much power to judges.

Norimitsu Onishi reports on life, society and culture in Canada. He is based in Montreal.

The Macy’s Parade Has Been Marred by War, Wind and Weather

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

It isn’t always easy to keep New York City’s Thanksgiving parade on track. Here’s a look back at notable moments and mishaps.

IN PHOTOS

A crew inflating the Linus the Lionhearted balloon in 1991, the year that a sudden gust of wind blew a different balloon — Betty Boop — into the trees along Central Park West. Credit... Sara Krulwich/The New York Times

Supported by

By Ishani Desai and Keith Bedford

Keith Bedford has photographed several editions of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, in good and bad weather.

The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has overcome rain, snow, a pandemic, emergencies and protests to delight millions across New York City and beyond nearly every year since 1924.

But on Wednesday night, Macy’s announced that the parade had to be postponed because of heavy rain and wind, forecasted to reach 58 miles per hour. Americans did not begin their holiday morning on Thursday by watching balloons, marching bands and pop stars on glittering floats move through Manhattan. Instead, the parade will begin at 8:30 a. m. on Saturday.

With the parade’s postponement for the first time in 55 years, here’s a look at some notable moments and mishaps through the event’s history.

The parade went on a three-year hiatus in 1942, prompted by the materiel needs of the World War II effort. When it returned to the route in 1945, above, young people cheered and applauded in the sunshine. “For the generation born during the war it was the opening of a new wonderland,” The New York Times reported. Nearly 30,000 crammed into Times Square.

In the 1927 parade, Felix the Cat stuck its tongue out at onlookers as it bobbed through the city, held aloft by handlers dressed as clowns. At the parade’s end, officials released Felix the Cat and other balloons, leaving their fates to the whims of the weather. Felix’s end was particularly dire: He bumped into a high-tension wire in West Norwood, N. J., and burst into flames.

The parade has had other brushes with bad weather. In 1971, intense gusts grounded the Macy’s balloons. The marching bands played on, and families turned out to see them.

The 1997 parade was marred when a gust of wind knocked a six-story Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, injuring four spectators. One woman, Kathy Caronna of Manhattan, was critically injured and spent 24 days in a coma. Three others were also hurt.

In 2005, windy conditions drove a 515-pound M&Ms balloon into a light pole in Times Square. Two people — a 26-year-old woman, who was using a wheelchair, and her 11-year-old sister — were injured.

The two crashes each prompted calls for safety reforms.

The Covid-19 pandemic had upended a normal world, cloaking everyone in uncertainty, but one ritual went ahead in 2020: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Sort of. The organizers truncated the parade’s route to one block, down from two miles. High school bands stayed home. Police officers were assigned to ward off any crowds eager for a glimpse. It felt to many like a sign of hope when the parade returned in 2021.

A Thanksgiving snowstorm hit New York City in 1989 for the first time in 51 years. Wind gusts tore at the seams of giant balloons and punctured Snoopy’s nose.

Rain fell on the parade in 2024, but many onlookers smiled anyway.

Following the rescheduling of Thursday’s parade, the Buzz Lightyear balloon waited to be deflated until Saturday morning, when the event is scheduled to kick off. The joy was not over, just postponed.

An earlier version of this article misstated the length of time that Kathy Caronna was in a coma after an accident at the 1997 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. It was 24 days, not 24 hours.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Ishani Desai is a reporter covering breaking news and other topics, and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

With Dancing Robots, Russia Projects a Future Shaped by A. I., Not War

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Russian officials see artificial intelligence as a way to solve the country’s pressing problems. But Russia’s technological development has been constrained.

By Ivan Nechepurenko

Reporting from Russia’s flagship tech conference in Moscow

The humanoid robots shimmied and leaped in perfect synchronicity with the flesh-and-blood dancers behind them. President Vladimir V. Putin, eyes wide at times, took in the spectacle from the audience at Russia’s flagship technology conference.

In this display and many others at the event, called A. I. Journey, the country’s future was presented as being shaped not by the war in Ukraine, but by the development of artificial intelligence. Russia, Mr. Putin said in his keynote speech on Thursday, wants the adoption of A. I. to encompass “all spheres of the economy and people’s lives.”

Yet even as Russian officials look to the technology to offset a range of problems like labor shortages, the country’s technological development has been constrained.

Russian A. I. models depend on American and Chinese hardware that has become harder to obtain and more expensive because of sanctions. Immense spending on the military has diverted resources. Technology talent has left Russia because of the war. Security officials monitor domestic A. I. models to ensure that they comply with censorship rules.

And this year, a new challenge emerged after Ukrainian drones attacked some of the country’s most powerful data centers.

Still, Mr. Putin and senior technocrats remain determined to push Russia forward in A. I.

During the conference, German O. Gref, the head of Russia’s largest bank, Sberbank, unveiled the latest model of its flagship GigaChat bot, claiming that it approaches the capabilities of leading Chinese models such as DeepSeek.

The bank has woven the model into daily life in Russia. Some Moscow restaurants offer A. I.-assisted menus, and museum exhibitions use A. I.-powered guides to explain the works on display.

The model remains censored. For instance, GigaChat declines to give concrete examples of what Mr. Putin’s opponents criticize him for, saying it is a “sensitive” topic.

A Russian data scientist involved in the bot’s development said that the security services watched closely to make sure that the model complied with a loosely defined set of “traditional values.” The developer spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly.

Mr. Gref has pitched the bank’s model as the only genuinely domestic option, arguing that it can therefore be used in sensitive fields such as defense, according to a Russian official involved in developing digital infrastructure. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

Even as Russia and China have drawn closer in recent years, there is unease in Moscow over growing too dependent on Chinese technology. In his speech, Mr. Putin said Russia was “betting on sovereign foundational models.”

“We must not end up in a situation we have already experienced, when someone presses a button for us and everything stops working altogether,” he said.

At the conference, Russian officials and business leaders struck an effusive tone about A. I., suggesting in speeches that the technology could help solve many pressing problems at once. Endless screens showcased how A. I. could improve Russia’s court system, health care and even pothole repair.

Officials argued that the technology could make up for labor shortages caused by Russia’s demographic challenges. The country is projected to lose roughly 820,000 people to population decline this year, according to a leading demographer. That includes some of the hundreds of thousands of soldiers who have been killed over nearly five years of war in Ukraine, according to recent estimates.

“For Russia — as we are developing amid serious demographic challenges and a shortage of labor resources — such technologies are a real opportunity to overcome limitations and strengthen our potential,” Mr. Putin said in his speech.

Although Western sanctions are a hurdle to Russia’s A. I. development, technical specifications released with the GigaChat model underscored how Russian companies had managed to procure advanced chips. Aleksandr A. Vedyakhin, the first deputy chairman of Sberbank, declined to comment on how the company obtained the chips, saying only, “We are doing it somehow.”

Still, while Russian companies may be able to get some of the hardware they need, many of them, including those owned by the state, use American and Chinese models in their work, instead of developing their own.

According to Stepan Gershuni, a Russian technology investor and entrepreneur, “it isn’t just about computing capacity — it’s also about access to capital, access to talent and companies’ willingness to do it.”

“A serious effort to build a competitor today would require investments in the single-digit or tens of billions of dollars,” Mr. Gershuni said in response to written questions. “In the current economic climate, Russian businesses simply don’t have that kind of money. I can’t speak for the government, though it seems they are spending their money elsewhere.”

Since invading Ukraine, Russia has poured hundreds of billions of dollars into its military.

In addition to the financing shortfalls, the war has left Moscow scrambling to protect the domestic technology infrastructure. This fall, Ukrainian drones struck several data centers, including a facility being developed by Sberbank. The company’s main rival, Yandex, had three data centers hit and damaged.

But Kremlin officials have argued that Russia has advantages in the A. I. age, including its vast energy reserves and remote territory.

On Tuesday, Mr. Putin approved a program to build data centers in Russia’s coal-mining regions of Kuzbass and Yakutia, areas far from the front line in Ukraine. Depleted coal pits and shafts there could be used to shield the facilities from attack.

Kirill A. Dmitriev, the Kremlin’s senior envoy on talks with the United States, said at the conference that cheap domestic energy gave Russia “an exclusive global advantage as the lowest-cost power supplier for data centers worldwide.” He added that Moscow could build data centers for both the United States and China.

“In the current geopolitical climate, that may sound like a fantasy,” Mr. Dmitriev said. But in a few years, he added, “countries will realize that managing complex A. I. systems requires capabilities Russia can provide that others simply cannot.”

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting.

Ivan Nechepurenko covers Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia. He divides his reporting time between Moscow and Tbilisi, Georgia.

In Congress vs. Trump, the Loser May Be Federal Contractors

The New York Times November 27, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The incoming Democratic majorities have begun targeting businesses and other outsiders in their planned inquiries, but the president has threatened to fire them if they comply without his permission.

By Luke Broadwater

Reporting from Washington

When the House Jan. 6 committee in 2022 encountered roadblocks from Donald J. Trump’s inner circle, investigators sought answers from his outer circle, sending interview and records requests to businesses and individuals outside government.

Many complied, including telecommunications companies, social media sites and government contractors, turning over documents and phone records that helped supply material for televised hearings that painted a damning portrait of Mr. Trump’s role in the mob attack on the Capitol.

The Trump administration is hoping to cancel a sequel before it can be made.

Faced with incoming Democratic majorities gearing up for an array of investigations, the White House plans to vigorously fight any congressional oversight it views as illegitimate. And Mr. Trump has warned contractors in an executive order that they must seek permission from the White House before complying with a congressional oversight demand or risk being fired.

Businesses and other outsiders will soon find themselves stuck in the middle.

On one side, Congress has a constitutional duty to conduct oversight of the administration and can vote to hold in contempt those who refuse to comply with its subpoenas. Such a vote can result in jail time, as two Trump allies, Stephen K. Bannon and Peter Navarro, experienced after refusing to testify in the Jan. 6 committee investigation.

A vote to hold someone in contempt is referred for prosecution to the Justice Department, which is controlled by Mr. Trump and would be unlikely to follow through. Still, a contempt of Congress finding carries significant reputational damage, and the statute of limitations for the offense is five years, well past Mr. Trump’s term. Congress also has the constitutional power of the purse and could punish recalcitrant contractors financially.

On the other side is Mr. Trump. Famously vengeful, the president has made no secret of his plans to go after those who cross him. His second term has been defined, in some ways, by his revenge tour and his administration’s investigations, funding cuts and executive orders against a variety of institutions, including law firms and universities.

“I feel bad for contractors,” said Jim Secreto, the former chief investigative counsel to Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York. “They’re going to get squeezed by both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue, and it’s not going to be a pleasant experience.”

Mr. Secreto, who worked in the White House Counsel’s Office under President Barack Obama, said presidents had used a number of strategies to stonewall congressional investigations. Often, in response, Congress will try to find a different way to get the information.

“Congress can just keep going and going until it finds a willing party,” Mr. Secreto said. “OK, the agency won’t provide information, go to the private sector. The contractor won’t provide it, go to the contractor’s bank. Then go to the contractor’s I. T. provider. Eventually you’ll get to someone that says: ‘Look, I don’t want to get crosswise with Congress. I’m just going to give them the information.’”

Poised to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, Democrats believe they have a mandate to thoroughly investigate the Trump administration after their lopsided wins in midterm elections in which polls showed government corruption was a top voter concern.

Democrats plan to cast a wide net. If there are potentially corrupt dealings between the Trump administration and private business, both sides should be investigated, they argue.

Last week, Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, sent a dozen notices to members of Mr. Trump’s family, Vice President JD Vance and other current and former administration officials asking them to preserve documents on a host of issues.

And Senators Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, and Adam B. Schiff, Democrat of California, demanded answers from lobbyists who they said had played an instrumental role in funneling corporate donations into Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom project.

This week, Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, signaled that investigations were likely to involve many private-sector companies that have done business with Mr. Trump or his family.

Mr. Raskin announced that he was expanding his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, demanding records from Hadrian Automation, Juul Labs, Polymarket and GrabAGun Digital Holdings. Mr. Raskin said he was investigating whether the president’s son and his business partners had helped steer federal contracts or regulatory decisions to companies in which they had a financial interest or had used advance knowledge of decisions to profit.

Bill Burck, a lawyer for 1789 Capital, said he had reached out to Mr. Raskin to point out what he called “the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors.”

“These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence,” he said in a statement.

Whether they decide to cooperate or fight, companies will often have to spend significant resources on lawyers to navigate a congressional inquiry.

Machalagh Carr, the former top lawyer in the House under Speaker Kevin McCarthy, a Republican, said the greatest pain to companies would be from having to deal with the investigation itself.

But the Supreme Court has said congressional inquiries must have “a valid legislative purpose,” and Ms. Carr warned Democrats against trying to expand them beyond that.

“The process is the punishment,” she said. “But the expansion of oversight into nonlegislative questions has led the courts to continually limit congressional subpoena authority and enforcement power. If Congress continues to overreach, especially into private companies and private individuals, the courts are likely to continue this pattern.”

Susanne Sachsman Grooms, who served as chief counsel to the House Oversight Committee under three Democratic leaders, said each company that received a letter from Congress would face tough decisions about how to comply, especially if Mr. Trump takes a clear action such as asserting executive privilege over the material sought.

“A subpoena is a very clear law, but then, if you have a formal assertion of executive privilege, that’s also pretty clear,” she said. “The pain points and the pressure points in these battles all point toward the entity in the middle.”

Luke Broadwater covers the White House for The Times.

It’s the Most Lucrative Time of the Year (for Influencers)

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A growing part of a brand’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday marketing strategy rests on paying top dollar for social media influencers to post videos.

By Aruni Soni and Kim Bhasin

If Brie DElia, a fashion influencer, weren’t constrained by the number of hours in a day, she could have made $78,000 this month.

Every day over the last few weeks, Ms. DElia, 26, has received over a dozen brand deals related to Black Friday and Cyber Monday emailed to her inbox. The offers ask her to make videos promoting products like straight-leg jeans and fall trench coats and post them on her TikTok and Instagram pages. Sometimes she receives requests that can total up to $30,000 in a single day.

“I’m making the bulk of my income at this time,” Ms. DElia said, squeezing a call in between her day job at a licensing company and an evening planning out a Black Friday deal video for her follower base of 168,000 on TikTok and 52,000 on Instagram.

For many online creators, the last two months of the year are the most lucrative, as businesses rush to compete for shoppers’ attention with holiday sales. Retailers count on sales driven by social media, and creators work to make the most of that brief but frenetic window — one in which they can double or even triple their monthly income.

“This is the Super Bowl for them,” said Madison Weaver, co-founder and chief marketing officer of the Creator Society, a marketing and talent management company.

The influencer frenzy shows just how much holiday shopping has changed in recent years for retailers. The battle for consumer attention has shifted to different social media strategies, away from traditional television, print and radio ads. Social ad revenue grew 32.6 percent this year, and the industry now represents 40 percent of all digital ad revenue, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau, a trade group.

Unilever, one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies, now has nearly 300,000 people recommending its products, like Dove soap and Liquid I. V. hydration packets. That’s up from around 10,000 two years ago. Fernando Fernandez, the chief executive of Unilever, told investors in April that the company was still figuring out how to deploy influencers most efficiently.

“This has been a significant change in the infrastructure behind our model of consumer reach and engagement,” Mr. Fernandez said. “We have increased the level of investment, but there is still a lot to do to maximize the return on that spending.”

Most online creators make their money either by being paid to promote products in videos and social media posts (brand deals) or by earning commissions on items followers purchase using specialized website links attached to their online profiles, known as affiliate links. They can earn thousands of dollars for a single Instagram reel or Substack post.

LTK is a creator commerce platform that many influencers use to share links to the products they’re promoting. Nearly a quarter of all retail sales driven through creator recommendations on LTK in 2025 were generated in November and December, the firm said.

One of Ms. Weaver’s clients is making $200,000 to $250,000 this month from brand deals alone, up from $80,000 to $100,000 earned during other months of the year. Ms. Weaver said the Creator Society might typically charge $5,000 for an Instagram reel but could bump that number up to $6,500 this time of year.

“I will as much as double rates if we’re getting down to the wire,” she said.

Melanie Wilking-Ekeler, a 27-year-old content creator who makes a third of her income during the last three months of the year, said she was working with 10 brands this month, up from three at other times.

“The quantity of brands I’m working with is larger during this time, when a lot of companies are running these sales at the same time,” she said. Ms. Wilking-Ekeler has 709,000 followers on Instagram and 3.8 million on TikTok.

Her days are chock-full of attending meetings, submitting ideas for her posts to companies for approval, filming videos and editing them. When asked how many hours she had contributed to creating content every day this month, she said, “I feel like it never shuts off — but filmmaking is the shortest part of what I do.”

For Kit Keenan, 27, the rush for holiday gigs begins in late July and early August, as companies map out their seasonal marketing plans. She is mostly focused on food content and released her own cookbook this year, sharing Thanksgiving recipes and gift guides for home goods with her nearly 500,000 followers on Instagram.

It’s crucial not to overload fans with ads in their feeds, she said, which means she needs to post other content regularly to keep them interested.

“It’s definitely the busiest time of year for me, and it’s a balance of making as much organic content as I possibly can to balance that out and to not have my followers feel fatigue from me posting brand partnerships,” Ms. Keenan said.

Christina Elezaj, a 32-year-old fashion influencer who used to work a corporate job at LinkedIn and now collaborates with brands such as Walmart and L’Oréal, said there was a last-second scramble for brands to spend their marketing budgets. Influencers will sometimes sign a deal to make content and post something on the same day.

“I remember my boss saying, ‘We either use it or we lose it,’” Ms. Elezaj said. “If there’s a natural, organic opportunity to have a creator who already loves the product promoted during these sales, it seems like a win-win.”

As brands pump more money into the creator economy, the largest part of that growth is in ad dollars put toward short-form videos, unboxings, “get ready with me” content and other types of posts online. Businesses plan to increase the amount they spend with creators on those types of videos to $25 billion by 2030, up from $5 billion in 2020, according to a recent report by Madison and Wall, an advertising advisory firm.

Companies will also sometimes pay double the amount for a video post if a creator agrees to exclusively promote their products for a fixed period before and after the post, said Sreya Halder, a 25-year-old online creator. After gaining 445,000 followers on TikTok, Ms. Halder can pull in up to $9,000 for a video, she said.

This is her first year working with brands on Black Friday deals, but the pressure has already ramped up. Ms. Halder, who also runs her own fashion and tech business, said she “crashed out” when the offers began rolling in early this month.

“I had never experienced the holiday waves, but then as soon as that first, second week of November came, within four days we had all these deals, and it was for over the course of the next couple of months,” she said.

Ms. Halder had to make sure that her holiday travel plans aligned with the deals and that she had time to film all her videos. Some offers required her go into a store to film a video a day after the initial outreach.

“It’s a great time to be a creator, but it’s also very, very chaotic,” she said.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Before there was Tom Wolfe, there was Charlotte Curtis, who turned Park Avenue into news.

Credit... Matt Dorfman

Supported by

By Ginia Bellafante

Ginia Bellafante, who frequently writes about wealth and class, has been obsessed with Charlotte Curtis since finding a copy of her collection “The Rich and Other Atrocities” on eBay during the pandemic.

This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

On a January evening in 1970, Charlotte Curtis arrived at Leonard and Felicia Bernstein’s two-story penthouse on Park Avenue without an invitation. The couple was hosting a fund-raiser in support of 21 members of the Black Panthers who had been indicted on flimsy allegations of conspiring to blow up several New York City buildings. The party was not the first or last held that season to raise money for the arrested activists, who were eventually exonerated. But it would stand as the only one to sustain the interests of history.

Nearly 90 guests mingled between the two grand pianos in the Bernsteins’ vast living room: artists and writers — Otto Preminger, Adolph Green, Peter Duchin, Sidney Lumet — along with socialites and leaders of the Panthers’ New York chapter. The party was closed to the press, but Curtis, then nine years into her tenure as a reporter and editor at The New York Times, was brought along, the story goes, by an actress friend who lived in her Greenwich Village building. Wearing a chic but inconspicuous black dress, she stood with her notebook in the corner, near soaring windows framed by green velvet drapes.

The party began stiffly but gained momentum, the disparate groups, Curtis wrote, “studying one another cautiously over the expensive furnishings, the elaborate flower arrangements, the cocktails and the silver trays of canapés.” Leonard Bernstein, then at the height of his fame as conductor of the New York Philharmonic, navigated the crowd in Black Watch tartan slacks. One Panther assured a white woman that she would not be killed just because her husband was an avowed capitalist.

Curtis recorded everything. The piece that appeared the next morning under her byline, absent embellishment or condescension, was a portrait of elite obliviousness. Especially damning were bits of a conversation she caught between the heiress Cynthia Phipps and the Panther organizer Henry Mitchell. Mitchell was complaining that he often waited six or seven minutes for a dial tone on his phone.

“I have the same problem. They really ought to do something about it,” Phipps said.

Mitchell, though, was talking about interference from F. B. I. wiretaps.

Bernstein had also made himself vulnerable to derision. Part of the proceedings involved a formal question-and-answer session between him and Donald Cox, the Panthers’ “field marshal.” Curtis quoted Cox claiming that if Black people were denied “full employment,” then the Panthers would “take the means of production and put them in the hands of the people.” And then Bernstein’s reply: “I dig absolutely.”

Reading Curtis’s story, the Bernsteins were furious — both at the content, which they felt was snide, and at the placement in the society pages, which they viewed as trivializing. The piece ran on The Times’s wire service as well, which meant it was printed in papers around the world, exposing the couple to wider denunciation.

Remarkably, the Times editorial board also weighed in, accusing “the politico‐cultural jet set” of romanticizing the militant Panthers in an act of “elegant slumming.” Protests broke out in front of the Bernsteins’ building. In Miami, Jewish picketers who considered the Panthers antisemitic demanded the cancellation of a documentary in which Leonard Bernstein was central.

Six months after the fund-raiser, Tom Wolfe, who had also crashed the party that night, published his own take in New York magazine. “Radical Chic,” his gleeful 25,000-word evisceration of the cosmopolitan left, soon and forever supplanted Curtis’s straightforward account in the cultural memory, but in a sense he had just built upon her lead. As Wolfe later explained admiringly, “It wasn’t anything she wrote that infuriated them. It was that she put down exactly what they said. That’s always what seems cruelest of all, to hold up a mirror to people that way.”

For Curtis, the piece was merely another expression of her news-making approach to society coverage. Long considered disposable and unserious, it became a chronicle of dubious belief systems and mindless self-regard. At villas and parties and horse races and resorts, the rich showed Curtis who they really were. When she interviewed Warren Avis, founder of the rental-car company, at his enormous vacation house in Acapulco, for example, he told her that he “wanted a house where you’d never see the servants and you don’t.”

Back in 1961, when Curtis was hired by The Times as a fashion reporter, it would have been impossible to foresee the kind of influence she would eventually leverage. Nearly everyone else in the newsroom with any authority was male, and the society pages, where she was later relegated, provided little more than wedding announcements and travel itineraries.

It was Clifton Daniel, the paper’s assistant managing editor at the time, who encouraged her ambition. A pharmacist’s son who had married Harry Truman’s daughter, Margaret, Daniel maintained an outsider’s fascination with moneyed subcultures and believed that Curtis could write about the rich in a way that was neither tediously prosaic nor deferential — as “sociology.”

His instincts were right. Curtis, a Vassar graduate and the daughter of a wealthy Ohio family, took herself beyond New York, drawing meaningful distinctions among the various social orders of Denver and Boston, San Francisco and Miami. In 1966, she covered Truman Capote’s historic Black and White Ball at the Plaza Hotel, a gala that famously broke open the longstanding social barriers between uptown and down, assembling poets, intellectuals, socialites, movie stars, businessmen and the Maharani of Jaipur. Curtis published the 540-person guest list in the paper, making it impossible for anyone to lie about whether they had gotten an invitation. She had received one.

By the early 1970s, Curtis had become the most powerful woman at The Times. In 1974, she was named editor of the Op-Ed page, the first woman to hold the position, one she would occupy for the next eight years. The page was still a new venture for the newspaper. It required an editor of independent mind, one comfortable publishing a range of opinions, including ones with which she disagreed. As she had done with the lifestyle pages, Curtis aligned the section with the preoccupations of the moment, calling on younger contributors like Erica Jong to write about a culture untangling the old mores. This led to misperceptions. Just as socialites were surprised that someone who looked like a compatriot could embarrass them in print by publishing what they had actually said, feminists were confused by Curtis’s resistance to public advocacy.

In 1986, a year before she died at the age of 58, The Times conceded to pressures to incorporate “Ms.” as an honorific. Curtis was skeptical. “This afternoon the managing editor is going to have a meeting to take up the matter of Ms., pronounced miz, the new title for ladies,” she wrote to her husband. “The liberated ones want to be called Ms. I don’t.”

The same year she was named Op-Ed editor, seven women at The Times brought a class-action suit against the company for gender-based pay disparities. They won but Curtis, to lasting consternation, had not supported their case, claiming that as a manager she had to remain neutral.

And yet these public intimations of ambivalence did not line up neatly with the private reality. In 1968, she covered a protest of the Miss America Pageant in Atlantic City that had been organized by the feminist activist Robin Morgan. Decades later, in a letter to The Times, Morgan said that when she went to check on demonstrators who had been arrested, she discovered that they had been released on bail, the cash put up by a woman named Charlotte Curtis. When Morgan called to thank her, Curtis asked to keep her breach of journalistic ethics between them.

“Those dreary gray guys running The Times,” she told Morgan, would not be amused.

Ginia Bellafante writes features, profiles and social criticism for The Times.

In the 1960s and ’70s, Charlotte Curtis was a household name — in a very particular kind of household. She was a wealthy and socially prominent woman who often covered the wealthy and socially prominent quite critically. What would she have made of the current moment in all its veneration of money and power? What would she make of Instagram?

Five Big Questions for the 2028 Presidential Race

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Will JD Vance and Marco Rubio run? What about Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez? And, of course, what role will President Trump play?

By Tim Balk

The midterm election is barely behind us, but in some ways the 2028 presidential race has already begun.

The start of the holiday season — long a time for ambitious politicians to sort out their plans and lay the groundwork for White House bids — has brought a flurry of activity and speculation. Debates are being scheduled, likely candidates are recruiting top aides and everyone in politics is waiting for some of the biggest names to reveal whether they are running or not.

Both parties are expected to have crowded and competitive primaries, as Democrats hunt for new leaders and Republicans ponder who should fill the void that President Trump will leave behind.

Here are five burning questions about the presidential race to come.

Mr. Trump’s vice president, Mr. Vance, and his secretary of state, Mr. Rubio, are both potential heirs to the president’s political movement and offer two distinct visions of Republican politics.

Mr. Trump has long enjoyed asking allies who would make a better presidential candidate between Mr. Vance, a former Ohio senator with a populist brand, or Mr. Rubio, a former senator from Florida with hawkish foreign policy views who has accumulated many titles in the president’s second administration.

But it’s not clear they will definitely run. If one or both decline, it would probably encourage other Republicans to join the race.

Mr. Vance took a risk after the midterms, publicly blaming Mr. Trump’s war in Iran for their party’s sweeping losses. Mr. Trump has been frustrated with Mr. Vance over the critique, leading some Republicans to see a rise in the stock of Mr. Rubio, who has cast the war as necessary for U. S. national security.

But Mr. Vance’s analysis could also help clear a 2028 lane for him as a Republican willing to oppose some of the president’s unpopular foreign policy decisions.

Mr. Vance has said that he will decide next year whether to run. Mr. Rubio, who ran for president in 2016, has said that Mr. Vance would be a strong candidate. He has shied away from questions about 2028.

“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” Mr. Rubio told The New York Times this month. “I just won’t do it.”

Potential candidates from each side of the country could alter the course of the Democratic primary.

On the West Coast, Ms. Harris — the former vice president, who published a memoir late last year — said this spring that she “might” run. In her most recent public remarks on the issue, an interview this month with the Swiss newspaper Tages-Anzeiger, she said her decision would primarily hinge on her family.

If she runs, it could discourage campaigns by other Democrats who are likely to rely on African American voters. Still, it is too early to say which potential contenders would have the advantage with Black voters. At least one possible leading candidate, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, has said he will not run if Ms. Harris does — though he said more recently that he would decide in January on a bid.

On the East Coast, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez — a New York congressional representative and one of the country’s most high-profile progressives — has shied away from some of the steps politicians typically take before a White House run. No book is in the works.

But the progressive lane appears wide open, and left-wing Democrats have been clamoring for Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 37, to take up the mantle of Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is 85 and has all but ruled out running again.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez suggested to The Times in September that she might have a “very unique political window,” and that she might only “get one shot.”

She has also been considering a 2028 run for the seat of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York. It is not clear if Mr. Schumer, 76, who is in a fight for the party leadership post in the Senate, will run for re-election in 2028.

If Ms. Ocasio-Cortez does not run for president, it would probably set off a scramble among progressive Democrats to find another standard-bearer.

Two other Democrats could also play a considerable role in shaping the primary field: Senators Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock of Georgia, who are both seen as potentially formidable but who have not telegraphed their interest in running as clearly as some of their counterparts in the party.

The midterms are over, and time is ticking down for big names to make their decisions.

Second-term presidents have sometimes sought to stay out of their party’s presidential contests.

In 2008, President George W. Bush, then deeply unpopular after an economic downturn and a half-decade of war in the Middle East, did not attend his party’s national convention, saying that he needed to monitor a hurricane bearing down on the Gulf Coast. (He addressed the gathering by video.)

Republican strategists say it is unlikely Mr. Trump will take a similar approach, given his desire for the spotlight and the steps he has already taken to pit Mr. Vance and Mr. Rubio against each other.

If Mr. Trump does seek a central role, that could create a challenge for Republican candidates, especially if the president’s approval rating remains poor. Efforts to seek separation from Mr. Trump’s least popular policies could risk drawing public criticism from the longstanding head of the party.

This potential dynamic already seemed to surface last week at a joint news conference that featured Mr. Trump, Mr. Rubio and Mr. Vance — and that carried whiffs of a tryout between the two potential successors.

Near the end, the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, lavished praise on Mr. Trump. The president, grinning, proposed that perhaps Mr. Miller was a better option than either Mr. Vance or Mr. Rubio.

For Democrats, the midterm primaries looked like the season for fighters.

Democrats picked a pugnacious progressive, Abdul El-Sayed, over a centrist to be their Senate nominee in Michigan. They backed a fiery populist, Graham Platner, as their Senate nominee in Maine (his campaign imploded after a rape allegation that he denied). And they elevated outspoken democratic socialists in several House primaries.

But the Nov. 3 general election offered a different picture. While Mr. El-Sayed and other left-wing brawlers triumphed, it was moderate unifiers who delivered Democrats some of their most unexpected victories. Adam Hamilton, a pastor and a centrist, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Kansas in nearly a century. Roy Cooper, a moderate and low-key former North Carolina governor, won his battleground state’s Senate race by about 20 percentage points.

It is unclear what the mood of Democratic voters will be as 2028 approaches: Will they favor more combative politicians like Mr. Newsom and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez? Or unity-focused figures like Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg?

Republican voters, who have flocked to Mr. Trump’s polarizing leadership style for more than a decade, will also decide whether they want someone in his mold — or if they want to chart a different path.

Both parties agree: More than anything else, the midterms were about the economy and high prices.

But strategists across the political spectrum predict that another issue, artificial intelligence, will be central in 2028, as the unpopular but widely used technology increasingly affects markets, jobs and infrastructure.

A. I. burst onto the midterm stage in September, as researchers issued warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat. The data centers that power the technology and drive up energy prices also became a pressing matter in certain races.

But neither party has coalesced behind a vision on how to approach A. I. Mr. Trump, who favors a light touch, has been at odds with some Republicans. Some potential 2028 presidential candidates in the party, including Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida and Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, are vocal critics of the A. I. industry.

Republicans got a taste of possible fights to come in recent days, when the A. I. giant Nvidia reinstated its scandal-plagued leader, Jensen Huang, at the urging of Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance — prompting fierce pushback from some Republicans, as global stock markets whipsawed.

Democrats are also fractured. Some, like Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, have called for a total pause on the technology’s development. Many other Democrats oppose such drastic action. And some, including possible presidential contenders, have shied away from even articulating policy positions on A. I.

A. I. is a wild card in many ways. Is it a bubble that will cause a stock market crash? Does it pose a severe threat to national security? Will it lead to widespread job losses? Will rogue A. I. agents create disruptions in the next two years that change the political picture?

Democrats, Republicans and the technology’s creators are all unsure. And polls indicate that the public is split on which party is better equipped to handle those questions.

Elder Care Is Unequally Shared. But Not Among Gen Z.

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

New data shows that young adults are increasingly caring for older relatives, and young men are just as likely as young women to take on these roles.

By Claire Cain Miller

Women are the default caregivers for aging relatives, as was recently brought to national attention by a piercing “Saturday Night Live” sketch. But there’s evidence that the gender gap is disappearing in Generation Z.

More young adults — in their teens and 20s — are serving as unpaid family caregivers than in previous generations, and young men are just as likely as young women to take on these roles, a variety of data shows.

“Grandsons and granddaughters are equally likely to be engaged in that type of caregiving,” said Karen Fingerman, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin who studies family and aging. “That could bode well for the future when they are involved in caregiving for their own parents.”

It’s a notable change, because the norm for women to care for aging adults is so entrenched worldwide. In the United States, many of them are in the sandwich generation — caring for children while also caring for an aging parent.

But in a growing number of families, those children are also helping to care for older relatives. It’s happening as baby boomers grow older, parents have children later, and more Americans live in multigenerational households.

Two new studies, along with earlier findings, show that among young adults, the gender split is much closer to equal, reflecting changing attitudes about caregiving and gender roles.

One, published Thursday in the journal Frontiers in Health Services, found that 15 percent of people ages 18 to 24 provided regular care to a family member or friend with a health problem, most of them for a grandparent or parent. Nearly half were men. It was based on a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention survey that included 23,090 young people from 2021 to 2023.

And in a survey by New America and the research institution NORC that was published this month, men and women ages 18 to 29 were equally likely to report ever providing care for an adult friend or family member — nearly a third had done so — while for adults 30 and over, women were more likely to have done so than men.

Jack Boyden, 20, a college junior in Orlando, Fla., helped care for his grandfather, Laurance, starting when he was 16. Laurance, then 91, had developed memory issues, and Mr. Boyden quit his fast food job to be his chauffeur, companion and errand runner.

“I thought it was my duty as a grandson,” Mr. Boyden said. “When your family’s becoming ill, you kind of drop whatever it is you’re doing.”

Growing up, he said, he saw his grandfather regularly but hadn’t developed a close relationship. That changed on their drives.

“It was a great opportunity, being able to take care of him and grow a more personal connection with him,” he said of his grandfather, who died two years ago. “It was good to just have a friend to talk to.”

He said he thinks it aligns with gender norms for men to be caregivers, in the same way that men are expected to be providers for family. And while some older people were surprised he was doing it, he thinks young people would find it normal.

“I do think there’s more men in my generation who would be more apt to take a break to care for their family,” he said.

Overall, young men have more egalitarian attitudes about gender and caregiving. As fathers, they spend more time than previous generations taking care of their children.

The New America survey found that extends to elder care. Of men ages 18 to 29, 77 percent said gender doesn’t play a role in who’s best suited to care for an adult — 11 points higher than the share of young women who said that.

Young adults are more likely to help their aging relatives with housekeeping, meal preparation, errands and transportation, according to a survey released last week by KFF. They are less likely to make medical or financial decisions or help with personal care, like bathing or dressing.

Caregiving can take a toll on young people, researchers said, disrupting their lives just as they are going to school, starting careers and dating, and developing their independence and sense of self.

The new Frontiers study found that compared with young people without caregiving responsibilities, caregivers reported more mental and physical health problems, more drinking and smoking, and less schooling. There is some evidence that those who spend a lot of time caregiving when they’re young complete less education and have lower earnings later.

Time spent caregiving “raises a lot of questions with regards to what trade-offs are people making with regards to their time,” said Katherine Miller, an assistant professor at Johns Hopkins studying public policy and long-term care.

But caregiving is also deeply rewarding, she and other researchers noted. While it’s harder to quantify, there are benefits to young people, like developing self-efficacy, closer relationships with family, and skills like work-family balance and empathy.

Policies to support caregivers — which are already limited in the United States — rarely include young people, researchers said. Broader programs could cushion them from some of the consequences of caregiving.

For example, federal unpaid family leave in the United States could be expanded to cover caring for grandparents, they said, or young people could get academic credit for their caregiving time.

And, researchers said, support for long-term care needs — like paid leave, insurance and subsidized in-home or residential care — could help both aging adults and their family caregivers.

I've been wondering if gender norms about who provides elder care would change with the younger generations, the same way norms around fatherhood have changed. Then, after covering the "S. N. L." sketch about Sister, I heard from a few different researchers that men in their teens and 20s were just as likely as young women to care for aging relatives. I’m curious whether this will continue as they age.

Claire Cain Miller is a Times reporter covering gender, families and education.

I Prosecuted Government Corruption. We’re in Trouble.

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Kate Gilbert

Ms. Gilbert was an acting deputy chief in the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division.

As a federal prosecutor in the Justice Department, I spent over eight years prosecuting corrupt and abusive public officials. I went after police officers and prison officials for rape, fatal beatings and cover-ups. I know how effectively the federal government can root out corruption, even among its own ranks.

Americans are clamoring now for these sorts of prosecutions. Corruption drove more midterm voters to the polls than almost any other issue, including the cost of living, data centers and the war in Iran. Nearly 90 percent of Americans say government corruption is widespread, the highest percentage on record.

Democrats in Congress have promised to use their oversight authority to investigate Trump administration officials. Congressional investigations can uncover critical information, but these efforts probably won’t fully satisfy American voters fed up with corruption in both parties. People are demanding consequences. If congressional efforts reveal criminal misconduct, Congress generally relies on the Justice Department to prosecute it. But federal prosecutors will struggle to prosecute any corrupt official — not only now, but also in 2029, under a new administration.

When I was at the Justice Department, I relied on expert investigators and skilled attorneys to join me in following the facts wherever they led. When we received a credible tip, we spent months or years running down leads, gathering documents, interviewing witnesses and, where the facts merited, filing charges against abusive public officials regardless of partisan politics. Our cases came together thanks to countless support staff members.

But since January 2025, over 21,000 criminal prosecutors, investigators and other staff members have left the Justice Department. The office that led prosecutions of traditional corruption cases went from 36 prosecutors to two last year. The unit that held officials accountable for constitutional violations has also seen its numbers plummet.

The effects of this sudden vacuum are staggering. In the first six months of 2025 alone, the department dropped more than 23,000 federal criminal investigations. This number includes cases involving traditional corruption as well as abuse of authority, which I used to handle. I worry that these abuses could now go unpunished. Justice Department buildings now feel ghostly: empty offices, quiet hallways.

Even if a new president commits to rebuilding the Justice Department and dedicates lots of resources to corruption cases in 2029, the prospects for comprehensive federal enforcement are dim in the short term.

First, there is the question of personnel. Current and former department officials have alleged that partisan politics have infected the hiring process. When similar allegations surfaced in 2006, it took the department two years to investigate them and issue findings.

And the tens of thousands of public servants who recently left are not necessarily coming back. Some entered early retirement. Many have had to move on.

Even if the Justice Department were able to staff up quickly in 2029, corruption investigations are resource-intensive and time-consuming. It can take years to build a case, and attorneys will have to race against the statute of limitations clock, which is typically five years.

The exodus of career workers is not limited to the Justice Department. Over 4,000 tax inspectors and 3,000 I. R. S. agents have left the Treasury Department. More than 20 independent inspectors general who were watchdogs for federal government agencies are now gone. New leaders committed to rooting out corruption have very few tools at their disposal.

But that’s just at the federal level. State law, like federal law, prohibits a wide range of corrupt and abusive behaviors by government officials. Many state and local prosecutors could prosecute corrupt officials, but they don’t have the resources. Many lack investigators who have worked on “paper cases” — investigations that involve spreadsheets, rather than drugs or physical evidence.

This problem is solvable. Congress and state governments can start by allocating the funding needed to conduct investigations and train investigators and prosecutors at the state and local levels. Since most states and counties elect their district attorneys and attorneys general, these prosecutors are more directly accountable to voters than are federal prosecutors. And when they win a case against a corrupt official, the president can’t overturn the conviction with a pardon.

It could take at least another presidential term to build back the Justice Department. By then, the statute of limitations will have passed for the perceived corruption that propelled voters to the polls this month. So especially until we have an agency with the credibility and integrity to attract the best and brightest candidates, we must look locally. The stakes could not be higher. Research shows that people who live in societies they perceive as deeply corrupt eventually resign themselves to corruption. When people believe the system is rigged, they vote less, donate less to political candidates and parties and participate less in political systems. They begin to favor authoritarianism.

Americans haven’t thrown their hands up just yet. But if those now in power fail to punish corruption, this country may well give up on democracy altogether.

Kate Gilbert is a former federal prosecutor and the founder and executive director of Partnership for Public Accountability.

Spending Money in This Economy Means Constantly Doing the Math

The New York Times November 27, 2026

Within strong consumer spending lie the decisions many families are making to stretch their dollars to cover the meals, trips and activities they value most.

Kristen Abt checking the turkey that she prepared for an early Thanksgiving dinner. Credit... Rajah Bose for The New York Times

Supported by

By Sydney Ember

Many Americans are thinking twice about visiting family this holiday season. They are attending fewer concerts and buying less meat.

But they are spending as much as ever.

Though prices continue to climb and consumers are concerned about affording daily life, many are making more trade-offs in their spending rather than cutting back outright.

These tactics help explain why consumer spending has remained healthy this year, economists say, despite rising inflation driven by higher energy prices and the artificial intelligence boom. And it bodes well for the holiday shopping season, which economists and retailers expect to be strong.

Christina Ailor, 38, has altered her budget calculations to offset soaring gas prices brought on by the war in Iran, and account for higher grocery and utility costs. She and her partner, who live in Swarthmore, Pa., decided not to buy their usual season tickets to a local theater. They are doing a big shop at a grocery store in town instead of going to the farmers’ market and a co-op so that they have to make only one car trip.

Her partner usually visits his mother on the other side of the state for Thanksgiving, but this year they decided to spend the holiday at her father’s house nearby to avoid the travel costs. They had planned a potluck so no one had to be responsible for the entire meal.

Even with their financial constraints, she and her partner have adopted something of a carpe diem attitude toward spending, in part because they both have jobs. She works in pharmaceutical market research, and he works at a university research center. They go to concerts, just less often, and they are planning to drive to Washington, D. C., in December to see her sister and celebrate her nephew’s first birthday.

“There’s just a lot more math that we weren’t really doing before,” Ms. Ailor said.

In addition to higher energy prices, which have pushed up the price of gas, food and other goods and services, Americans in recent years have endured elevated interest rates as well as new tariffs that made some goods more expensive. Through it all, consumer spending has remained surprisingly solid, propping up the overall economy. Retail sales, which are not adjusted for inflation, rose 0.2 percent in October from the previous month, according to the most recent data from the Census Bureau.

The spending resilience has been powered by wealthier households that have benefited from an ebullient stock market and rising home prices. But recently, lower- and moderate-income consumers have appeared to be spending more freely as well.

Credit card data from Bank of America shows that spending growth for households with lower incomes outpaced that for richer households in October. Their discretionary spending, on items such as restaurant meals and travel, has also picked up.

A driver has been the labor market, where unemployment has been low and layoffs have been relatively rare. That has kept incomes stable and given many consumers confidence in their ability to spend. Larger tax refunds this year also gave many households an infusion of cash, benefiting lower-income consumers in particular. Even hiring, which had been concentrated in health care, has broadened to sectors including construction and manufacturing.

Household finances have also been relatively healthy, which has supported spending. The credit card delinquency rate has trended down slightly, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s quarterly report on household debt and credit. And the personal saving rate has been lingering around its lowest point in four years, indicating that consumers may be less concerned with maintaining substantial cash reserves.

At the same time, consumers appear to be trading down more, especially on groceries, suggesting they are seeking out values to make up for higher gas prices and other costs.

“If you’re a consumer, you need to be savvy in this environment,” said Michelle Meyer, the chief economist at Mastercard. “And I think that’s what they’re showing us.”

David Tinsley, an economist at the Bank of America Institute, said the fact that consumers were being forced to trade down could be why they were feeling gloomy about the economy and affordability. Frustration over higher prices helped power Democrats to victories up and down the ballot in the midterm elections this month.

“Although people are spending, they’re still being forced to make quite painful trade-offs,” he said. “They are trying to squeeze dollars out of groceries and clothing, et cetera, to go spend on other items — that’s not necessarily something they are overjoyed about doing.”

Megan Sapp-Nelson, 47, an academic librarian from Urbana, Ill., said figuring out her spending had been “kind of Tetris,” in part because she used a lot of her savings this year to buy a house. Rising costs have further strained her budget.

To compensate, she purchased a deep freezer so she could buy more food in bulk. She and her partner, a government employee, have given up weekend trips to cities like St. Louis and Chicago to see live music and go out. They decided they would not buy each other gifts for Christmas this year, nor would they visit family for the holidays because they felt they could not afford train tickets.

She is paying for her 9-year-old daughter to take a gymnastics class but only because she no longer has to pay for tutoring.

“I wouldn’t say overall we’re spending less,” Ms. Sapp-Nelson said.

There are some risks that could knock consumer spending off course. Inflation has been increasing faster than wage growth for months, eroding spending power. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates next month to tamp down stubborn price increases, which could add financial strain for households. Investors could sour on A. I., deflating stock portfolios.

But broadly, economists anticipate that households will maintain their spending into next year. Americans are already getting some relief from lower gas prices, which fell below $4 a gallon earlier this month for the first time since July, according to AAA, the auto club.

A sustained drop in fuel prices could free up an extra dose of spending for consumers like Kristen Abt.

Ms. Abt, 39, drives about 50 miles one way from her home in rural Metaline Falls, Wash., to the hospital where she works as a nurse. She and her husband, a substation wireman at a hydroelectric dam, have cars that run on diesel. Since the beginning of the year, she said, their monthly fuel costs have grown to around $800 from $437.

That has forced them to look for savings in other areas. Whereas Ms. Abt used to go for hikes or to hot springs on her days off, she said, she has been venturing out much less so she doesn’t have to worry about filling up her tank as often. She and her husband have discussed forgoing their weekend trips to see family and friends. For Christmas, she is considering making gifts rather than buying them.

Still, Ms. Abt said she had cut back mostly on leisure expenses. Her plans for Thanksgiving, including driving 113 miles to her parents’ house, did not change. She and her husband still spend liberally on groceries and going out to eat.

Should diesel prices fall by even $2 a gallon, she said, she would be more comfortable spending again on everything else, too.

“I would feel more freedom to spend a little bit more frivolously on my wants,” she said, “versus pulling back and saying, ‘Oh, do I really have it in my budget this month to spend a little extra money on things that aren’t necessary for my life?’”

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.
